projectDetails.name: AstroFire 3D
projectDetails.summary:
AstroFire 3D is an interactive fire safety console, 3D Unity WebGL simulator, and Super Intelligence (SI) copilot built on open NASA space combustion data.

On Earth, hot air rises and gives fire a teardrop shape, but in space flames form quiet blue spheres that behave very differently. Standard ground tests miss these risks, and NASA’s data is scattered across technical databases (PSI and NTRS). To solve this, we built a physics engine grounded on 79 verified BASS-II tests from the ISS (R² = 0.91 for flame-spread prediction). We then added 71 more ISS flight states to train a physics-informed neural network that predicts whether a flame survives, reaching 95.3% cross-validated accuracy and catching 97.7% of sustained fires. We also rank six NASA campaigns (BASS-II, Saffire, SoFIE, SAME, FLEX and SPICE) by relevance to four space habitats.

Users test 7 real NASA materials across the ISS (0g), Moon (0.16g), Mars (0.38g), and Earth (1g), adjusting oxygen and airflow to see burn speed, minimum oxygen limit, CO and CO₂ gases, live 3D flame behavior, and generate an analysis report. As an extra feature, we integrated microgravity heat transfer research from Brazil, our homeland, to size water-mist extinguisher suppression. Every result separates direct NASA data from estimates, supporting safer space missions and fire safety on Earth.

Make the next giant leap safer!
projectDetails.details:
AstroFire 3D is an interactive 3D microgravity combustion simulator, physics-informed AI platform, and fire-safety engineering console built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Flame in Freefall). Its purpose is to transform empirical records from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) into an accessible, real-time decision tool for spacecraft cabins and partial-gravity habitats.

Fire in space behaves nothing like fire on Earth. Without buoyancy-driven convection, hot gases do not rise: flames in quiescent microgravity (0g) form slow, faint blue spherical diffusion balls, yet even a gentle cabin ventilation breeze (4–10 cm/s) or partial gravity (Moon at 0.16g, Mars at 0.38g) can feed fresh oxygen into the reaction zone and cause a flame to spread faster or ignite at lower oxygen concentrations than on Earth. AstroFire 3D bridges this gap by combining a deterministic physics engine, a custom Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), real-time 3D Unity WebGL combustion animations, and an operational fire-extinguisher sizing calculator within a single unified web console.

Project & Repository Access

Live Application (3D Simulator & Console): https://astrofire-3d.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository (Backend, PINN, Frontend, 3D Unity & Contracts): https://github.com/leandro-elias-fontes/AstroFire-3D-hackathon

The Problem

Over decades of orbital research, NASA has conducted high-precision combustion experiments inside spacecraft gloveboxes and Orbital Test Beds—such as BASS-II, Saffire I–VI, SoFIE, FLEX, and SAME. Because every burn in microgravity requires astronaut crew time and launch mass, the resulting datasets are fragmented across heterogeneous tables, technical reports, and PDFs, often with small sample sizes (e.g., 79 verified state transitions in BASS-II).

For engineers, researchers, and students, interpreting how a given material behaves across different gravity regimes (0g ISS, 0.16g Moon, 0.38g Mars, 1.0g Earth), oxygen concentrations, and cabin airflows requires cross-referencing multiple reports and analytical equations. Furthermore, numbers in a spreadsheet alone do not convey the operational danger of a nearly invisible blue 0g flame—nor do they answer the immediate crew-safety question: if a fire starts under these conditions, how much water mist and how much time will it take to extinguish it?

The Gap

Advances in AI and browser-based 3D simulation create new opportunities to explore aerospace fire-safety archives, but generic LLM wrappers or black-box neural networks are not suitable for spacecraft safety:

  1. Hallucination and Offline Risk: Wrapping an external LLM API can fabricate physical numbers, violate conservation laws, or fail when offline during judging or mission operations.
  2. Small-N Overfitting: A conventional black-box neural network trained on 79 experimental rows easily overfits and violates thermodynamics—such as predicting sustained fire below a material's Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI).
  3. Lack of Operational Suppression Sizing & Partial-Gravity Data: NASA's PSI archive contains no solid-material combustion tests conducted in partial gravity (0.16g Moon or 0.38g Mars), and existing tools rarely translate combustion physics into actionable fire-extinguisher requirements (water volume and discharge time) tailored to reduced-gravity boiling physics.

Our Solution

AstroFire 3D solves these challenges with a zero-dependency, sub-5ms deterministic Python backend (FastAPI + Pydantic V2) paired with our own custom Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), a real-time Unity WebGL 3D combustion chamber, and a Suppression Sizing Module that integrates NASA data with Brazilian microgravity thermal research.

Every simulation explicitly declares its scientific boundary:

  • Empirical Match (empirical_bass2): Directly retrieves verified ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox measurements from BASS-II (PSI-25, DOI: 10.60555/4qc4-de67, CC0-1.0) across 7 spacecraft materials (PMMA clear slabs, thin films, clear/black rods, SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric, Nomex III fire barrier, and Japan wax candles). We also audited dataset licenses, strictly excluding PSI-10 due to its lack of an open license.
  • Physics-Bounded Interpolation (interpolated_from_ntrs): When testing custom environmental combinations or partial gravity, the engine computes Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI), flame spread rate (Vf), and toxic gas byproducts (CO ppm and CO2 %) using analytical equations from NASA/TM-20210011385, Saffire I–VI, SoFIE, FLEX, and SAME.

Our Core Differentiators

1. Custom Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) with High Accuracy

Instead of relying on external AI APIs or black-box models, we engineered our own Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) and Physics-Informed Classifier from scratch in pure Python math (backend/app/ml_pipeline.py). We embedded the governing physical laws from NASA/TM-20210011385 directly into the feature space and loss function alongside 24 physics collocation boundary points:

  • Olson Eq. (6.1): U-shaped microgravity Limiting Oxygen Index boundary (XO2(a) = 6e^-0.5a + 0.0167a + LOImin).
  • Bhattacharjee Eq. (2.2)–(2.5): Thermally thin/thick inverse thickness scaling (Vf ∝ τ^-α) and radiative quench velocity (Vg,cr).
  • T'ien Concurrent/Opposed Flow Limits: High-velocity Damköhler blow-off boundaries.

Validated with Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation on the 79 ISS empirical states (running full training in ~650 ms on CPU), our custom network achieved:

  • 94.94% Classification Accuracy, 95.31% Precision, 98.39% Recall, and 96.83% F1-Score in distinguishing sustained flame spread from radiative quench/extinction.
  • R² = 0.9117, RMSE = 0.1747 mm/s, and MAE = 0.0549 mm/s in predicting microgravity flame spread rates (Vf).
2. Real-Time 3D Microgravity Chamber & Original Voxel Animation

To make invisible 0g combustion intuitive, we built an interactive 3D combustion chamber in Unity (WebGL) paired with original 3D voxel models (Earth, ISS, Moon, Mars, RocketShip, and Fire Extinguisher) sculpted by our team in MagicaVoxel. The 3D animation is driven in real time by four physical outputs from our backend (flame_geometry, burn_rate_mm_s, flame_color_hex, and oxygen_factor). In quiescent 0g, the custom particle shader renders a spherical #3B82F6 blue diffusion flame; as airflow or gravity increases, it stretches into an elongated, soot-radiating #F97316 orange plume, and smoothly quenches into dissipating smoke over 600 ms whenever oxygen drops below the material's LOI.

3. Beyond NASA Data: Brazilian Microgravity Research (UFSC/INPE) & Fire Extinguisher Sizing

To answer how much water and time are required to put out a fire in space, we went beyond NASA's datasets and incorporated Brazilian microgravity thermal research conducted by the Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC) and the National Institute for Space Research (INPE) aboard the VSB-30 sounding rocket, combining it with NASA's Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (FWM PFE) qualification data (NTRS-20130011664, 2,720 mL tank) and microgravity boiling reports (NTRS-20030003652).

In 0g, the lack of buoyancy keeps vapor bubbles from detaching quickly from heated surfaces, forming an insulating vapor barrier that drops thermal cooling efficiency to 68% compared to Earth (1g = 100%). Using a √g interpolation model across gravity regimes, our Suppression Sizing Module calculates:

  • Gravity-Bounded Cooling Efficiency (%) (68% in 0g, 80.8% on the Moon, 87.7% on Mars, 100% on Earth).
  • Estimated Flame Power (kW) derived from burn rate, sample geometry, and polymer heat of combustion (ΔHc).
  • Exact Water Mist Volume (mL) and % of the 2,720 mL ISS Extinguisher Tank required to quench the reaction heat (2,450 J/mL adjusted by cooling efficiency).
  • Estimated Discharge Time (seconds) needed to extinguish the fire—including operational alerts that confined electronics racks in 0g can take up to 60 seconds because fine mist cannot curve around obstacles without natural convection.

How It Works

  1. Mission & Habitat Configuration: Users select from mission presets (ISS Microgravity, Lunar Habitat, Martian Base, Earth Lab) or manually adjust gravity (g), oxygen concentration (% O2), cabin airflow (cm/s), and spacecraft material.
  2. Deterministic & PINN Evaluation: Clicking Simulate sends the parameters to our FastAPI backend, which checks for an exact BASS-II empirical match or runs our PINN + physics-bounded interpolation engine, returning the simulation state in under 5 ms.
  3. Interactive 3D Combustion Stage: The Unity WebGL chamber updates immediately, animating the flame's color, geometry, spread rate, and smoke/quench behavior in real time alongside our original MagicaVoxel spacecraft and extinguisher assets.
  4. Suppression Sizing & Telemetry Console: The console displays flame spread rate, LOI margin, CO/CO2 toxicity estimates, and the exact water mist volume (mL) and discharge time (seconds) required to extinguish the fire.
  5. Automated Engineering PDF Reports & BASS-II Explorer: Users can inspect the underlying 79 verified BASS-II experimental records and export a formatted engineering PDF report (@react-pdf/renderer) documenting the scenario, scientific boundaries, and suppression calculations.

Implementation Details

DATA PIPELINES & CUSTOM ML (backend/)

  • Datasets & Cleaning (backend/data/): Ingests and cleans BASS-II (PSI-25) experimental records into structured CSV/JSON baselines (bass2_empirical_verified.csv, bass2_empirical_verified.json) and stores trained model artifacts (pinn_model_weights.json, pinn_validation_metrics.json).
  • Custom PINN Pipeline (backend/app/ml_pipeline.py, backend/train_model.py): Pure-Python implementation of the Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network and Physics-Informed Classifier with Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation, trained and experimented in Google Colab with zero heavy ML runtime dependencies.
  • Physics & Suppression Engine (backend/app/physics_engine.py): Implements Olson, Bhattacharjee, and T'ien analytical bounds, √g cooling efficiency interpolation from UFSC/INPE VSB-30 and NASA NTRS data, and FWM PFE water volume and discharge time calculations.

BACKEND & API CONTRACT (backend/app/, contracts/, api/)

  • API Service (backend/app/main.py, api/index.py): FastAPI + Pydantic V2 service exposing deterministic simulation endpoints, investigation presets (investigations_presets.py), and automated tests (backend/tests/test_api.py).
  • Strict JSON Schema Contract (contracts/simulation_schema.json): Synchronizes backend outputs, frontend telemetry, and 3D simulator payloads.

3D SIMULATION & ASSETS (unity-fire-simulation/)

  • Engine & Shaders: Built in Unity (WebGL) with C# scripts and custom particle/flame shaders driven by backend telemetry.
  • Original Voxel Art: Custom 3D models (Earth, ISS, Moon, Mars, RocketShip, Extinguisher) modeled in MagicaVoxel (unity-fire-simulation/Assets/MagicaVoxelModels/).

FRONTEND (frontend/)

  • Stack: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Ajv (runtime JSON Schema validation against contracts/simulation_schema.json), @react-pdf/renderer (engineering PDF export), and Vitest + Testing Library for unit and route testing.

Impact

AstroFire 3D transforms fragmented microgravity combustion archives into a transparent, verifiable, and operationally useful engineering tool. By pairing a high-accuracy, physics-grounded neural network (94.94% accuracy, R² = 0.9117) with real-time 3D visualization, the platform makes the counterintuitive physics of space fires immediately visible to students, researchers, and mission designers.

Furthermore, by integrating Brazilian microgravity boiling research (UFSC/INPE VSB-30) with NASA's FWM PFE data, AstroFire 3D bridges the gap between theoretical combustion science and practical crew survival—quantifying the exact water mist volume and discharge time needed to suppress fires in 0g, lunar (0.16g), and Martian (0.38g) habitats.

Conclusion & Next Steps

AstroFire 3D demonstrates how deterministic physics, custom Physics-Informed Neural Networks, real-time 3D WebGL simulation, and international microgravity research can work together without relying on hallucination-prone black-box LLMs.

As our next technical milestones, we aim to:

  1. Expand the PINN dataset by integrating raw time-series and image data from SoFIE, Saffire IV–VI, and FLEX to cover thicker materials, depressurized atmospheres, and droplet suppression dynamics.
  2. Extend the 3D simulator from single-sample glovebox geometry to multi-material habitat rack layouts where ventilation wakes and obstacle shadowing affect flame spread and water mist reach.
  3. Collaborate with NASA combustion scientists and PSI maintainers to validate our PINN boundary assumptions and partial-gravity interpolation curves (0.16g and 0.38g) against upcoming lunar and Martian habitat standards.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Firesync
projectDetails.summary:
firesync is a web platform that turns NASA fire data into decisions for fire commanders and crews. It shows where hot spots are burning now, whether that is normal for the place and time of year, and which areas carry the highest fire risk in the next 14 days.

It addresses the challenge by joining two sensor records into one. VIIRS records about six times more detections than MODIS, so we convert MODIS Aqua to the VIIRS scale with factors calibrated in the 13 years both sensors flew. The result is a consistent 24-year series, with estimated months marked and their uncertainty range available. A model trained only on past data estimates the 14-day risk per area: tested on the Amazon (2021-2024), it warned of 51 in 100 significant fire outbreaks, usually 10 days ahead.

It matters because commanders decide with little time. Knowing early where fire is likely can help place crews before it spreads. If early warning helped Amazon crews cut burned area as Cerrado brigades did (12%), that could mean about 290,000 hectares (710,000 acres) and 3.8 million tonnes of CO2 less in a year like 2024 (June to August): a hypothesis to test in a pilot.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

firesync answers three questions for the people who decide where to send fire crews: Where is fire burning now? Is it unusual for this place and time of year? Where is the risk highest in the next 14 days?

  • Fire now. A map of the last 24, 72 or 168 hours of NASA hot spots, as H3 hexagons (about 1,770 km² each) or points, with the intensity class of each detection. An icon marks the areas that are above the usual for the season (Attention and Critical).
  • Is it normal? The last 7 days and the month to date are compared with the median of the same dates (within ±15 days) in earlier VIIRS years. The alert level (Normal, Attention, Critical) follows rule v1, versioned in config/alert_rules.json.
  • Where next. A 14-day risk for every area, in four tiers (very high, high, medium, lower). The “Where to look first” list ranks areas by risk, and high-risk areas enter the list even when there is no fire there now.
  • 24-year calendar. The user draws an area (polygon or rectangle), picks one of the six biome regions, or types a point and radius, and sees a months × years calendar of fire detections from January 2003 on one scale. Estimated months (MODIS era) are hatched and carry an uncertainty range. A month with a satellite outage is shown as missing data, which is different from zero.
  • Ask the data. A chat assistant answers questions such as “is the Pantanal above normal this week?” in the language of the question. It does not write numbers itself. It calls the same API functions as the screen (calendar, recent window, map, risk), and every figure in the answer is checked against what those functions returned, with the sources shown.
  • Downloads. CSV tables, a PNG of the calendar and an audit package (ZIP) with the raw counts by cell, the conversion factors of every scenario, the formula and the filters, so anyone can rebuild the calendar.

How it works

  1. Data. NASA FIRMS active fire detections for Brazil since November 2000: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2 (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), from the yearly country files and the near-real-time API.
    • Standardized before counting. The FIRMS columns of both sensors are brought to one format: satellite name, acquisition date and UTC time, day or night pass (daynight), and the brightness columns, whose names change with the source. Confidence comes on different scales (MODIS 0 to 100, VIIRS low, nominal or high). MODIS is mapped to the same three classes (below 30 low, 30 to 79 nominal, 80 or more high), and the two scales are never compared directly.
      • Only vegetation fires (type 0) with fire power (FRP) above zero are kept.
      • Exact duplicates are removed.
      • Low-confidence detections are kept apart. VIIRS low-confidence night detections are dropped because of the South Atlantic Anomaly.
      • Pixel size (scan, track) is not filtered.
      • Only Aqua is used on the MODIS side, because it crosses at about the same time of day as S-NPP.
      • NOAA-20 is treated as equal to S-NPP.
      • Fire power is left out of the factor on purpose. In the MODIS-only years, the fires MODIS missed have no FRP recorded, and FRP is not comparable between the two sensors.
      • In the 13 overlap years (2012 to 2024), we count Aqua and S-NPP detections per H3 cell and divide the sums. This gives one factor per biome, month and pass for each year: 1,860 factors.
      • Days with a data gap in either satellite are left out.
      • A condition with too few detections borrows from the neighbouring months, then from the whole year.
      • A MODIS-era month is the median of the 13 scenarios, with a 5th to 95th percentile range.
    • It uses 10 variables, all from daily VIIRS detection counts per cell: fire in the last 7, 14 and 30 days, trend, neighbouring cells, the same season in earlier years, week of the year, and position.
    • It was trained only on earlier years and tested year by year.
    • A separate job writes the scores to the database, and the API only reads them.

Benefits

  • A decision aid for fire commanders and crews: which areas to look at first today, and where to prepare resources in the next 14 days.
  • Context, not just a map. Today’s fire is shown against what is normal for the place and the season, with 24 years of NASA data read as one series.
  • Honest numbers. Estimated months are marked and carry an uncertainty range. The alert rule is versioned, and every number can be rebuilt from the audit package.
  • Open and easy to reach: open source, no login, works on desktop and mobile, in English, with colour scales that are readable with colour-vision deficiency.

Intended impact

What we measured (Amazon, 2021 to 2024, with the model trained each year only on earlier years):

  • It warned of 51 in every 100 starts of significant fire (10 or more VIIRS detections in 14 days).
    • Of those, 42 were warned 3 days or more ahead and 33 7 days or more ahead.
    • Among the warned, the median lead time was 10 days.
    • 49 in every 100 still arrive without a warning.
  • When it flags an area (probability of 50% or more), significant fire followed in 78% of cases. It flagged 74% of the areas that had significant fire. In Brazil as a whole, the figures are 76% and 66%.
  • Looking only at the 20% of areas with the highest score each week, a brigade covers 66% of the significant fire. The top 10% of areas cover 42%. A random choice captures only as much as the share of areas chosen.
  • NASA’s burned-area product agrees: the “very high” tier holds 75.5% of the area burned in the next 14 days (see “How we checked it”).

What we estimate as a scenario, not as a result.

  • The inputs:
    • Brigades in conservation units of the Cerrado reduced burned area by about 12% (Oliveira et al., via Aliança da Terra and Embrapa).
    • The Amazon burned about 2.4 million hectares from June to August 2024, an extreme drought year (IPAM).
    • that the Cerrado effect also holds in the Amazon;
    • that warning ahead makes brigades more effective (the study measures having brigades, not having a warning);
    • that an average year would give less.
  • It is a hypothesis to test in a pilot with a fire brigade.

How we checked it

Every check had its pass or fail criterion fixed before the run, and we tried to refute each result before reporting it.

  • The harmonized series, year by year. We left one overlap year out, rebuilt the factors with the other years and compared the estimate with the real VIIRS count of the year left out. In the Amazon the error is about 6% a year, and the uncertainty range holds the real value about 8 times in 10.
    • Result: the two series have the same shape in all six biomes:
      • monthly correlation of 0.94 to 0.99;
      • the same peak month (within one month) in 83% to 100% of the years;
      • 4 or 5 of the 5 worst years in common.
    • The bias we declare: INPE’s series is almost Aqua itself (monthly correlation of 0.998). This comparison checks the shape of the curve and the 2012 sensor switch, not the size of the factor. The year-by-year test above is what checks the factor.
    • INPE is compared only by the shape of the curve, never by absolute value, because it counts on the scale of one satellite.
    • The 2012 switch leaves no artificial jump in the Amazon (−0.6%), and a jump of up to about 7% in the Cerrado, Caatinga and Pantanal. In the Atlantic Forest (−12.7%) and the Pampa (+12.3%) the step is larger, and we say so in the method.
    • Result: our model ranked areas better in every year.
      • 59% to 64% of its top 10% areas had significant fire, against 25% to 31% for INPE’s index.
      • AUC of 0.94 to 0.95, against 0.74 to 0.81.
      • in areas with no fire in the previous 30 days;
      • in each biome;
      • with 3-day and 7-day horizons;
      • with the cell maximum instead of the mean;
      • in each year apart.
    • This does not make INPE’s index a poor danger indicator: it answers a different question. Adding it to our model gave no gain, so it is an external benchmark and not an input.
    • The “very high” tier is 11% of the predictions and holds 75.5% of all the area burned in the following 14 days.
    • 69% of the places that burned had been flagged high or very high.
    • The score separates burned from unburned places with an AUC of 0.898, between 0.880 and 0.904 in each year.
    • This hit rate is a floor: MCD64A1 misses small burns and pixels under cloud or smoke.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data pipeline and models: Python (pandas, PyArrow, GeoPandas, pyogrio, Shapely, h3, psycopg, scikit-learn).
  • Database: PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS 3.4 and the Uber H3 grid.
  • API: Python, FastAPI and Uvicorn, in a hexagonal architecture.
  • Front end: TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet with Leaflet-Geoman, D3 (d3-scale, d3-scale-chromatic), GSAP, three.js for the opening globe, Archivo typeface.
  • Assistant: tool calling over the API’s use cases, through OpenAI-compatible chat completion APIs with a fallback chain of providers.
  • Tests and delivery: pytest, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright user journeys, GitHub Actions, Docker Compose, Cloudflare Workers and Cloudflare Tunnel.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. The site is static, and the API and jobs run on one small virtual server.

The creative aspect

  • Joining two sensors without hiding the doubt. Instead of hiding the 2012 sensor switch, firesync converts MODIS to the VIIRS scale with 13 calibration scenarios. It hatches the estimated months on the calendar and gives each one an uncertainty range. The opening of the site shows the MODIS-to-VIIRS band folding into the calendar.
  • “Is this fire normal?” Today’s fire is compared with the same dates in earlier years, in plain language, with a verdict in one sentence.
  • Early warning for places with no fire yet. The risk list brings areas to the top before the first detection.
  • Everything can be rebuilt. A versioned alert rule and an audit package for every query let a judge or a scientist recompute the numbers.
  • A descent from the planet to the decision. The opening takes the user from the globe, with the Aqua and Suomi NPP satellites in orbit, down to a full-screen map with the tools of a commander.

Factors the team considered

  • Detections are not fires and not burned area. One large fire produces many detections. We count detections, and say so on screen.
    • 52% of the high-detection periods followed a week rated Normal.
    • 49 in every 100 starts of significant fire still arrive without a warning.
    • The risk model uses only VIIRS detection counts, with no weather forecast.
    • NASA POWER weather data and more MODIS history were tested. They did not improve the model under criteria fixed before the runs, so they are not in the product.
    • The Pantanal has few areas and an anomalous 2020, so its results carry a warning.
    • The model covers less outside the fire season (62% in the Amazon).
  • The conversion assumes the sensor ratio of 2003 to 2011 was similar to 2012 to 2024, which cannot be tested. In exceptional years (2020 and 2024 in the Amazon) the estimate errs more.
  • Sensor change. S-NPP is the VIIRS source until October 2026, and NOAA-20 from November 2026. The risk model was tested for the switch with no harm.
  • Independent references. The series and the risk model were compared with INPE and with NASA burned area, with the biases of each comparison declared (see “How we checked it”).
  • People under pressure. Large touch targets, shape and text besides colour, a colour scale readable with colour-vision deficiency, and no login.
  • The virtual assistant stays inside the data. It answers only with figures returned by our own API, and shows its sources.
  • A decision aid, not a decision. The tool ranks where to look. It does not replace field information, wind, or the judgment of the commander.

Next steps

  • Field updates from the fire line. A login area for fire commanders and crews to report the conditions of each fire in real time (active, controlled, out, front advancing). The map would then join what the satellite sees with what the crews see on the ground.
    • We tested the index as an input to the risk model, and it did not help: 13 years hold few El Niño episodes, and the effect differs by region.
    • It would enter as a clearly labelled “what if” scenario, not as part of the measured model.

Machine learning and AI tools

Machine learning inside the product. firesync uses two machine-learning models, both trained only on NASA data.

  • The 14-day risk model (gradient boosting, scikit-learn). It exists because a fixed rule cannot weigh ten fire signals at once across six biomes and every season.
    • Against the best simple rule we found (fire in the last 30 days plus the average of the same season), it gains about 2 points in the top 10% of areas, in 8 of 8 years.
    • Against INPE’s fire-risk index, it gains about 30 points.
    • The gain over the simple rule is small, and we say so. Most of the skill comes from recent fire, and new information (weather forecast, vegetation dryness) is what could raise it.
  • A detection classifier that learns the chance that MODIS saw each VIIRS fire, from fire power, temperature, confidence, month, day or night, biome and pixel size. It does not produce the conversion factor. It shows which fires MODIS misses (mostly the weak ones) and serves as a cross-check of the factor.

AI tools to build it.

  • The idea, the method and every pass or fail criterion are the team’s, and were fixed before the runs.
  • We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Antigravity and Lovable) to write and review code and documents from those decisions, test-first where possible.
  • Every change entered through a pull request with automated tests.
  • The AI-assisted parts are listed file by file in the “Uso de IA” table of the repository README.
  • No image, video or audio in the project or in the demo was generated by AI.
  • The optional virtual assistant in the site calls a language model at run time and gets every figure in its answers from our own API.

projectDetails.name: CORA - Crew Operations Readiness Assistant
projectDetails.summary:
CORA (Crew Operations Readiness Assistant) is an onboard-first health telemetry prototype for space crews. It combines simulated wearable signals, manual measurements, daily check-ins, personal pre-flight baselines, and historical NASA environmental references to provide an explainable next operational action.

The system collects and evaluates local evidence even when communication with Earth is unavailable. It distinguishes normal, deviating, stale, invalid, and missing data; recommends actions such as routine monitoring, rechecking a measurement, or reviewing before a critical task; and safely synchronizes queued evidence with Earth once the link returns.

CORA addresses the challenge by helping astronauts monitor relevant health indicators, assess their own readiness, and act without waiting for ground support. This is important for long-duration missions, where isolation, distance, delayed communication, and environmental hazards make local autonomy essential.
projectDetails.details:
CORA is a health-monitoring platform for astronauts designed to keep working even when communication with Earth is limited or unavailable.

The idea started with a simple question: if an astronaut notices a change in their health during a mission, what can they do while waiting for support from the ground team? To explore this, we created a system that brings together simulated wearable data, daily check-ins, and manual health entries.

Instead of only displaying numbers, CORA compares current readings with each astronaut’s personal pre-flight baseline. This helps identify when something is unusual for that individual and provides a clear operational suggestion: continue the routine, monitor the situation, or review their status before a critical task.

The main feature of the project is that it continues working onboard without an Earth connection. Data is stored locally and, once the link is restored, it is safely synchronized with a ground-team dashboard. This prevents information loss and helps the team understand what happened during the communication gap.

We built CORA using Python and FastAPI for the onboard and Earth services, PostgreSQL for data storage, and React with TypeScript for the interface. We also created a wearable simulator and used Docker to run the full system.

CORA is not intended to diagnose diseases or replace medical professionals. It is a demonstration of how health data, personal context, and resilient communication can help astronauts make more informed decisions during long, isolated missions with delayed contact with Earth.

projectDetails.name: Ares Base
projectDetails.summary: The project consists of an educational game that incorporates trade-offs to engage children in interactive training and organic learning, allowing them to acquire real-world knowledge about resource management and Martian colonies.
projectDetails.details:
Ares Base is an educational 3D game created by AndromedaProject to introduce children to the exciting world of space exploration. In the game, players become astronauts on a five-day mission to Mars, where they must take care of a space base, manage resources, complete daily tasks, and solve unexpected problems.

Every day, players receive instructions from Earth and explore different areas of the base. They must take care of a greenhouse by watering plants and adjusting lighting, visit an observatory to discover real NASA astronomy images, monitor solar panels to keep the base powered, and check the magnetic shield. They may also face unexpected events, such as sandstorms and communication failures, making each day a new challenge. At the end of the mission, players receive a report showing their activities and discoveries.

The main benefit of Ares Base is that it turns learning into an adventure. Instead of simply reading about science, children interact with different systems and learn by doing. They discover why water and energy must be carefully managed, how plants can be grown in space, and why astronauts need to monitor their surroundings. The game also introduces topics such as astronomy, solar radiation, oxygen, and life-support systems.

Our goal is to make science more fun and accessible while encouraging curiosity, creativity, problem-solving, and responsibility. We want players to understand that exploring Mars is not just about traveling to another planet; it is also about working together, taking care of resources, and keeping everyone safe.

Ares Base was developed with the help of artificial intelligence tools. The project started as an application with information and static images created using Lovable. After discussions and new ideas, our team decided to transform it into a more interactive 3D game. We used Lovable, ChatGPT with Codex, and Claude during development, and later ported the project to Unity. We also considered NASA resources, including its APOD API for astronomy images and its Veggie experiments as references for the greenhouse.

What makes Ares Base creative is the way it combines different scientific subjects into one adventure. Players can explore the universe, grow food, manage energy, and protect their base, all while experiencing some of the responsibilities of an astronaut. Real NASA images also help connect the game to actual space exploration.

During development, AndromedaProject considered its young audience and the importance of making the experience easy to understand and enjoyable. We discussed how to introduce scientific concepts gradually, how to make tasks interesting, and how unexpected events could challenge players without making the game frustrating. We also planned visual improvements, including colorful environments, friendly characters, intuitive interfaces, and engaging animations.

Ultimately, Ares Base aims to bring the adventure of space exploration closer to children. By combining science, creativity, and gameplay, we hope to inspire young players to become curious about the universe and discover that even a small astronaut has big responsibilities!

projectDetails.name: Earth Information Jukebox — Angular Lovers
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web experience developed by Angular Lovers to make NASA Earth science more engaging through sight, sound, and exploration.

Inspired by NASA's Earth Information Center, our application transforms real nighttime satellite imagery into music generated in real time. Users can explore an interactive globe, select NASA night-lights images from 2012 or 2023, and listen as visual brightness is translated into musical notes. A synchronized visual indicator and textual descriptions explain how each region contributes to the sound.

Built with Angular, TypeScript, Canvas2D, and the Web Audio API, the project combines scientific visualization with a reproducible sound-generation system. Its purpose is to explore new ways of communicating Earth information, supporting multisensory learning and making complex visual material more approachable.

By turning images into an interactive musical experience, we invite people to discover our changing planet from a different perspective.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth Information Jukebox lets people explore a globe and listen to NASA night-lights imagery. It was designed from the start to be a more accessible way to experience Earth science, including for people with low vision. The application opens on the Earth and then offers a separate image-sonification panel. The user chooses the 2012 or the 2023 annual image and presses Play. A highlighted region and a text reading follow the playback, so it is always clear which part of the image is being heard.

HOW IT WORKS

Playback is a spatial scan through one annual image. The relative brightness of the image controls the notes and the gain of the voice, and the horizontal position in the image controls the stereo panorama, so the pattern of the image can be followed by ear as the sound moves between left and right. No audio starts automatically. The sound panel has Play/Pause, Restart, Mute, Volume, Speed and Spatial position controls, and the whole site can be operated from the keyboard.

BENEFITS

NASA's Earth Information Center presents our changing planet mostly through sight. This project offers the same imagery in three forms, image, audio and text, so a person does not need to see fine visual detail to follow the data. The text reading can be used without sound, the highlighted region gives a single clear point of focus instead of a dense map, and comparing 2012 with 2023 becomes something a person can hear as well as see.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want Earth science to reach people who are left out when data is only visual, especially blind and low-vision users, and to give everyone a more engaging, multi-sensory way to experience how human presence on Earth appears from space.

TOOLS AND DATA

- Angular 18 and TypeScript, with HTML and CSS, on Node.js 22, including server-side rendering

- Automated checks: Angular tests in headless Chrome, Node tests and a production smoke test

- Data: two annual night-lights images derived from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio SVS 5276, the original visualization linked by its Earth Information Center version, SVS 5313. A manifest in the repository records the exact resources, hashes, transformation and credits.

- Globe geography from Natural Earth

- [AUDIO TECHNOLOGY, e.g. the browser's Web Audio API or the library used]

- AI assistance was used and is documented in AI_USAGE.md and in the project metadata.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The project treats the image itself as the score. Instead of placing a soundtrack over a visualization, it reads brightness as melody and loudness and reads geography as stereo space, inside a jukebox where each year is a record to play and compare.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- An accessible site first: the first keyboard link skips straight to the sound panel; globe destinations, direction buttons and arrow keys select a point; plus/minus change zoom and Home resets the view; reduced motion disables the automatic rotation of the globe.

- User control: sound never starts on its own.

- Honesty about the data: the sound represents RGB image brightness, not calibrated radiance, and black pixels may have several meanings. Globe coordinates do not control the audio, because a geographic transform has not been validated. Source, formulas and limitations are shown in the app under "Method, credits and limitations".

- Credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio and its contributors retain the credits listed in the manifest, and no NASA endorsement is implied.

- Remaining work: human listening tests, screen-reader testing and mobile-device acceptance still need confirmation.

projectDetails.name: GeoSafra
projectDetails.summary: GeoSafra is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers compare crop rotation strategies using NASA Earth observations, local field information, and their own priorities. Farmers map a field, describe its soil and crop history, and choose goals such as conserving water, reducing erosion, improving soil health, or diversifying income. GeoSafra combines historical climate and satellite information with transparent agronomic rules to compare the current rotation with alternatives, highlight climate risks, and explore planting windows. An AI-assisted explanation layer translates the analysis into accessible insights, while keeping scores grounded in explicit rules and data. By making complex information easier to understand, GeoSafra helps growers explore more resilient choices for their next season. Results show data gaps and limitations and support discussion with local agronomists.
projectDetails.details:
GeoSafra turns NASA Earth observations into accessible information to help farmers explore crop rotation strategies suited to their fields, practical constraints, and priorities.

HOW IT WORKS

Farmers locate and map their field, enter crop history and local soil information, and identify priorities such as conserving water, reducing erosion, improving organic matter, fixing nitrogen, producing forage, or diversifying income.

The platform combines these inputs with historical climate and satellite information. NASA POWER weather data support the analysis of water balance, reference evapotranspiration, dry spells, temperature extremes, and planting windows. SRTM elevation data inform terrain and erosion indicators, while HLS and MODIS vegetation observations provide additional environmental context.

An agronomic rules engine filters unsuitable crops and compares the current rotation with alternative strategies. Scores consider water availability, soil structure, nitrogen, erosion, organic matter, pest cycles, forage, income, market fit, and climate resilience. Farmer priorities influence the relative importance of these criteria.

AI-GENERATED INSIGHTS

An AI-assisted explanation layer translates analytical results into clear language, helping producers understand the benefits, trade-offs, and risks of each alternative. Numerical scores are calculated from explicit rules and data; AI helps communicate their meaning.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

GeoSafra aims to make complex Earth-observation information useful for everyday agricultural planning. By presenting alternatives and explaining their differences, the platform supports informed discussions about crop diversification, soil protection, water management, and adaptation to climate variability.

The interface is available in Portuguese and English, and users can explore the platform without creating an account.

TECHNOLOGY AND CREATIVITY

GeoSafra was developed using Laravel and PHP for the web application, and Python for data processing and analytical services. The platform combines interactive field mapping, NASA Earth observations, an agronomic rules engine, and an AI-assisted explanation layer.

Its creative contribution is connecting observations from space with local field information and farmer priorities. Instead of presenting isolated environmental indicators, GeoSafra brings them into a practical workflow where growers can compare crop rotations, understand trade-offs, and explore alternatives through clear explanations.

DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS AND LIMITATIONS

We considered climate variability, soil conditions, crop history, equipment availability, market suitability, and competing farmer priorities. We also considered differences in spatial resolution, missing observations, and uncertainty.

Regional climate grids and satellite pixels do not replace local measurements. GeoSafra communicates data gaps and limitations, and its scenarios explore changes to historical conditions rather than predicting future weather. Results support decision-making and should be reviewed alongside farmer experience and local agronomic advice.

AI tools also assisted development, writing, visual assets, and synthesized narration in project materials. Dataset credits and methodological details are documented at:
https://geosafra.softrix.com.br/metodologia

projectDetails.name: ARARA — Radar Water Monitor
projectDetails.summary: ARARA turns NISAR, the NASA–ISRO L-band radar satellite, into a water-change monitor that anyone can read. Floods, droughts and reservoir swings often happen under clouds, exactly when optical satellites are blind; radar measures water day or night, in any weather. For each monitored area, ARARA reads every NISAR pass, separates water from land and compares it with the driest pass of the period, showing where water advanced or retreated, how much, which municipalities were affected and how much it rained before, each number with a confidence level. When the radar cannot separate water from land, ARARA says so instead of showing a number. The pipeline is region-agnostic; we deployed it first in southern Brazil, a region hit by recurring floods, and validated it against official data from Brazil's National Water Agency (ANA): flood area in Porto Alegre tracks the official river gauge (r = 0.95 on 5 of 6 passes, same peak date), and reservoir area at Furnas matches ANA's official level–area curve within 1%. The pass-by-pass water history ARARA builds helps find the areas that flood first and can feed flood-prediction models.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

Water changes — floods, droughts, reservoirs filling and emptying — shape the lives of millions of people, but the worst moments usually happen under heavy clouds and rain, exactly when optical satellites cannot see the ground. River gauges measure the water level at one point, not where the water spread. Civil defence, river-basin committees, reservoir operators and city halls need to know where water advanced or retreated, how far, and who was affected. Radar can see through clouds, but its data is hard to access and interpret.

What ARARA does

ARARA is a water-change monitor built on NISAR, the NASA–ISRO L-band synthetic aperture radar, which measures water day or night, with or without clouds. For each monitored area, ARARA:

• reads each NISAR pass over the area and separates water from land;

• compares every pass with the driest calm pass of the period and maps the extra water (flood) or the water lost, counted only on low terrain;

• flags possible flooded vegetation, adds the rainfall of the previous days (NASA GPM IMERG) and lists the affected municipalities with their population;

• gives every number a confidence level with its reasons (wind, coverage, agreement with Sentinel-2);

• writes a plain-language summary generated from the numbers.

The interactive globe ranks the monitored areas by measured flood area. Each area has a pass-by-pass timeline, a slider that compares any pass with the driest one, the municipalities affected at the peak, a downloadable history (CSV) and an automatic full study. When the radar cannot separate water from land, ARARA says so and publishes no number instead of a wrong one.

Where we applied it

The processing pipeline does not depend on a specific place: an area is a configuration, and the same method measures rivers, floodplains and reservoirs. We deployed it first where it matters most to us: southern Brazil, a region hit by recurring floods, with nine flood-prone areas monitored in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and Paraná, plus reservoir studies in Minas Gerais and on the Brazil–Uruguay river basin.

Validation against official data

• Porto Alegre (Guaíba): NISAR flood area vs. the official ANA river gauge 87450020 at the time of each pass: r = 0.95 on 5 of 6 passes (August–October 2026), with the flood peak on the same date as the river peak (3 October). One pass diverges (low river, more water detected, after 85 mm of rain); it is documented, not hidden.

• Furnas reservoir (Minas Gerais): NISAR water area vs. ANA's official level–area curve at the official daily level: 1.0% mean absolute error on 7 calm dates; sensitivity of 47 km²/m measured vs. 45 km²/m in the official curve.

• Barra Grande and Machadinho reservoirs, experimental: NISAR caught two reservoirs rising 14 m and 9 m in 12 days of winter rain, on the right dates (r = 0.98 and 0.85), but underestimates the area in these narrow canyons. We publish it as experimental, with the reason.

Benefits and intended impact

ARARA turns open NASA radar data into a water history that a city, a basin committee or a reservoir operator can read: where water arrived or receded, when, and which municipalities were exposed. Repeated passes build a record of the places that flood first, which can guide prevention and feed flood-prediction models. Because radar does not depend on clear skies, it fills the gap exactly when optical images fail — in any cloudy, flood-prone region of the world.

Creativity and what we considered

Instead of a pretty map, ARARA treats trust as a feature: every number is measured, has a confidence level and a validation path, and the app prefers "unmeasured" to a wrong number. We separated measurement from cause (radar says where there is extra water, not why), checked every claim against official data (ANA, ONS, IBGE), and kept the results reproducible: data, scripts and regression results are in the repository.

Limitations

• NISAR products are still provisional; our series start in June 2026.

• A flood that lasts the whole period is invisible, because it is part of the reference (the driest pass).

• Smooth land (rice fields, marshes) can look like water to the radar; in five of the nine monitored areas the radar did not separate water from land, and ARARA shows no number there.

• The Porto Alegre gauge series used for validation starts in mid-August 2026.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, h5py, rasterio and related libraries) for the NISAR processing pipeline; Java 21 and Spring Boot with PostgreSQL for the API and the pass-by-pass history; JavaScript with Leaflet and globe.gl for the interactive globe and maps; Docker, Caddy and Traefik for hosting. Data from NASA Earthdata / ASF DAAC (NISAR L2 GCOV), NASA GPM IMERG, ANA, ONS, IBGE, Copernicus Sentinel-2 and GLO-30 HAND.

Use of AI

We used AI tools (Anthropic's Claude) as assistants: to help us understand the NISAR data (product structure, HDF5 layout, radar concepts such as backscatter and decibel conversion), to help build the application (code, tests, documentation and review) and to help edit the demo video. The interpretation of the problem and the idea behind ARARA are our own: tracking water with radar, the choice of floods and reservoirs as first use cases, and validating against official data. AI-assisted outputs were reviewed and tested by the team, and all reported results come from real NISAR data processed by our pipeline.

• Demo video: edited with AI assistance and marked with a visible "AI-assisted edit" watermark; its background music and sound effects were generated with AI-assisted code; the narration is our own voice.

• ARARA logo: created with AI assistance.

challengeDetails.title: Dancing with the SARs
challengeDetails.excerpt: Earth's surface is an endless dance of natural processes and human activities, but these changes are often difficult to visualize, understand, and communicate. From wetland loss to forest wildfires, earthquakes, farming activities, glacier movement, and more, Earth is in a constant waltz of surface changes. Your challenge is to build an interactive application that uses radar remote sensing data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to track and visualize one or more types of surface change at locations around the world.

projectDetails.name: AETHER: Mission Architect
projectDetails.summary: AETHER: Mission Architect is an interactive educational game that allows users to experience the challenges of designing a space mission. Players take on the role of mission architects, making strategic decisions about scientific objectives, mass, power, communications, orbital constraints, reliability, and budget. Each decision affects the mission's performance and overall success. By transforming complex aerospace engineering concepts into an engaging simulation, AETHER makes space exploration more accessible and encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific curiosity. The project aims to inspire students and aspiring engineers to understand the real-world trade-offs involved in planning successful space missions.
projectDetails.details: Sobre o Projeto AETHER: Mission Architect é um simulador interativo de engenharia aeroespacial desenvolvido durante o NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. O jogo coloca os jogadores no lugar de arquitetos de missões espaciais e engenheiros de sistemas, desafiando-os a projetar, equilibrar e lançar missões viáveis por meio de análises sistêmicas reais de trade-offs. Em vez de tratar a exploração espacial como uma tarefa simples de arcade, o simulador transforma restrições autênticas de engenharia — como orçamentos de massa, limites financeiros, delta-v (Δv), geração de energia e capacidade de carga útil — em decisões estratégicas e práticas impulsionadas por dados abertos da NASA. Características-chave Engenharia de Sistemas e Reais Trade-offs: Cada componente selecionado (sistemas de propulsão, tanques de combustível, painéis solares, instrumentos científicos e blindagem térmica) impacta diretamente a massa total, custo e eficiência da missão. Integração de Dados Abertos da NASA: Incorpora parâmetros orbitais reais dos corpos do Sistema Solar, constantes gravitacionais e curvas de desempenho dos veículos lançadores. Modos Single-Player e Multiplayer: Single-Player: Cenários progressivos de missões orbitais e interplanetárias e desafios de engenharia. Multiplayer: Modo colaborativo/competitivo onde os membros da equipe gerenciam subsistemas distintos da espaçonave para alcançar um objetivo de missão compartilhado. Simulação e Validação de Lançamento em Tempo Real: Testes ao vivo dos projetos de missões, exibindo telemetria, consumo de propelente, janelas de lançamento e sucesso ou falha na inserção orbital. Fontes de Dados Abertos da NASA Para garantir precisão científica e valor educacional, AETHER: Mission Architect utiliza conjuntos de dados oficiais da NASA e referências técnicas: NASA Data Source Application in Simulator Horizons & Solar System Dynamics do Laboratório de Propulsão a Jato da NASA (JPL) Elementos orbitais, períodos de revolução, excentricidade e parâmetros gravitacionais dos corpos celestes. Curvas de capacidade de carga e especificações de desempenho do Programa de Serviços de Lançamento da NASA (LSP) em diferentes órbitas alvo (LEO, GTO e trajetórias de escape interplanetário). NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) Modelos conceituais para orçamentos de massa, sistemas de energia elétrica e dimensionamento de propulsão química/elétrica. Abra a pasta do jogo/localizada dentro deste diretório. 2. Se os arquivos forem comprimidos (.zip), extrair todo o conteúdo para uma nova pasta. 3. Execute o executável principal do jogo (por exemplo, AETHER.exe, ou abra index.html no seu navegador web se estiver executando a versão Web). Nota: Se o Windows SmartScreen exibe um aviso porque o executável foi compilado durante o hackathon, clique em "Mais informações" e depois em "Execute mesmo assim". Apresentação, Vídeo de Apresentação e Slides da Equipe: Incluídos dentro dos slides/pasta deste pacote de submissão. challengeDetails.title: Space Mission Design Game
challengeDetails.excerpt: Designing a space mission requires careful consideration of competing demands, including mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communications, and orbital constraints. For students who  rarely get to experiment with an entire mission from concept to operation, these trade-offs often remain abstract. Your challenge is to create an interactive game that allows participants to design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission while making engineering decisions, managing limited resources, and evaluating how each choice shapes the success of their mission.

projectDetails.name: Project Artemis Adventure
projectDetails.summary: Artemis Adventure is a short, decision-making game set at an outpost on the Moon. Players take on the role of a junior commander on their first 5-day mission. Each day, players must choose two actions such as cleaning solar panels, adjusting life-support systems, or preparing shields since it is impossible to do everything. Four resources must be managed: energy, oxygen, food, and health, all of which directly impact the success of the mission. The game also features emergencies, such as solar storms, based on real-world events recorded in NASA’s DONKI database. Through the consequences of their own choices, players learn how resource scarcity, radiation, and careful planning shape life on the Moon. Our solution addresses the challenge by blending science with fun, transforming complex concepts into a hands-on adventure for children aged 7 to 12. Our goal goes beyond simple instruction, we aim to inspire the next generation of scientists and explorers from an early age.
projectDetails.details:
Game Overview

Before starting, players choose a landing site. There are three options inspired by candidate regions for the Artemis missions: the Sunlit Crater Rim, the Shadowed South Pole, and the Central Plains. Each location has its own advantages and risks, as well as determining when lunar night begins and which resources are available at the start of the mission.

1. Morning Briefing

Mission Control presents the tasks for the day, including the cost and potential reward of each activity. It also provides important warnings, such as an approaching lunar night or a solar storm forecast for the following day.

2. Base Modules

The game takes place on a lunar base composed of five modules: Life Support, Greenhouse, Bunker, Power, and Habitat.

3. Completing Tasks

Each task is an interactive minigame. Examples include cleaning and adjusting the orientation of solar panels, calibrating batteries, replacing CO2 filters, cultivating algae, watering plants, preparing meals, removing lunar dust, and reinforcing the base's shielding.

Performance is essential: with up to 20% error, the player receives the full reward. Above that threshold, the reward decreases, while excessive mistakes result in losing the task entirely.

4. Resource Indicators

The game features four main indicators: Energy, Food, Oxygen, and Health.

Every night, the base consumes supplies. If any resource falls below 25, the crew's health begins to deteriorate. If a resource reaches zero, the mission is aborted.

5. Space Weather Events and Emergencies

Emergencies occur randomly throughout the mission.

  • Solar Storm: Modeled using real events from NASA's DONKI database.
  • Meteor Shower: A randomly selected module is targeted, and the player has 20 seconds to activate the emergency lever.
  • Navigation Computer: Provides access to space weather information, the mission log, forecasts, base status, and real DONKI data.

6. Learning Through Gameplay

Each minigame begins with a tutorial card explaining a real-world scientific fact about why astronauts perform that activity, with information sourced from NASA or ESA.

The first time players enter a module, an introductory card explains its purpose and presents a relevant scientific fact and its source.

7. Final Mission Report

At the end of the mission, players receive a summary of their results, a timeline highlighting the most important moments based on their most impactful decisions and the trade-offs involved, and information about the real NASA DONKI event used as the basis for that playthrough.

Benefits

  1. Learning by Doing: Players understand firsthand how energy, air, food, and health depend on one another.
  2. Scientific Content with Reliable Sources: The game includes 20 real scientific facts, each connected to NASA or ESA data and sources. Solar storms also use real data from NASA's DONKI API.
  3. Accessibility: The game runs directly in a computer's web browser.

Impact

Our goal is to bring children aged 7–12, as well as the general public, closer to space missions and the realities of living and working on the Moon.

We teach systems thinking and decision-making by allowing players to experience the consequences of their choices, which directly influence the success of the mission.

The game can also be used as a complementary educational tool in the classroom. Our game goes beyond simple instruction: we aim to inspire the next generation of scientists and explorers from an early age.

Tools and Technologies

Game Development

  • Godot Engine with GDScript.
  • JSON for data storage and management.

Art and Audio

  • Pixel art using a unified palette (APOLLO).
  • Python Pillow for art processing and generation scripts.

NASA Data and Scientific Sources

  • NASA DONKI.
  • NASA API (api.nasa.gov).
  • NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS).

Development and Collaboration

  • Git and GitHub.
  • Balancing bots developed in GDScript.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

Claude Code: Used as a programming assistant to help write and review code.

Local Image Generation Pipeline: Used to generate artwork for the rooms, minigames, cards, and title screen. The generated images were then converted into pixel art using the APOLLO palette and refined manually or through scripts. Some assets, such as the astronaut, were drawn pixel by pixel.

Factors Considered by the Team

Scope for a 48-Hour Development Period

Our initial plan was designed for a seven-day development period, with 10 rooms and 19 minigames. We reduced the scope to five days, five rooms, and 15 minigames, prioritizing a complete and polished game over a larger prototype.

Scientific Accuracy

Every scientific fact was verified against NASA or ESA sources, and solar events are obtained directly from DONKI.

Learning Curve and Accessibility

Tutorials before each minigame and a morning briefing displaying the cost and reward of each task help players understand the mechanics and make informed decisions.

Game Balancing

The game was tested using balancing bots designed to simulate different types of players: smart, average, random, and clumsy players.

projectDetails.name: Astro Health BR — Autonomous Space Health Monitoring
projectDetails.summary:
Astro Health BR has developed a prototype for an intuitive platform designed to monitor the health of astronauts on missions to Mars. During long-duration space travel, the crew faces extreme isolation, communication delays with Earth, and unprecedented physiological stressors—making rapid, independent access to medical support essential.
Our prototype addresses this challenge by centralizing real-time biometric tracking into a clear, adaptable dashboard. In addition to presenting vital signs in an accessible format, the system provides actionable protocols and instructions tailored to each phase of the mission, ensuring that astronauts can identify anomalies early and act with precision, even millions of miles away.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

AstroHealth Monitor is an onboard health decision-support dashboard built to answer one critical question during spaceflight: "What do I do now, and why?" It tracks each crew member day by day and hour by hour across three mission phases: Orbital Station, Transit to Mars, and Mars Base.

At its core, a deterministic rules engine performs personal baseline triage by evaluating daily biomarkers and logs—including blood pressure, resting heart rate, glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood, resistance training, cumulative radiation, and neuro-ocular symptoms—against each astronaut's own baseline and a 7-day rolling window. Based on these comparisons, the system classifies each day as Normal, Warning, or Critical and identifies the affected physiological domain (cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, neuro-ocular, behavioral, musculoskeletal, or radiation). Alongside daily tracking, a simulated smartwatch streams continuous hourly telemetry (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, SpO2, HRV, and stress) that evolves dynamically from hour to hour in response to logged pain, applied countermeasures, and accumulated fatigue.

These data streams feed into a 0–100 cumulative readiness model that starts from the day's baseline condition, depletes as physiological strain accumulates, and recovers exponentially during sleep, rest, and countermeasures. Regardless of the numerical readiness score, explicit safety rules automatically cap or suspend Extravehicular Activity (EVA) whenever critical conditions such as fever, hypoxia, severe pain, or a critical alert are detected. On alert days, a decision-first interface immediately surfaces "Today's Decision," presenting what happened, the recommended action, and the exact measurements triggering the alert side by side with the astronaut's personal baseline, while an alert pop-up mirrors the same guidance so crew members never have to search for next steps.

Crew members also interact with an anatomical body map that highlights affected organs on front and back views with concise clinical explanations, while allowing astronauts to click any of 15 body regions to report discomfort type and intensity directly into the readiness and triage models. When an alert occurs, an AI copilot receives a compact telemetry summary to explain in plain language why the physiological change happens in spaceflight, recommend countermeasures, and indicate whether the case can be managed onboard or requires escalation to flight surgeons on Earth; if connectivity is lost, a local deterministic engine generates the exact same structured guidance offline. Additionally, a predictive trend panel flags gradual multi-day deterioration before it becomes an active alert (treating radiation as a cumulative mission dose), a data-quality panel recommends follow-up exams when telemetry is missing or inconclusive, and daily missions, experience points (XP), and an exercise coach support adherence to the 60-minute daily resistance training protocol.

BENEFITS

AstroHealth Monitor provides true onboard autonomy during deep-space missions where one-way communication delays to Mars can reach approximately 20 minutes, giving crews immediate, explained clinical guidance without waiting for ground support. By evaluating changes against each astronaut's personal baseline rather than generic population averages, it delivers individualized precision while maintaining clarity under high stress through a single unified status, one clear action, and consistent evidence across every screen. Its offline-first design ensures resilience when external AI services or Earth communications are unavailable, while predictive trend tracking and data-quality alerts catch emerging risks and diagnostic gaps before they escalate into medical emergencies.

INTENDED IMPACT

The project aims to shorten the loop between a physiological deviation and an informed, timely action on long-duration space missions, making complex biomedical telemetry actionable for non-physician crew members. Beyond spaceflight, this offline-first, baseline-driven approach translates directly to remote and austere environments on Earth, including Antarctic research stations, maritime vessels, offshore oil platforms, low-connectivity rural telemedicine, and home monitoring of chronic conditions.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

The backend was developed in Python using FastAPI, pandas, and NumPy, supported by a structured Excel (.xlsx) mission dataset. The frontend was built with TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts, and Lucide icons. Clinical synthesis relies on the Groq API (model openai/gpt-oss-120b) configured with a system prompt grounded in NASA Human Research Program (HRP) and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) references, paired with response caching and a 3.5-second timeout before falling back to the local deterministic engine. Python with OpenCV and Pillow was used for image processing to segment and generate the 15 interactive body map regions. No physical hardware was used, as the wearable device and hourly sensor stream are simulated entirely in software.

CREATIVE ASPECT

AstroHealth Monitor combines a phase-adaptive mission-control interface—whose color palette and ambient background shift dynamically between Orbital Station, Transit to Mars, and Mars Base—with a readiness model that behaves like a living physiological system, wearing down under cumulative strain and recovering hour by hour during sleep and countermeasures so astronauts can see the direct impact of their actions. Its adaptive decision-first layout prioritizes clinical guidance and baseline evidence ahead of gamification on alert days while bringing daily missions, exercise goals, and XP forward on routine days, complemented by a dual-purpose anatomical body map that serves simultaneously as an alert display and a low-friction symptom reporting interface.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

The team designed the triage categories, cumulative tracking, and countermeasure protocols around the five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile closed environments. To account for communication latency and signal loss, the system follows an offline-first architecture in which cloud AI enhances plain-language synthesis rather than acting as a single point of failure. Clinical safety and interface consistency were prioritized by governing EVA eligibility with explicit rules, aligning the top status bar, protocol view, and alert pop-ups, and explicitly displaying an "Unknown" health status rather than "No Alert" whenever telemetry is missing. To prevent alarm fatigue, pop-ups appear only when clinical status changes rather than while browsing past mission days. Finally, the team ensured full transparency and accessibility by disclosing that all datasets are simulated and thresholds require medical validation (explicitly stating the app is a prototype rather than a certified medical device), clearly labeling all AI-generated assets in the interface (astronaut portraits, background videos, logo artwork, and LLM-written guidance), spelling out technical acronyms like Extravehicular Activity (EVA) on first use, and designing responsive layouts for desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.

projectDetails.name: Outpost — Space Survival and Exploration Simulator
projectDetails.summary:
**Outpost** is an interactive educational simulator designed to explore the challenges of human survival in space environments. The project places users in the role of an astronaut, allowing them to interact with the systems of a fictional space outpost.

The platform features resource management, an interactive cockpit, piloting missions, and a multilingual interface, combining exploration, decision-making, and educational experiences.

Its main objective is to introduce users to the technological and operational challenges involved in establishing and maintaining human habitats beyond Earth. By transforming space exploration concepts into an interactive experience, Outpost encourages curiosity about science, engineering, technology, and the future of human space exploration.

The project aims to make space-related learning more accessible, engaging, and immersive.
projectDetails.details:
1. What the Project Does and How It Works

Outpost is an interactive space survival and exploration simulator designed to introduce users to the challenges of living and operating in space environments.

Users take on the role of an astronaut and interact with a simulated space outpost through different features, including resource management systems, an interactive cockpit, piloting missions, and multilingual interface options.

The simulator combines interactive elements with educational concepts related to space exploration, encouraging users to make decisions and understand the complexity of operating a space habitat.

2. Benefits and Expected Impact

Outpost aims to make space exploration concepts more accessible and engaging, particularly for students and people interested in science, technology, engineering, and space exploration.

Its educational approach encourages curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and awareness of the challenges associated with human space missions.

The intended impact is to create an accessible learning experience that helps users better understand the responsibilities and difficulties involved in maintaining human presence beyond Earth.

3. Technologies and Development Tools

The project was developed using web technologies:

  • HTML5: Structure and organization of the simulator.
  • CSS3: Visual design, interface styling, and responsive elements.
  • JavaScript: Interactive functionality and simulator mechanics.
  • GitHub: Source code management and project collaboration.
  • GitHub Pages: Public hosting and deployment.

Artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic), were also used to support brainstorming, programming, debugging, problem-solving, and documentation.

4. Creative Aspects

The main creative aspect of Outpost is its combination of an educational experience with interactive space simulation.

Instead of presenting space exploration exclusively through static information, the project allows users to experience selected aspects of astronaut activities through a simulated environment.

The combination of resource management, cockpit interaction, piloting missions, and multilingual accessibility creates an engaging approach to introducing space-related concepts.

5. Design Considerations and Development Decisions

During development, the team considered usability, accessibility, educational value, and technical feasibility.

The interface was designed to provide an understandable experience while maintaining a space exploration aesthetic. The multilingual functionality was included to make the simulator accessible to a broader audience.

The team also considered the importance of creating an experience that could run through a web browser without requiring specialized hardware or software installation.

Outpost represents an educational exploration of the challenges of human spaceflight, combining interactive web development with an interest in the future of space exploration.
