projectDetails.name: Project Forsaken Elite
projectDetails.summary: Solar Atlas is an interactive web platform turning NASA's hardware left on the Moon, Mars, and deep space into visual stories, connecting engineering design to science to inspire STEM students.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work? Solar Atlas functions as an interactive guide and digital museum of the Solar System dedicated to NASA's historical space artifacts—equipment that fulfilled its missions on the lunar and Martian surfaces, or probes that continue traveling through deep space.

Upon accessing the application, users navigate through different destinations (the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space) and historical eras to explore each piece of equipment in detail:

Guided Narrative (Storytelling): Instead of presenting dry technical spec sheets, each artifact (such as the Apollo Lunar Modules, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Surveyor and Viking probes, or the Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight rovers) is given an engaging narrative that explains why it was built, the extreme challenges it faced, how it operated, and its current status.

Bridge Between Engineering and Science: The platform breaks down complex systems—such as heat shields, radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs), seismometers, and spectral cameras—into educational and visual explanations, demonstrating how each piece of hardware enabled fundamental discoveries (such as confirming past water on Mars or revealing the internal structure of the Moon).

Visual Exploration and 3D Models: It integrates visual references and official NASA 3D resources so students can inspect the anatomy of the spacecraft and understand their scale and functionality.

What benefits does it bring and what is the intended impact?

Democratization of Space Science: It removes the barrier of dense technical reports and academic textbooks, delivering rigorous scientific content in clear, exciting, and jargon-free language for school-age youth and casual enthusiasts.

Pedagogical Support for Educators (STEM): It provides science, physics, and technology teachers with a ready-to-use interactive classroom tool, making it easier to teach concepts of aerospace engineering, robotics, and astronomy.

Emotional Connection and Inspiration: By presenting inactive equipment not as "discarded scrap," but as robotic pioneers and archaeological heritage of humanity, the project sparks scientific curiosity and encourages young people to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).

Tools, programming languages, hardware, and software used

Artificial Intelligence and Prototyping: Google AI Studio and Gemini API for structuring the application's architecture, curating educational content, and adapting technical engineering language into educational storytelling tailored for students.

Front-End Development: React, TypeScript, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and Tailwind CSS / CSS3 to build a fast, responsive Single-Page Application (SPA) with an immersive aesthetic inspired by space telemetry interfaces.

Design, Icons, and Typography: Google Fonts and Lucide Icons to ensure high readability, accessible contrast, and an intuitive visual hierarchy.

Infrastructure and Deployment: Cloud hosting via Google AI Studio Apps (https://atlas-solar.ai.studio/), enabling instant browser access across computers, tablets, and smartphones with no installation required.

How is the project creative? The project subverts the common perception of "abandoned equipment" by treating every inactive probe, lander, and rover as a historical character and a living monument to human engineering. Instead of listing dates and specifications in a static table, the Solar Hardware Atlas creates a space exploration experience where students uncover the "invisible legacy" of each machine—showing that a silent rover covered in Martian dust still tells the story of how we learned to navigate another world.

What factors did the team consider?

Age and Language Appropriateness: We calibrated the depth of the text to captivate school-age students and beginners while maintaining 100% fidelity to historical facts and real NASA mission data.

Accessibility and Performance: We designed a lightweight, intuitive, and responsive web interface, ensuring that schools or users with modest internet connections and devices can navigate the experience smoothly without lag.

Balance Between Scope and Depth: We selected iconic missions distributed across the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space to illustrate both the technological evolution since the 1960s and the diverse functions of space hardware (landing, mobility, sample collection, communication, and seismic measurement).

Versão em Português

O que ele faz e como funciona?

O Atlas Solar funciona como um guia interativo e museu digital do Sistema Solar dedicado aos artefatos espaciais históricos da NASA — equipamentos que cumpriram suas missões na superfície lunar e marciana ou sondas que seguem viajando pelo espaço profundo.

Ao acessar a aplicação o usuário navega por diferentes destinos (Lua, Marte e Espaço Profundo) e épocas históricas para explorar cada equipamento em detalhes:

Narrativa Guiada (Storytelling): Em vez de apresentar fichas técnicas áridas, cada artefato (como os módulos lunares Apollo, o Lunar Roving Vehicle, as sondas Surveyor e Viking, ou os rovers Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity e InSight) ganha uma narrativa envolvente que explica por que foi construído, os desafios extremos que enfrentou, como operava e seu estado atual.

Ponte entre Engenharia e Ciência: A plataforma decompõe sistemas complexos — como escudos térmicos, geradores termoelétricos de radioisótopos (RTGs), sismômetros e câmeras espectrais — em explicações didáticas e visuais, demonstrando como cada peça de hardware permitiu descobertas fundamentais (como a confirmação de água no passado de Marte ou a estrutura interna da Lua).

Exploração Visual e Modelos 3D: Integra referências visuais e recursos tridimensionais oficiais da NASA para que estudantes possam inspecionar a anatomia das espaçonaves e compreender sua escala e funcionamento.

Quais benefícios isso traz e qual é o impacto pretendido?

Democratização da Ciência Espacial: Elimina a barreira dos relatórios técnicos e livros acadêmicos densos, entregando conteúdo científico rigoroso em uma linguagem clara, empolgante e livre de jargões para jovens em idade escolar e entusiastas casuais.

Apoio Pedagógico para Educadores (STEM): Oferece a professores de ciências, física e tecnologia uma ferramenta interativa pronta para uso em sala de aula, facilitando o ensino de conceitos de engenharia aeroespacial, robótica e astronomia.

Conexão Emocional e Inspiração: Ao apresentar equipamentos inativos não como "sucata descartada", mas como pioneiros robóticos e patrimônios arqueológicos da humanidade, o projeto desperta curiosidade científica e incentiva jovens a seguirem carreiras nas áreas de ciência, tecnologia, engenharia e matemática.

Ferramentas, linguagens de programação, hardware e software utilizados:

Inteligência Artificial e Prototipação: Google AI Studio e Gemini API para estruturação arquitetural da aplicação, curadoria de conteúdo educativo e adaptação da linguagem técnica de engenharia para storytelling didático voltado ao público estudantil.

Desenvolvimento Front-End: React, TypeScript, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 e Tailwind CSS / CSS3 para construir uma Single-Page Application (SPA) responsiva, rápida e com estética imersiva inspirada em interfaces de telemetria espacial.

Design, Ícones e Tipografia: Google Fonts e Lucide Icons para garantir alta legibilidade, contraste acessível e hierarquia visual intuitiva.

Infraestrutura e Deploy: Hospedagem em nuvem via Google AI Studio Apps (https://atlas-solar.ai.studio/), permitindo acesso instantâneo via navegador em computadores, tablets e smartphones sem necessidade de instalação.

Como o projeto é criativo?

O projeto subverte a percepção comum de "equipamento abandonado" ao tratar cada sonda, lander e rover inativo como um personagem histórico e monumento vivo da engenharia humana. Em vez de listar datas e especificações em uma tabela estática, o Atlas do Hardware Solar cria uma experiência de exploração espacial onde o estudante descobre o "legado invisível" de cada máquina — mostrando que um rover silencioso coberto de poeira marciana ainda conta a história de como aprendemos a navegar em outro mundo.

Quais fatores a equipe considerou?

Adequação de Faixa Etária e Linguagem: Calibramos a profundidade do texto para cativar estudantes em idade escolar e iniciantes, mantendo 100% de fidelidade aos fatos históricos e dados reais das missões da NASA.

Acessibilidade e Desempenho: Projetamos uma interface web leve, intuitiva e responsiva, garantindo que escolas ou usuários com conexões e dispositivos modestos possam navegar pela experiência sem travamentos.

Equilíbrio entre Escopo e Profundidade: Selecionamos missões icônicas distribuídas entre a Lua, Marte e o Espaço Profundo para ilustrar tanto a evolução tecnológica desde os anos 1960 quanto a diversidade de funções do hardware espacial (pouso, locomoção, coleta de amostras, comunicação e medição sísmica).

projectDetails.name: Future Foundation
projectDetails.summary:
Orbit is a health self-monitoring system that turns each astronaut into the first responder for their own health, even when the nearest doctor is 20 light-minutes away.

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, delays and blackouts make real-time medical support impossible, while risks like bone loss, vision changes (SANS), radiation, and isolation develop slowly and silently. Astronauts can take measurements but are not doctors, so they need help interpreting them.

Orbit combines a 2-minute daily check-in, wearable data (heart rate, SpO2, eye attention) and radiation readings. Each value is compared with the astronaut's own baseline and, where they exist, official NASA limits, then shown on a clickable body map with a color, an icon and a word for every state. Every alert explains its rule, its evidence and the recommended action, in supportive language rather than diagnosis.

The prototype runs offline with simulated data and includes a crew view and an offline assistant. Next step: syncing compact reports to flight surgeons when a communication window opens.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES / HOW IT WORKS

Orbit is a health self-monitoring system that helps astronauts assess and act on their own health during long missions, even without contact with Earth.

1. Collect: Orbit Glasses (concept) use EEG and EOG sensors to detect fatigue, stress and inattention, and deliver alerts through bone conduction so the crew can still hear their surroundings. The system also tracks heart rate, radiation dose and blood oxygen, plus a short daily check-in for hydration, fatigue, appetite and blood tests.

2. Understand: a 3D Digital Twin shows each body system color-coded green (nominal), yellow (monitor) or red (act), inspired by the radiation thresholds NASA used on Artemis II. Trend charts show how each indicator changes over time.

3. Act: each alert comes with one clear action. An AI assistant guides triage, and compact reports are sent to flight surgeons when a signal is available.

Other features: gamification, crew view and a radiation tracker.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mars is up to 4 - 22 minutes away by message, with up to two - three weeks of no contact during solar conjunction. Orbit gives astronauts medical autonomy, detecting silent conditions like bone loss, cardiovascular changes and vision problems early. On Earth, it can support remote communities, polar stations, aircrews, elderly people living alone and disaster zones.

CREATIVITY

- A wearable that monitors the brain and eyes while keeping hearing free.

- Every alert is linked to one of NASA's 17 official spaceflight risks.

- A color system based on a real NASA protocol.

- Designed to work offline and sync with Earth when possible.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, with support from Lovable, Claude Code, Traycer, Claude and ChatGPT. The demo uses synthetic mission data, and the Orbit Glasses are a hardware concept.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Communication delays, astronauts not being doctors, underreported symptoms, accessibility (color, icon and text), and safety: Orbit supports decisions but does not diagnose, and flight surgeons stay in the loop.

projectDetails.name: Project Gaiapus
projectDetails.summary:
Gaiapus connects NASA Earth observations with crop decisions and a practical path to local sensing. Built for Field Shift, our multilingual app combines NASA POWER weather, including IMERG rainfall, with crop calendars and soil assumptions in a reproducible FAO-56 water balance. Maps, 3D views and rainfall scenarios make soil-cover and water trade-offs visible.

Our custom hardware design pairs a solar-powered ESP32-S3 controller with a protected capacitive probe for soil moisture and temperature at 15 and 40 cm, plus air temperature, humidity and local rainfall. LoRa links stakes to a shared gateway, avoiding cellular connections at each sensor. A rechargeable LiFePO4 battery, deep sleep, buffered readings and on-demand LEDs support the goal of affordable monitoring in remote fields. We developed PCB and enclosure designs and tested firmware logic in simulation; field calibration and live app integration remain next steps.

In our six-season historical simulation for Sorriso, Brazil, adding brachiaria to soybean-maize provides about 115 extra crop-cover days annually, with nearly unchanged average water reserves before the next soybean planting. These results depend on stated assumptions.

Gaiapus makes sources, limitations and alternatives visible so farmers and agronomists can assess adaptation choices together.
projectDetails.details:
Repository: https://github.com/LuksbellN/Gaiapus-APP


Gaiapus helps farmers and agronomists compare crop choices, soil cover and water availability. Built for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, our web application combines Earth observations, daily simulations and interactive visualizations. Users select a location, check available evidence and compare scenarios through maps, 3D views and technical reports. The interface supports Portuguese, English, Spanish, French and German on desktop and mobile.


Gaiapus planning interface: illustrative soybean development, daily water balance and scenario indicators linked to the selected simulation.

NASA POWER supplies meteorological inputs, GPM IMERG provides rainfall, and Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery supports RGB and NDVI views in demonstration areas. IBGE agricultural statistics, USDA NASS records and INMET station observations support yield research and rainfall evaluation. We preserve source provenance, geographic scale and limitations.

Our deterministic FAO-56 water-balance model combines weather and stage-dependent crop coefficients to track soil-water storage, evapotranspiration, drainage and water deficit. Future-planning scenarios replay historical weather trajectories to explore seasonal variability, rather than predict weather on specific dates. The 3D scenes illustrate modeled crop stages and soil conditions.

In Sorriso, Brazil, we compared three strategies over six historical seasons (2015/2016–2020/2021): soybean-maize-fallow, soybean-maize with brachiaria cover, and soybean followed by long fallow. Under the same weather and a 55 mm available-soil-water assumption, brachiaria added approximately 115 days per year with a crop or cover present, while average reserves before the next soybean planting remained nearly unchanged. Rainfall sensitivity tests use 80%, 100% and 120% of the historical sequence. These are modeled calendar and water outcomes; yield, profit, erosion and carbon benefits were not measured.

Historical Sorriso comparison, averaged over six seasons. Brachiaria adds approximately 115 crop or cover days, while modeled reserves before soybean planting remain similar under the stated assumptions.

Separate machine-learning research compares Ridge regression, gradient boosting and neural networks against historical yield baselines, with temporal and geographic separation during evaluation. In our retrospective test for 2022–2024 across 790 Brazilian municipalities, the selected soybean model reduced mean absolute error from approximately 714 to 582 kg/ha. We also document experiments that did not outperform their baselines. Yield-estimation accuracy does not establish the benefits of changing management.

The application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre and Three.js/React Three Fiber, with a Node.js/Fastify API and Python scientific services. scikit-learn and PyTorch support model research. Docker containers run on Microsoft Azure; Supabase provides authentication and PostgreSQL storage. Technical reports use deterministic templates linked to simulation artifacts, preserving results across languages. Claude and Codex assisted code, tests, documentation and translation under team review.

Our hardware design provides a path toward local sensing: a solar-powered ESP32-S3 stake with soil moisture and temperature sensing at 15 and 40 cm, air temperature, humidity and rainfall. LoRa links stakes to a shared Wi-Fi/MQTT gateway to reduce connectivity requirements. We developed KiCad PCB designs, mechanical CAD and C/C++ firmware with PlatformIO/Arduino. Custom-board manufacturing, calibration, physical validation and secure telemetry integration remain pending; the application's sensor workflow uses explicitly labeled synthetic readings.

CAD render of the Gaiapus controller and rain-gauge assembly. Manufacturing, calibration and live telemetry validation remain pending.

Gaiapus connects regional observations, transparent simulations and local-sensing design in one accessible workflow. We considered missing data, publication delays, uncertainty, privacy, mobile usability, energy, connectivity and cost. Our intended impact is better-informed adaptation decisions with agronomists. Calibrated hardware and supervised field trials are the next steps toward evaluating practical water, yield and financial benefits.

projectDetails.name: Happy Farmers
projectDetails.summary:
Happy Farmers is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers in Minas Gerais, Brazil, choose their next crop rotation under a changing climate. The farmer draws a field on a satellite map, adds what was planted before, sets priorities for water, soil and income, and confirms the soil texture. The tool returns the three best rotations for today's climate next to the current rotation, each with its rank in the climate projected for around 2060.

The engine runs on NASA POWER (climate, 2005–2024), NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (three climate models), MODIS (vegetation), SRTM (terrain) and GLDAS (soil texture). Brazilian sources (INMET, IBGE, Conab, CEPEA, ZARC and Embrapa) add ground measurements, yields, prices and local farming rules. Its rules are transparent: every number on screen can be explained, each rotation lists benefits, risks and information gaps, and close scores are flagged as a technical tie.

Climate conditions keep shifting, and the ranking shifts with them: around 2060, rotations with beans and cotton fall behind, and in a dry year the usual soybean and maize rotation loses 27% of its revenue. Happy Farmers turns open NASA data into a decision farmers can discuss with their agronomist before planting.
projectDetails.details:
Happy Farmers' Project Solution

Happy Farmers is a web-based decision-support tool for crop rotation in the Brazilian Cerrado. A farmer draws a field on a satellite map, sets priorities and receives the three best rotations for today's climate, next to the rotation already in use. Each one shows how it ranks in the climate projected for around 2060. This first version covers fields in Minas Gerais, Brazil.

How Does Our Solution Work

1. Define the field. The farmer draws the boundary on satellite imagery or imports a GeoJSON file. The tool calculates the area and locates the field.

2. Add the crop history (optional). The most recent crops become the current rotation, which stays on screen as the reference for comparison.

3. Plan the next planting. The farmer chooses the month the field becomes available and whether to plan one or two crops.

4. Set priorities and soil. The farmer weights water, soil and income. The tool suggests a soil texture from NASA GLDAS, and the farmer confirms or changes it. Texture sets how much water the soil holds.

5. Get the climate for that exact spot. The tool fetches 20 years of daily NASA POWER data for the field's location and applies the change projected by three NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models (SSP2-4.5). The result represents the climate of around 2060.

6. Simulate every rotation. For 10 crops grown in the region, the engine simulates each sequence of one or two crops day by day in its planting window: crop water demand, soil water balance, temperature and rainfall fit, heat stress during flowering, and sequence rules (crop repetition, shared pests and diseases, nitrogen credit after a green manure).

7. Compare. Up to three rotations with the highest scores appear as cards. Each card shows today's score, the rank around 2060 and the range of that rank across the three climate models, with its benefits, risks and information gaps. A monthly calendar shows planting, harvest, water deficit and days of bare soil. Scores less than two points apart are flagged as a technical tie.

8. Explore. What-if sliders test less rain or more heat. At the demo field, a real dry year (2020/21) is a third scenario. An optional AI chat explains the numbers on screen; it never produces them.

What the Data Shows: Our Demo Field

Our demo field is a 219-hectare farm in the Triângulo Mineiro region of Minas Gerais.

Heat. Days above 35 °C rise from 34 per year today to about 70 per year around 2060. The three climate models agree on warming: +1.3 to +2.3 °C in the average daily maximum.

A technical tie at the top. With the field available in October, soybean followed by sunn hemp (78.2), soybean followed by maize (77.9) and soybean followed by sorghum (76.5) score within two points of each other. The tool flags the tie instead of declaring a winner.

Heat reshuffles the ranking. With the field available in February, common bean followed by soybean falls from 4th to 9th place around 2060: hot days during flowering cut the bean's heat fit from 77 to 45 out of 100. Maize followed by cotton falls from 8th to 17th.

A dry year. In the real dry season of 2020/21 (813 mm of rain, against an average of 1,236 mm), soybean followed by maize loses 27% of its revenue, from R$ 13,003 to R$ 9,438 per hectare, and drops from 2nd to 4th place.

Satellite plus ground. A weather station 40 km away (INMET A520) records nights 1.2 to 2.5 °C colder than the NASA POWER estimate. The tool applies this correction near the station and shows it to the farmer.

Bare soil. Ten years of MODIS vegetation data show signs of bare soil or crop residue in August (50% of years) and September (60% of years).

Benefits

Farmers compare rotations on water, soil and income before planting, with their own priorities, in plain language and with a glossary of scientific terms.

Agronomists get a transparent starting point: every score comes from documented rules, and each rotation lists the risks and the data that need local validation.

Communities gain access to climate projections that rarely reach the field in a usable form.


Our Goal

Our goal is to turn open NASA data into a decision farmers can discuss with their agronomist before planting. The tool supports local knowledge and does not replace it.

We are open about its limits. This version covers Minas Gerais, and the planting calendar comes from one region of the state. Revenue is gross, before production costs. Scores less than two points apart are a tie. The projected change in rainfall is not statistically significant: the three models agree on warming but disagree on rain. Vegetation history, slope, the dry year and the range across climate models are available only for the demo field. Some crop values are provisional and are flagged on screen.

Datasets we considered and left out. SMAP soil moisture (9 to 36 km, top 5 cm) is the natural next check for our modelled soil water. GPM IMERG would improve rainfall extremes. ECOSTRESS and Landsat would feed a map of zones inside the field, which we did not build.

Next steps: check the modelled soil water against SMAP, bring the engine's daily mode to the screen (frost days and extreme rain are already counted), add planting calendars for other regions and include production costs.


Tools and Technologies Used

Coding languages: Python (scoring engine, data pipeline and API), Rust compiled to WebAssembly (interface) and JavaScript (map and browser integration).

Frameworks and libraries: FastAPI, pandas, xarray, Rune and rune-kit, Leaflet and Leaflet-Geoman, Vite.

Infrastructure: Docker, Railway, GitHub Actions running automated tests on every change (178 engine tests).

Scoring engine: rules and arithmetic only, with no machine learning, so every number can be traced back to its source.

AI: an optional chat uses a large language model (Anthropic Claude) only to explain the engine's results.

node.title: Harmonia
node.excerpt: In pursuit of creativity and harmony.

projectDetails.name: Project Harmonia
projectDetails.summary:
Harmonia is a web app that turns NASA satellite images of Earth into music, so people can hear what they cannot see.

It loads true-colour imagery from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS instruments through NASA GIBS, then divides each image into a grid of squares. Each square becomes a chord, following simple rules: brighter areas play higher notes, and mostly white areas such as clouds and ice play the highest; warm colours give major chords and cold colours minor chords; similar colours sound harmonic and mixed colours clash; and a square’s position sets whether the sound comes from the left or the right. People explore with a mouse, the arrow keys or a screen reader, or press Play to hear the whole image. A piano and meters show what is being played, and the page works in English and Portuguese.

The Earth Jukebox challenge asks for Earth science that is multisensory and accessible. 
Our project works as a new way to see images, works mixing music theory and color aspects of the image to create a sound.
We reached the objective of the challenge because we have implemented a way to translate sight into sound and this is important because the work can be used by blind people, and has much potential to expand.

Harmonia's source code, tests and documentation were written with Claude Code directed by our team. Our team defined the concept and the image-to-sound rules, chose the NASA images and tested the result. All images are real NASA satellite imagery
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

Our project gives a way to people interpret images, using sound.

How does it work?

The project works mixing basic music theory with color patterns. Associating details of the image with sound.

What benefits does it have?

This project can help people to see any image with the ears, including NASA vital information data.

The idea can help blind people to have an exciting experience with interpretating images with sound.

What do you hope to achieve?

We hope to achieve a software that helps people to see in a different way.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We used Claude AI to develop the code.

projectDetails.summary: H.E.L.I.O.S. is a bilingual health-monitoring software prototype designed to help astronauts track health trends, review medical information, and support autonomy during long-duration space missions.
projectDetails.details:
H.E.L.I.O.S. is a bilingual health-monitoring software prototype designed to support astronaut autonomy during long-duration space missions. It integrates medical histories, laboratory results, physiological trends, and self-reported symptoms into a unified interface, helping astronauts monitor health changes over time.

Our approach combines software engineering, scientific research, and human-centered design. Inspired by NASA's Human Research Program and technologies such as the NASA Analyzer, HELIOS proposes personalized biomarker monitoring, contextual health information, protocol-based alerts, and offline medical record storage. Developed using React, TypeScript, and Tauri, the interface supports English and Brazilian Portuguese.

projectDetails.name: Project iluminat horizontes
projectDetails.summary:
Planetary Explorers is a collaborative platform that connects robotics, citizen science, and space exploration. We propose a system through which children, students, schools, and universities can build their own robotic exploration vehicles using Arduino or other microcontrollers, equipped with sensors to collect environmental and terrain data, including temperature, atmospheric pressure, humidity, terrain inclination, elevation, and surface characteristics.

The collected data is transmitted to a digital platform, where it is compared with NASA's scientific and geospatial datasets from Mars and the Moon to identify terrestrial environments with similar characteristics.

Our solution aims to expand the identification of terrestrial analog environments for space research and mission simulations while democratizing access to science and technology. Our key innovation is transforming the public into active participants in space exploration through a global collaborative network for data collection, scientific discovery, and hands-on learning.
projectDetails.details:
Planetary Explorers – A Collaborative Platform for Extraterrestrial Terrain Analog Mapping and Space Exploration Simulation

What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project was conceived around a fundamental question: how can we bring society closer to space exploration while contributing to the challenges of planning and preparing future missions to the Moon and Mars?

We propose the development of an open, collaborative technological platform that integrates robotics, citizen science, STEM education, environmental sensing, and planetary exploration.

The concept is to enable children, students, schools, universities, and technology enthusiasts to build their own robotic exploration vehicles using a DIY (Do It Yourself) approach, based on Arduino or other compatible microcontroller platforms.

These vehicles will be equipped with environmental and terrain-monitoring sensors capable of collecting multiple parameters, including temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, wind speed, terrain inclination, elevation, surface morphology, and soil characteristics such as sand, rocks, sandstone, and other geological formations.

Once collected, the measurements will be transmitted to a centralized digital platform, where the information will be processed, organized, and compared against scientific and geospatial datasets made available by NASA concerning the surfaces of Mars and the Moon.

Through geospatial analysis and multi-parameter similarity assessment, the platform will identify terrestrial environments that exhibit comparable physical and morphological characteristics to selected extraterrestrial locations.

The results will be displayed through interactive maps, allowing users to visualize potential terrestrial analog sites and understand their similarities to specific regions of Mars and the Moon.

For example, a student operating a robotic vehicle across a sandy environment in Brazil could discover that the terrain presents morphological characteristics comparable to a particular region of Mars or the lunar surface.

What benefits does the project provide?

The primary benefit is democratizing access to space science, robotics, and scientific research.

Through an accessible and modular architecture, participants can independently build robotic vehicles, develop embedded systems, program microcontrollers, integrate environmental sensors, and contribute to a collaborative scientific data network.

Beyond its educational value, the platform aims to establish a crowdsourced database of terrestrial environments that may serve as analogs for extraterrestrial terrain conditions.

By gathering measurements from geographically diverse locations and contrasting environmental conditions, the project will expand the availability of field data for comparative planetary science and terrestrial analog research.

What is the intended impact?

Our vision is to transform the public from passive observers of space exploration into active contributors to scientific discovery.

Imagine students collecting environmental and terrain data across the sand dunes of São Luís, Brazil, semi-arid regions, the Atacama Desert in Chile, frozen environments in Canada, and other extreme terrestrial landscapes.

Each participant can contribute measurements from their local environment, helping build an international network for terrestrial terrain characterization.

These datasets could support researchers, educational institutions, and space exploration organizations in identifying and evaluating potential terrestrial analog environments for planetary research, technology testing, and mission simulation.

The project also seeks to strengthen global STEM education by making planetary science accessible through hands-on experimentation.

Our goal is to allow children and young people to experience what it means to be scientists, engineers, and planetary explorers, demonstrating that meaningful contributions to space exploration can begin right here on Earth.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project integrates hardware, embedded software, robotics, environmental instrumentation, and geospatial data analysis.

The main technologies include:

- Arduino and other compatible microcontrollers for robotic vehicle control.

- Environmental sensors for temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and wind measurements.

- Inclinometers, altitude sensors, and terrain-monitoring instruments.

- Electric motors, electronic components, and mechanical structures for robotic mobility.

- C programming language for embedded systems development.

- Code::Blocks and Visual Studio Code as software development environments.

- A web-based platform for data transmission, processing, storage, analysis, and visualization.

- NASA scientific datasets, planetary maps, and geospatial resources for comparative terrain analysis.

The system architecture is designed to support different microcontroller platforms, allowing flexibility, modularity, scalability, and broader community participation.

What makes the project creative and innovative?

The most innovative aspect is the integration of DIY robotics, citizen science, and planetary terrain analog research into a single collaborative ecosystem.

Traditionally, scientific information about Mars and the Moon is obtained through specialized space missions, orbital instruments, robotic landers, and scientific exploration systems.

Our proposal introduces a complementary approach: a distributed terrestrial exploration network in which ordinary people can build their own robotic vehicles, collect environmental measurements, and contribute to a shared database of terrestrial analog environments.

We are not simply teaching people how to build robots. We are creating an opportunity for participants to investigate how terrestrial environments compare with the landscapes of other planetary bodies.

The project combines open-source hardware, accessible programming, environmental data acquisition, collaborative scientific participation, and planetary geospatial analysis.

It transforms the concept of learning through robotics into an active contribution to the broader field of space exploration.

What factors did the team consider?

Throughout the development process, our team considered several fundamental aspects:

- Financial accessibility and ease of replication of robotic vehicles.

- Compatibility with different microcontrollers, sensors, and hardware architectures.

- Measurement reliability, calibration, and data standardization.

- Geographic and environmental diversity of participating locations.

- Safety and ease of use for children, students, and educational institutions.

- Integration with NASA scientific and geospatial datasets.

- Platform scalability and international participation.

- Potential applications in scientific research, comparative terrain analysis, and planetary mission simulations.

Our vision for the future

We envision a global platform where thousands of people, across different countries and environments, can build their own planetary exploration vehicles and contribute to an international network for terrestrial analog characterization.

Every robotic vehicle becomes a learning instrument. Every student becomes a potential contributor to scientific discovery. Every dataset becomes an opportunity to better understand the environments beyond our planet.

Our mission is to transform human curiosity into technology, education into science, and terrestrial exploration into a bridge toward the exploration of space.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Kultive IoT: NASA Remote Sensing Soil Telemetry Data Fusion
projectDetails.summary:
Kultive IoT
Kultive IoT is a hybrid agricultural monitoring system that bridges macro-level space technology with micro-level ground telemetry.

What We Developed
We built low-cost field stations using ESP32 microcontrollers to measure localized soil moisture and stream real-time telemetry via MQTT. On the macro layer, our system automatically ingests root-zone soil moisture (0–100 cm) from the NASA SMAP L4 satellite (NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/008) and precipitation data from NASA GPM IMERG via Google Earth Engine. A FastAPI/Python backend calibrates orbital satellite estimates against physical ground readings using linear regression to eliminate spatial bias[1], feeding a Flutter mobile application featuring interactive maps, dynamic marker color changes, and automated drought push notifications[1].

How It Addresses the Challenge
It overcomes the fundamental trade-off between coarse-resolution regional satellite maps (~9 km) and isolated ground-sensor point readings by unifying spaceborne climate context with field-level precision.

Why It Is Important
It transforms complex NASA Earth observation data into direct, real-time irrigation decisions in the palm of the farmer's hand—optimizing water consumption, preventing crop failure, and fostering agricultural sustainability
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Kultive IoT is a hybrid agricultural intelligence and precision irrigation solution that performs data fusion across two complementary layers:

  • Orbital Layer (Macro): Automatically retrieves root-zone soil moisture (0 to 100 cm) from the NASA SMAP Level-4 satellite (NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/008) and accumulated precipitation from NASA GPM IMERG via Google Earth Engine.
  • Ground Layer (Micro): Deploys low-cost field stations based on ESP32 microcontrollers with capacitive moisture sensors installed at root depth, transmitting real-time telemetry via MQTT.
  • Data Fusion & Linear Regression Calibration: Because satellite observations cover a broad spatial resolution (~9 km to 11 km) while physical sensors measure specific points in the field, a FastAPI/Python backend cross-references historical timelines and applies linear regression (Linear Scaling). The algorithm calculates slope (\(m\)) and additive offset (\(c\)) to eliminate spatial bias and calibrate satellite estimates according to local soil physics.
  • Interface & Alerts: The calibrated data is delivered to a Flutter mobile application, displaying crop fields on interactive maps with dynamic color-coded markers and triggering local push notifications if soil moisture drops below critical levels (<20%).

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Resolves the Scale Discrepancy (Macro + Micro): Overcomes both the coarse detail of standalone satellite imagery (~9 km) and the lack of regional climatological context in standalone ground sensors.
  • High In-Soil Durability: Uses capacitive sensors to eliminate the electrolytic corrosion typical of resistive sensors, significantly extending field hardware lifespan.
  • Real-Time Critical Alerts: Instant visual and audio notifications alert farmers the moment a field enters critical drought stress (<20%).
  • Intuitive Cartographic Interface: Automatic color transitions for map markers (green/blue for adequate moisture, red for drought warning).
  • Ultra-Low Cost: Enables building each field node for an estimated hardware cost between R$ 80.00 and R$ 140.00 (~$15–$25 USD), taking advantage of completely free NASA Earth observation APIs.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Optimized Water Resource Management: Precise scheduling of irrigation pump activation, avoiding water waste when deeper root zones still retain sufficient moisture.
  • Risk Mitigation & Food Security: Protects sensitive crops (such as coffee plantations in Triângulo Mineiro, Brazil) against severe yield losses caused by flash droughts.
  • Democratizing Space Technology: Translates complex NASA Earth observation data into simple, actionable farm management decisions in the palm of the farmer's hand.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Spatial Data & Cloud: NASA SMAP L4 (NASA/SMAP/SPL4SMGP/008), NASA GPM IMERG, and Google Earth Engine API.
  • Hardware & IoT: ESP32 DevKit V1 microcontroller (Dual-Core, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth), Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor V1.2, 5V 1-Channel Relay Module (optoisolated), and 5V Submersible Mini Water Pump.
  • Protocols & Connectivity: MQTT Protocol (PubSubClient in C++ and mqtt_client in Dart) with Mosquitto/HiveMQ broker.
  • Backend & Data Science: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, and SQLite.
  • Frontend Mobile & Web: Flutter, flutter_map (Leaflet.js / ESRI World Imagery), flutter_local_notifications, and a responsive HTML5/CSS3/JavaScript web mockup.
  • Hardware Simulation: Wokwi simulator for virtual circuit testing of the ESP32 and sensors.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Calibrated Spaceborne-Ground Fusion: Mathematical creativity in using local field readings as point "ground truth" to correct the radiometric bias of satellite imagery through linear scaling.
  • Dynamic Map Markers: Real-time visual UI transitions on smartphone maps, dynamically altering pin color and pulse animations based on incoming MQTT payload states.
  • Hybrid Simulation & Prototyping: A fully functional prototype pipeline integrating the Wokwi hardware simulator connected to live MQTT brokers and mobile application mockups during development.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Depth & Scale Differences: The team accounted for the distinction between surface moisture (0–5 cm) and root-zone moisture (0–100 cm), choosing SMAP's Level-4 product to align with root-depth ground sensors.
  • Farmer Financial Feasibility: Focused on affordable, readily available hardware components in local markets paired with zero-cost cloud infrastructure.
  • Field Operational Robustness: Selected corrosion-resistant capacitive sensors and weatherproof IP65 enclosures powered by rechargeable battery/solar setups to withstand farm environments.
  • User Experience (UX): Simple map interface supporting quick status visualization and direct push alerts without requiring complex user setup.

projectDetails.name: MARS ADVENTURES: EDUCATIONAL SIMULATOR FOR SCIENTIFIC PRACTICES AND SPACE SURVIVAL
projectDetails.summary: Considering the growing number of virtual game users over the past decade, this project proposes the development of a game designed for children's aerospace education and training. The project was developed within the context of the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”. The player's objective is to complete missions involving survival, data collection, scientific research, data management, spacecraft and aircraft systems, and geological exploration. Throughout the narrative, scientific and technological topics are introduced, enabling players to learn different techniques and concepts while developing a basic understanding of aerospace engineering and natural sciences. Furthermore, in each mission, children perform activities to keep the space station operational, such as generating electricity using solar panels, monitoring crew health, investigating soil composition, treating water, and experimenting with different cultivation methods. The game was developed using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, as well as software development languages and technologies. Its design was inspired by the visual style of the game Stardew Valley, recreating regions of the planet Mars, specifically the Arcadia Planitia region. Interaction with the game encourages scientific, critical, and technological thinking, inspiring new generations of astronauts and scientists.
projectDetails.details:
NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE BRAZIL 2026

MARS ADVENTURES: EDUCATIONAL SIMULATOR FOR SCIENTIFIC PRACTICES AND SPACE SURVIVAL

Project: Mars Adventure

Institution: University Application School of the Federal University of Uberlândia, Brazil

Group: Technological Innovation, Research, and Studies Group (GEPIT)

Team: Space Explorers 

PROJECT DOCUMENTATION

Link to access the Drive Documentation: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1FAHbf50d-wRZ_GHg_zdKL6V4BJzoMCMS?usp=sharing

MARS ADVENTURES: EDUCATIONAL SIMULATOR FOR SCIENTIFIC PRACTICES AND SPACE SURVIVAL

This project aims to develop Mars Adventure, an educational digital game that combines adventure, survival and science, challenging players to remain on Mars by completing missions inspired by astronauts' activities and the obstacles involved in space exploration. Throughout the experience, activities will be developed related to the installation of solar panels, monitoring the astronaut's health, geological investigation, water identification and treatment, growing food in greenhouses, and protection against Martian environmental phenomena.

As a learning aid, the game features Capi, a capybara who acts as a tutor and virtual assistant, guiding the player through missions, explaining scientific concepts, and helping interpret the information presented. The choice of the capybara is related to its popularity and recognition as a symbol of cultural identification among young Brazilians, as well as contributing to making the experience more welcoming and accessible. In addition, the game will include a logbook system for recording events, observations and results of experiments conducted during the expedition.

The main benefit of the proposal is to bring scientific knowledge closer to the students' reality through a playful and interactive experience. In this sense, it seeks to stimulate curiosity, logical reasoning, problem-solving, and scientific thinking, as well as broaden understanding of the importance of space research.

Regarding technological development, the languages ​​JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, and CSS were used, in addition to tools such as Git and GitHub, intended for source code management and versioning, and artificial intelligence platforms such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, employed as resources to support programming and content creation. Antigravity and Cursor were also used, which assisted in the development of functionalities and the structuring of the game. The integration of these resources enabled the construction of the interfaces, interactive systems, and mechanics necessary for the proposed experience.

The originality of Mars Adventure lies in its integration of space survival, scientific investigation, and challenge-based learning. During development, aspects such as the scientific methodology for data collection in missions, age-appropriate language, information accessibility, challenge progression, and gameplay were also considered, aiming to transform complex scientific concepts into understandable and meaningful activities.

In light of the above, it can be concluded that Mars Adventure presents a proposal for integrating two axes, entertainment and education, using space exploration as a means for constructing scientific knowledge. Its application may contribute to sparking students' interest in science and technology, while simultaneously stimulating skills related to investigation, autonomy, and problem-solving. In this way, the project highlights the potential of digital games as tools to support learning and scientific dissemination.

projectDetails.name: Project L.O.G.
projectDetails.summary:
L.O.G. – Legacy of Giants is a cooperative, hybrid game for two players about the objects NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Alex flies a ship on a computer screen and sees a picture of the target object, but not its name. Neil holds the cards, printed on 3 A4 sheets or opened as a virtual deck, with real mission data but no picture. The two players talk, compare clues and remove cards until one is left. Then Alex types the position from the card, the ship travels there, and the team adds the object to the catalog. The 25 cards go from the Apollo 11 descent stage to the Ingenuity helicopter and Pioneer 10.

Most students have never heard of these objects, but they are part of the history of exploration. L.O.G. turns real mission data into a conversation, so students learn by reasoning together. It needs only a computer and 3 sheets of paper, and every source is listed in the references.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

L.O.G. – Legacy of Giants is a cooperative game for two players about the objects NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It is a hybrid game: one part is on a screen and one part is on paper. Each player has only half of the information, so neither player can win alone.

How it works

1. Alex flies the ship, which runs in a web browser on a computer. Alex sees a picture of the target object, but not its name.

2. Neil holds the cards: 3 printed A4 sheets, or the virtual deck, which also opens on a phone. Each card shows real mission data: category, place, mission, size, weight, position, launch year, the year the object was lost and its power source. Each card also has a short fact, told by the object itself. The cards have no pictures.

3. Alex can ask the ship's terminal for clues about size, weight, launch year, year lost, power or mission. Each clue costs experience points (XP), so the team tries to use as few clues as possible.

4. The two players talk. Alex describes the picture and reads the clues. Neil removes the cards that do not fit, until one card is left.

5. That card gives the object's position: latitude and longitude on the Moon or on Mars, or a distance in astronomical units (AU) for objects in space. Alex types it into the navigator. The ship travels there, and the team adds the object to the catalog. Three wrong positions end the mission.

The story

The game has five missions. Between missions, the L.O.G. Operations Center sends messages and reports to the players. Little by little, the reports suggest that Alex is not what Alex believes, and the players start to ask who Alex and Neil really are. When the ship has a sync error, Neil finds the password on the protocol card. Each password comes from a real moment in space history, such as the 1202 alarm during the Apollo 11 landing and "SCE to AUX" during the Apollo 12 launch.

The data

The deck has 25 object cards: 10 on the Moon, 10 on Mars and 5 in space. They are in five categories: rovers and vehicles, landers, probes and telescopes, spacecraft parts and debris, and objects. The deck covers every group of equipment listed in the challenge except the Lunar Roving Vehicles: Apollo lunar modules, ALSEP, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, and Kepler. It also has smaller objects, such as the Apollo 11 plaque and the Apollo 15 memorial.

The cards use real mission data, with every source listed in the references. Most values come from NASA sources: the NSSDCA catalog, NASA mission pages, press kits and technical reports. We calculated the distances of the objects in space for 14 November 2026 with NASA JPL Horizons. When NASA does not publish a value, we say so: the size of the Apollo 15 memorial comes from a news article (Slate, 2013), the size of the EASEP is our own estimate from its stowed volume (NASA RP-1036), and two weights are marked "N/A". We checked the values against their sources and corrected our first draft, for example InSight's landing longitude, Viking 2's latitude and Sojourner's power source. Every object picture in the game comes from the NASA Image and Video Library: 19 are real photos of the objects, and 6 are NASA illustrations, a NASA painting or a model. The clues in the terminal are calculated from the same data that is printed on the cards.

Why it matters

Most students have never heard of these objects, but they are part of the history of exploration. The challenge itself notes that school-age space fans usually hear only about active missions. L.O.G. gives students a reason to read real mission data: they need it to win. The game is made for students aged 13 and up, in classrooms, science clubs or at home. A pair of players needs one computer with a web browser and 3 printed A4 sheets, or one computer and one phone. Nothing needs to be installed, and the game is free to play online. The game is in English and Portuguese, so it can also reach students who are still learning English.

What is new

L.O.G. splits the information between a screen and paper. One player has the picture and the other has the data, so the students must describe, ask, compare and decide together. They practice a real science skill: comparing what they observe with what is recorded. The game works like a cooperative "Guess Who?", but every clue is a real fact about a real object. The objects also tell their own stories, because the short fact on each card is written in the first person.

How we built it

- The game: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no game engine, published on itch.io. We used Vite as a local development server.

- The cards: vector graphics (SVG) built by Python scripts from the card data, and exported as PNG files and as a print-ready PDF. The printed set has 27 cards on 3 A4 sheets, double-sided: 25 object cards, 1 protocol card and 1 rules card.

- The languages: one switch on the start screen changes the start screen, the ship and the virtual deck between English and Portuguese.

- Testing: an automated browser test (Playwright) played the first mission from start to end in English, and checked 31 screens for leftover Portuguese text.

- The demo video was recorded from the real game. Its voices are AI-generated (ElevenLabs).

Accessibility, cost and energy

- Cost: one printed set is 3 A4 sheets. The online game is free.

- Devices: the ship needs a computer; on a phone it shows "Not available on phones". The virtual deck works on phones, and the printed cards need no device at all.

- Energy: with printed cards, a pair of players needs only one screen.

- Reuse: one printed set can be shared and used again by many classes.

- Language: English and Portuguese.

What we want to achieve next

- Test L.O.G. with students in schools in Uberlândia and measure what they remember after playing.

- Give missions 2 to 5 their own fixed sets of objects. Today, these missions draw their objects at random from the deck.

- Add the Lunar Roving Vehicles and more objects from NASA's catalogs.

- Publish a short guide for teachers together with the print-and-play cards.

Use of AI

We used AI tools to speed up the work. The voices in the demo video were generated with AI (ElevenLabs). An AI assistant (Claude) helped us write, review and translate texts and parts of the code. Early design drafts of the card frame and of the card back were made with an AI image generator. The final cards do not use those images: the frame was redrawn as vector graphics by code, and the card back uses a real NASA photo (AS12-47-6918). The idea, the game rules and the story are our own. No AI-generated content uses or changes NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.

projectDetails.name: Mars Academy
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Academy is an educational and interactive game aimed at children, in which the player takes on the role of an astronaut and must survive for ten days on Mars after Earth collapses.
The game addresses the challenge of survival on the Red Planet by placing the child at the center of decision-making. During the mission, they must manage six vital indicators (oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation, and health) while exploring the environment, completing nighttime tasks to collect items, and facing time-limited emergencies. All of this is integrated with educational explanations and real space phenomena, using official NASA sources and solar activity data from the NASA DONKI API.
This project is important because it teaches children to think critically, manage scarce resources, and understand the consequences of their own choices. In addition to sparking interest in science and space exploration in a fun way, the story reinforces an essential message about the importance of caring for and preserving planet Earth by understanding the difficulties we would face on another planet.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Academy is an educational game of survival, decision-making, and minigames aimed at children aged 7 to 12, also designed for use by teachers in the classroom. The application runs directly in the browser on computers, tablets, and smartphones, with each playthrough lasting an estimated 10 to 20 minutes.

Play the game online here: https://mars-academy.lovable.app/
Check out the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Maryendlu/Nasa-Space-Apps-Lovelace

The narrative takes place in the year 2045, in a scenario where Earth faces crises of environmental degradation, climate change, and resource scarcity. To address this reality, NASA creates Project New Horizon and sends four astronauts to Mars on a ten-day expedition. Shortly after landing, communication with Earth begins to fail, meaning the support team can only arrive on the tenth day. The player takes on the role of Maya — a specialist in astronomy and natural sciences — or Milo — focused on technology, robotics, and exploration — young astronauts-in-training participating in the mission through a NASA simulation. Throughout the journey, the team is accompanied by three specialists: Andreas, an aerospace engineer responsible for energy, equipment, and life support; Laika, a biologist and astrobiologist in charge of water, soil, climate, and cultivation; and Lina, a space physician focused on health, nutrition, and radiation.

The gameplay is divided into daytime and nighttime periods. During the day, one of the specialists presents a real Martian problem, such as dust storms, water scarcity, oxygen failures, excess carbon dioxide, among others. The player has three action alternatives, none of which are perfect; protecting a specific resource always comes at the cost of another, requiring choices based on logic and consequences that are followed by scientific explanations. Survival is monitored by six indicators that start at 70: oxygen, water, food, energy, radiation, and health. Of these, radiation never decreases, so decisions aim solely to avoid adding risk levels. At night, the player explores the base and can complete up to three of nine optional minigames, such as reconnecting circuits, restarting the oxygen generator, and cleaning solar panels. Each minigame shares real NASA trivia, and any failures result only in the loss of the reward. Additionally, on random nights, surprise emergencies occur — such as pressure loss, battery fires, and water contamination — triggering an alarm with a 30-to-45-second timer; if time runs out, the mission is immediately terminated. A playthrough can end in three distinct outcomes: mission completed successfully, completed with difficulties, or terminated if oxygen, water, or health reaches zero or radiation reaches one hundred, displaying at the end a logbook with all choices for joint reflection.

The project accurately addresses the challenge of creating a mission trainer for young astronauts by proposing real trade-offs in every decision, integrating with real space weather through queries to the NASA DONKI API, maintaining full data transparency via a space weather dashboard, simulating the real signal delay between Mars and Earth through the Deep Space Network, ensuring high replayability, and providing pedagogical guidelines for teachers. The game's impact encompasses social awareness regarding the urgency of caring for our planet — reinforced by the final message "Teach the children. Shape the future. Save the Earth" —, the stimulation of critical thinking, prioritization, and resource management in education, and bringing children closer to real science and space agency technologies, such as MOXIE, Perseverance, and life support systems.

Regarding the technological resources and tools used in development, TypeScript was the main programming language utilized, while HTML and CSS structured the visuals and screen layouts. The storage of the storyline, choices, translations, and scientific sources was handled in JSON files. The screens and interactivity were built with React, using TanStack Start and Router for navigation, Vite for project execution and bundling, and Tailwind CSS for design and animations. Automated tests for game rules, emergencies, inventory, and languages were executed with Vitest, and code editing was handled in VS Code. Real-world data was obtained through the NASA DONKI API and other sources cited in the credits, while the soundtrack was sourced from Pixabay.com. We also used Artificial Intelligence tools, such as Lovable and Claude, to support technical implementation, assisting in generating and organizing code, building the interface, and creating images and videos. The project requires no special hardware, running smoothly in browsers on computers, tablets, and smartphones.

All decisions regarding the concept, script, in-game choices, aesthetics/design, player experience, objectives, mechanics, and solution validation were led entirely by our team, which also reviewed and adapted all content generated by AI tools to accelerate development without replacing the creative participation of the team members. Throughout the process, we primarily considered the target age group, striving to create an accessible, intuitive, and fun experience for children. We also prioritized the scientific accuracy of the information (based on NASA sources), the balance between difficulty and learning, continuous engagement throughout the entire game, and building an attractive visual interface and compelling narrative.

projectDetails.name: Mars View
projectDetails.summary:
Mars View: Hyperlocalized Navigation & Situational Awareness on Mars

What We Built
We developed Mars View, an interactive web platform helping astronauts plan and execute extravehicular walks (EVAs) across key Martian landmarks: Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons, and Valles Marineris. Integrating real NASA datasets into a single interface, it overlays topographic, thermal, radiation, and spectral layers, plus first-person optical imagery from NASA rovers. Built for both habitat planning screens and spacesuit helmet Heads-Up Displays (HUDs), it provides real-time tactical mapping.

How It Solves the Challenge
While tools like NASA’s Mars Trek excel at global views, planetary data remains fragmented for hyperlocalized human exploration. Mars View bridges this gap by unifying critical datasets at a human walking scale across diverse terrains. Overlapping elevation, temperature, and radiation levels helps astronauts spot terrain obstacles (cliffs, craters, boulders) and environmental hazards to choose safe paths, while first-person rover views offer immediate visual recognition of the horizon.

Why It Matters
Astronaut safety is NASA’s top priority. Operating in extreme environments in heavy spacesuits requires rapid, data-driven decisions. Mars View turns decades of robotic mission data into actionable field intelligence, minimizing risks and maximizing real-time scientific discovery—paving the way for humanity to become an interplanetary species.
projectDetails.details:
How It Works Mars View is an interactive web application covering Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons, and Valles Marineris that transforms fragmented planetary datasets into a unified, hyperlocalized tactical map. Users toggle multiple overlapping data layers—topographic, thermal, radiation, and spectral—while inspecting specific coordinates to view real first-person optical imagery captured by NASA rovers.

Benefits & Intended Impact By consolidating critical environmental and terrain data into a single interface, Mars View eliminates guesswork during Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) across varied Martian geologies. Its primary impact is maximizing astronaut safety and mission efficiency, enabling human explorers to avoid physical hazards (steep slopes, boulders, craters) and radiation hotspots while accelerating real-time scientific discoveries.

Tech Stack & Tools Built for high performance and cross-device responsiveness (habitat consoles to spacesuit HUDs), the platform was developed using TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3, powered by Node.js and modern web mapping/UI libraries. We integrated official NASA Open APIs (such as Mars Rover Photos) and planetary GIS datasets, using Git/GitHub for collaborative development.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered Our creative breakthrough lies in combining orbital multi-layered telemetry with ground-level rover photography across three distinct Martian biomes. Our team prioritized spacesuit mobility constraints on steep or rough terrain, high-contrast UI readability, and cognitive load reduction for astronauts under extreme conditions.

projectDetails.name: Project MaRaBeTha
projectDetails.summary: MaRaBeTha is an interactive 3D globe that tests 30 Earth-science hypotheses against long-term NASA satellite records. Each region tells a story: the Amazon and Ganges river mouths, Lake Chad, the Aral Sea, the Amazon Arc of Deforestation, the Greenland Ice Sheet, the Great Barrier Reef and others. They are grouped into four themes: coastal estuaries, water stress, forests and land use, and the cryosphere and atmosphere. For each region we state what we expect to happen to a variable such as chlorophyll-a, soil moisture, land surface temperature or NO₂. A Python pipeline collects monthly series from NASA Giovanni and AppEEARS, then runs a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, along with Sen’s slope and its 95% confidence interval. Each hypothesis ends up confirmed, contradicted, inconclusive or lacking data. The challenge asks for exactly this: a variable, a specific region, a long time series, a rate of change and a significance test. Our app makes the whole chain readable by non-specialists. It shows not only whether a place is changing, but whether that change is statistically real and what it means, and an AI assistant answers questions about the numbers on screen.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Users spin a 3D globe and open one of 30 study regions. Each region opens as a story in chapters: the place, the hypothesis, the evidence, “Is it real?”, what it means, and where to explore next. The evidence chapter shows the monthly satellite series with Sen’s trend line. “Is it real?” shows the corrected Mann-Kendall p-value, Kendall’s τ, the 95% confidence interval of Sen’s slope, the number of months, data completeness and the effective number of independent months. Each series also gets a data-quality grade (ready, use with caution, exploratory only, insufficient), so a gap-filled series is never shown as a solid result. Some stories contrast two regions with opposite outcomes, for example a dammed delta against a free-flowing river.

How it works.

  1. Collectors pull monthly series from NASA Giovanni and NASA AppEEARS (MODIS) for each region’s bounding boxes and store them in Supabase.
  2. trend-analysis (Python) runs Mann-Kendall with an AR(1) autocorrelation correction, Sen’s slope with confidence intervals, and completeness checks. It then gives each hypothesis a verdict and writes a versioned JSON report.
  3. trend-api (Python) computes a region’s analysis live from the database when a story opens, starts new data collections, and serves an AI agent (“Ask the data”) that answers questions with the region’s real numbers as context.
  4. The Next.js front end renders the globe and stories. It passes the agent the exact numbers the user is looking at, so a question like “what does this 16.7% mean?” gets a grounded answer.

Benefits and intended impact. Climate and land-use trends are often reported as headlines without uncertainty. MaRaBeTha shows the test and its caveats next to every claim, including when the data says “we can’t tell yet.” We want students, journalists, educators and policymakers to learn the habit of asking whether a trend is statistically real before trusting it. Anyone can also reuse the method on new regions and variables.

Tools and languages. TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, react-globe.gl and three.js on the front end, deployed on Vercel. Python for data collection, statistics and the API, hosted on Render, with Supabase (Postgres) for storage. Data comes from NASA Giovanni, NASA AppEEARS (MODIS) and NASA Blue Marble textures, with Natural Earth outlines and Wikimedia Commons photos credited under their licenses. An LLM agent (Gemini) powers the Q&A. The design was done in Figma, and GitLab and GitHub were used for collaboration.

The user can access: https://spaceappschallenge-tau.vercel.app
Our code is hosted in: https://gitlab.com/marabetha

Creativity. Instead of a dashboard, every region is a scientific investigation told as a story. The hypothesis comes first, the data second, and the verdict can be “contradicted,” so the app shows that science is allowed to be wrong. Regions are paired so that human pressure (dams, irrigation, urbanization) can be read against natural variability. The assistant knows what is on the user’s screen, so it explains the actual numbers rather than giving general answers.

Factors we considered.

  • Statistics: monthly satellite series are seasonal and autocorrelated, so we chose non-parametric tests and corrected for autocorrelation instead of relying on a naive regression.
  • Data gaps: a minimum of 36 valid months is required, and completeness is shown.
  • Honest labels: sample or demo data is always labelled as such.
  • Reliability: the API has rate limits and retries, and API keys never reach the browser.
  • Attribution: image licenses are credited.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: MINEIRØ - The Earth Experience
projectDetails.summary:
NASA's Earth and climate visualizations rely almost exclusively on sight, limiting access for visually impaired people. With that in mind, we built MINEIRØ - The Earth Experience: an accessible, multi-sensory projected room and live 3D web simulator that lets users hear and explore NASA data in real time.

Using only two projectors and one screen-reader-ready device (or any web browser via our online 3D simulator), visitors launch a guided space mission with bilingual neural voice narration and 3-point 8D spatial audio. Once in orbit, our engine samples RGB pixels and spatial coordinates from five official NASA SVS datasets (lightning, temperature, wind, CO, and NOx), translating each layer into distinct Web Audio instruments.

Why it matters: MINEIRØ makes complex climate science more inclusive for blind and low-vision explorers while enabling anyone in the world to create an accessible, large-scale NASA immersion.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works:

MINEIRØ - The Earth Experience transforms real NASA Earth observation data into a multi-sensory, accessible experience where blind, low-vision, and sighted explorers can hear and interact with planetary science in real time.

Our engine samples RGB pixel values, scientific colorbars, and geographic coordinates from five official NASA SVS datasets and translates them live through the Web Audio API:

- Lightning (SVS 5011): drives crystalline melodic notes with 8D spatial panning;

- Carbon Monoxide (SVS 5153): generates harmonic chord pads;

- Air Temperature (SVS 5147): controls musical tempo (BPM) and thermal pulse;

- Nitrogen Oxides (SVS 5154): shapes sub-harmonic bass lines;

- Near-Surface Wind (SVS 5148): synthesizes stereo airflow textures.

Why It Matters & Intended Impact:

Climate and space imagery usually depend on sight alone. MINEIRØ makes NASA data audible and navigable for visually impaired users through a screen-reader-ready tablet controller, high-contrast WCAG AAA mode, and bilingual neural voice narration (English and Brazilian Portuguese). Just as importantly, it is radically accessible to set up: requiring only two projectors and one controlling device (or any web browser via our online 3D simulator), anyone in the world can create a giant, inclusive NASA immersion.

Creativity & User Journey:

Rather than a static dashboard, MINEIRØ guides visitors through an interactive space mission across three projected surfaces (Left Wall, Right Wall, and Ceiling):

1. Mission Briefing & Boarding: An animated 3D astronaut guide (MINEIRØ) invites the visitor aboard while metallic blast doors seal the cabin, revealing a launch field porthole on the left wall and the rocket nosecone on the ceiling with spatial pneumatic audio.

2. 8D Liftoff & Zero Gravity: A 5-to-1 countdown triggers 3-point 8D thruster propulsion. In orbit, the ceiling opens to reveal deep space and passing meteors before the cabin dissolves into the 3D Earth globe and floating country flags.

3. Live Planetary Mixer: Visitors select countries and toggle the five NASA visual/audio layers individually like a Photoshop-style mixer.

4. Gamified Return: Ending the mission brings Earth closer and awards a mission recognition medal.

Tools, Software & Hardware:

- Software & Stack: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, Web Audio API, Motion (motion/react), topojson-client / world-atlas (Natural Earth cartography), Vitest (39 automated unit tests).

- Neural Audio & Accessibility: @mintplex-labs/piper-tts-web (ONNX Runtime Web with OPFS caching) and Web Speech API fallback.

- Hardware Setup: 2 projectors (L-corner wall + ceiling) + 1 tablet/device + 3-point stereo/8D speaker setup (or 100% browser-based 3D Room Simulator).

Factors Considered & SI Transparency:

We prioritized WCAG AAA accessibility, corner-pin homography calibration for real room walls, zero-latency fallback audio, and bilingual support. In accordance with NASA Space Apps SI guidelines, we acknowledge the use of Piper TTS neural voices (en_US-bryce-medium and pt_BR-faber-medium) for accessible narration, AI coding assistants with specialized engineering/design skills to accelerate code refactoring and testing, and AI-assisted generation for the decorative Earth horizon illustration on the entry portal. All system architecture, NASA SVS data-to-audio mapping, and final verification were directed and authored by our team.
