Climate projections are organized separately from observed data.

For temperature and sea ice, NASA GISS-E2.1-G model data within the CMIP6 context (member r1i1p1f2) are used. For CO₂, GISS/CMIP6 forcing files per scenario are utilized.

Sea level projections use a semi-empirical approach associated with Rahmstorf (2007), driven by model temperature and calibrated with NASA and IPCC AR6 references.

The scenarios considered are SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5. The platform visually and narratively differentiates observations from projections, clarifying that results from a single simulation do not represent deterministic forecasts for every future year.

6  SONIFICATION METHODOLOGY

 

Sonification involves transforming quantitative information into sound properties. In ORICHALCUM, environmental indicators are associated with frequencies, intensity, rhythm, timbre, stereo position, and harmonic organization.

The goal is to produce an auditory representation that preserves relevant relationships among the data, making it possible to recognize trends and changes over time.

 

6.1  SOUND PARAMETERS

 

Parameters utilized include:

a)  Frequency: represents variations in indicator values;

b)  Intensity: expresses the relative magnitude of changes;

c)  Duration: organizes the temporal representation of data;

d)  Stereo Position: differentiates values below and above the mean;

e)  Timbre: distinguishes environmental indicators;

f)     Harmony: represents general composition changes associated with environmental scenarios.

Base frequencies are compositional choices used to differentiate indicators rather than natural frequencies of environmental phenomena.

6.3  SONIFICATION OF QUANTITATIVE DATA AND VISUAL CHARACTERISTICS

 

In the functional platform, environmental indicators are also represented by specific musical elements:

a)   Temperature: drives the melody and harmonic organization. Increased warming shifts the composition from major musical organization to higher-tension modes, such as Locrian;

b)     CO₂: forms a continuous low-frequency sound layer, with distortion increasing

alongside the represented concentration;

c)   Sea Ice: represented by bells, whose frequency of occurrence decreases as ice extent shrinks;

d)  Sea Level: represented by sound waves that increase as sea level rises.

These relationships are project-defined sound metaphors and do not represent intrinsic physical musical properties of environmental phenomena.

The platform also encompasses the interpretation of visual characteristics such as color, brightness, spatial distribution, and movement, respecting the legends and scales of source images.

7  METHODOLOGY AND DEVELOPMENT STAGES

 

The development of ORICHALCUM was organized into incremental stages, starting with data structuring and advancing to the integration of processing, sonification, visualization, and accessibility.

The first stage consisted of identifying scientific sources and selecting environmental datasets. Subsequently, routines for acquisition, validation, cleaning, aggregation, and standardization were developed, organizing time series across different indicators.

The Python prototype established the first computational implementation. Within it, data are organized by area, indicator, and year; values are aggregated by annual mean; and indicators are standardized to enable comparative analysis.

Next, annual profile clustering via K-Means was implemented, followed by audio file generation and matrix visualizations. This step tested the conversion of quantitative data into sound stimuli.

The project's evolution led to the implementation of the web platform, integrating processed data with three-dimensional visualization, time-series charts, climate scenarios, and accessibility features.

Development steps involved:

a)  research and selection of scientific sources;

b)  acquisition and organization of datasets;

c)  validation, cleaning, and aggregation of series;

d)  standardization and statistical analysis;

e)  definition and documentation of sound mappings;

f)  development of the initial Python prototype;

g)  implementation of the web platform and interactive modules;

h)  integration of audio, globe, charts, and timeline;

i)  implementation of accessibility and narration features;

j)  verification of data consistency and integrated operation.

9  CONCEPTUAL ARCHITECTURE

 

ORICHALCUM’s architecture integrates data acquisition and organization, processing, analysis, sonification, and user experience.

Python scripts handle dataset acquisition and preparation, generating resources used by the application. In the browser, the data module combines observed records and projections based on the selected scenario.

PCHIP interpolation is used to produce smooth transitions between values, preserving the distinction between observed and projected periods. Before the first available record, values are identified as missing without artificial extrapolation.

The globe module uses Three.js and GLSL shaders to represent the planet in three dimensions. Implemented features include terrain displacement, visual representation of coastal areas, ice edges, transitions between annual atlases, moving clouds, GPU-calculated wind particles, and representation of ocean waves and currents.

Environmental layers include:

a)  temperature anomalies;

b)  clouds observed via VIIRS imagery;

c)  vegetation via MODIS Terra NDVI;

d)  thermal anomalies associated with wildfires;

e)  10-meter winds;

f)  ozone monitoring products;

g)  geostrophic ocean currents derived from sea surface height.

Base textures utilize resources such as NASA Blue Marble Next Generation, land/water masks derived from MODIS, and NASA Black Marble nighttime lighting.

The architecture synchronizes the timeline, data, audio, globe, charts, and accessibility features, ensuring that changes to a period or scenario reflect across all modules.

11  DEVELOPMENT OF THE FIRST PROTOTYPE

 

ORICHALCUM's first prototype was developed in Python using a CSV file named dados_ambientais.csv, structured with columns for area, indicador (indicator), ano (year), valor (value), and unidade (unit).

The code covers two main areas: pollution and warming. The pollution area groups indicators such as PM2.5, PM10, CO, NO₂, O₃, and SO₂. The warming area covers temperature, CO₂, ocean heat, sea level, and sea ice.

Processing includes validating mandatory columns, converting numeric fields, removing incomplete records, and aggregating repeated records by annual mean.

In the next step, each indicator is standardized via StandardScaler. Data are reorganized into an annual matrix with years as rows and indicators as columns. Missing values are handled via median imputation using SimpleImputer.

Clustering is performed using the K-Means algorithm with up to three clusters, random_state=42, and ten initializations. The clusters represent statistical similarities among annual profiles rather than universal scientific categories.

Sonification transforms standardized values into sound frequencies and intensities. Each year corresponds to a 900-millisecond block with indicator-specific base frequencies. Blocks are concatenated and exported into WAV files.

The prototype also produces matrix visualizations using OpenCV, converting standardized values into a visual color scale. Audio playback can be performed via Pyo when the library is available.

This initial implementation served as a foundation for project evolution and for integrating processing and sonification concepts into the functional web platform.

 

12  TECHNICAL LIMITATIONS AND CHALLENGES

 

Using environmental datasets involves challenges related to the heterogeneity of formats, units, temporal and spatial resolutions, observation gaps, and methodological differences between series.

K-Means clustering depends on variable selection, standardization, number of clusters, and data distribution. The generated labels represent computational categories relative to the analyzed set and do not carry universal scientific meaning.

Median imputation can smooth real variations. Similarly, statistical standardization facilitates comparisons but does not directly preserve original physical magnitudes. For this reason, original values and units remain available for consultation.

The described climate projections use a single model simulation, GISS-E2.1-G, and should not be interpreted as deterministic forecasts for every future year.

Sea level projections use a semi-empirical approach calibrated with NASA and IPCC AR6 references rather than direct GISS model output.

Some visual elements are illustrative. The representation of coastal flooding and ice edges may be visually exaggerated to aid perception. Ocean currents represent the 1985–2014 climate mean, while urban light growth is illustrative.

Sonification also involves artistic decisions. Base frequencies, musical scales, timbres, and sound effects are project-defined parameters rather than natural properties of environmental phenomena.

Documenting these limitations is essential to preserve scientific transparency and prevent misinterpretations.

Scientific transparency remains essential. Data provenance, transformation methods, artistic choices, and projection limitations must be presented clearly.

By integrating different forms of perception and interpretation, ORICHALCUM seeks to contribute to a more accessible, interactive, and inclusive scientific outreach.

 

17  EXPANSION PLAN — TEN MONTHS

 

To broaden The Earth Jukebox's reach over ten months, the Orichalcum Group intends to invest in international outreach, innovation, and strategic partnerships. This planning represents a future expansion phase of the platform rather than pending features of the currently implemented version.

A key initiative will allow users to create and share musical compositions based on environmental data, encouraging spontaneous project dissemination and active community participation.

Social media presence will also be strengthened through international challenges and partnerships with universities, schools, and content creators. These initiatives aim to bring the platform closer to diverse audiences and expand its use in educational and scientific contexts.

Expansion into new languages, especially Spanish, will be another priority. The group also intends to enhance accessibility resources, broadening usability for people with diverse needs, including visually impaired individuals.

Additionally, educational campaigns will be developed to present ORICHALCUM as a scientific learning tool, encouraging environmental data exploration through sound and visual experiences.

As initial goals, the project will seek to reach users in at least 30 countries and establish 10 to 20 partnerships with universities. Monitoring will be conducted through indicators of geographic reach, challenge participation, utilization of creation and sharing features, number of available languages, and established partnerships.

Through these steps, the Orichalcum Group aims to transform The Earth Jukebox into an international initiative, building an engaged community and laying the groundwork for worldwide recognition.

projectDetails.name: Project Planet Lohan
projectDetails.summary:
Fiz o programa e os testes rígidos. Os 8 testes passaram, tanto nas simulações quanto com dados reais da NASA.

O método compara duas fotos tiradas em sequência no pico da explosão, ajusta a escala, localiza a estrela e mede seu deslocamento com precisão de fração de pixel. Se o movimento superar o ruído da imagem, indica um possível exoplaneta; caso contrário, é alarme falso.

Fase 1 – Simulações:

- Detectou pelo menos 95% das estrelas em movimento, com no máximo 2% de alarmes falsos.
- Explosões mais fortes não geraram falsos alarmes.
- Fotos corrompidas foram recusadas.
- Nos testes com 100, 200 e 400 análises simultâneas, houve 0% de erros, 95% das análises ocorreram em até 50 ms e não houve crescimento de memória.

Fase 2 – Dados reais: Foram utilizadas 600 estrelas do telescópio Kepler, do arquivo da NASA. O programa acertou 99,5%, com 0% de erros, cerca de 2.400 análises por segundo e menos de 1 MB de memória adicional.

Limitação: As fotos foram reconstruídas a partir de dados reais, pois o arquivo da NASA contém números, não imagens de explosões. Portanto, os resultados confirmam a lógica, mas ainda precisam de testes com fotos reais de telescópios.

As soluções de desempenho foram adaptadas ao programa, incluindo limite de análises simultâneas e reaproveitamento de memória.

Os erros que impediam a pré-visualização foram corrigidos.  Na página, basta tocar em "1. Rodar simulações" e "2. Rodar com dados reais" para conferir os resultados.

projectDetails.name: Raiz Orbital: What to Plant After Soybeans?
projectDetails.summary:
Every year between January and March, soybean farmers in Brazil's Cerrado must decide what to plant after the harvest, just as the rains begin to end. Most repeat second-crop corn or leave the field bare, which degrades the soil and exposes farms to drought and heat losses, with almost no crop insurance.

Raiz Orbital is a responsive web app that answers one question for a specific field: "What should I plant after soybeans?" The farmer marks the field and the harvest date. Raiz Orbital replays 20 seasons of NASA observations (GPM IMERG, NASA POWER, SMAP, MODIS) and NASA climate projections for 2041–2060 (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6), combined with local soil data, to test six off-season options. It delivers a detailed X-ray of the land, one recommendation, a 3-year rotation plan with a Plan B for dry autumns, alerts, a printable report and a bilingual guide. Every number shows its source.

This is exactly what Field Shift asks for: NASA Earth observations, local soil, crop traits and farmer priorities turned into rotation strategies that strengthen soil health and adapt farms to a changing climate. Built in 48 hours in Uberlândia, Brazil. Eyes on the sky, roots in the ground.
projectDetails.details:
Raiz Orbital: What to Plant After Soybeans?

Eyes on the sky, roots in the ground.

Live app: https://frontend-production-62e614b3.up.railway.app (no sign-up; a demo field opens with one tap)
Source code on GitHub: https://github.com/Ricardo07g/nasa-challenge (README, product documents, tests and data pipeline)

1. The challenge and why we chose it

We chose Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data because it describes, word for word, a decision that farmers around us make every year. We live in Uberlândia, in the Triângulo Mineiro region of Minas Gerais, in the heart of the Brazilian Cerrado. Here, soybeans are harvested between January and March, and right after that every farmer faces the same question: what should I plant next, with the rains about to end?

Field Shift asks for a tool that combines NASA Earth observations, local soil information, crop characteristics and farmer priorities into crop rotation strategies that strengthen soil health and adapt farms to a changing climate. Raiz Orbital is our answer to that, built for one real region and one real decision.

How we got to the problem

We started from a question, not from a technology. Before writing code, we spent the first hours on product discovery, with one rule: only public, citable sources, and every number with its link.

  • Public universities, many of them in our own region: UFU (dry spells across 30 weather stations and the farm profile of the Triângulo Mineiro), IFTM with UFU (when the rains end), UFV (when the rains start), UFG and UFGD.
  • Research and technology centers: Embrapa (soil under the soybean–corn routine, water stress in corn and soybeans, satellite mapping of cropping systems), Inpe and Cemaden, ISRIC, NOAA and FAO.
  • Official statistics and surveys: IBGE, Conab, MAPA (ZARC), Ipea, and farmer surveys with published methods (ABMRA, McKinsey, Serasa).
  • Farmers' own words: regional press reports from Uberlândia and Uberaba.

Three findings shaped every decision. The off-season choice repeats every year with no field-level information, so the app answers that one question. Rain changes a lot from one farm to the next, so every result is computed for the field's own grid cell. Farmers trust their agronomist far more than AI, so the engine is deterministic, cites its sources and produces a report for the agronomist. The full research is public in our product discovery.

2. The problem

  • Brazil feeds the world with soybeans. About 4 in every 10 soybeans on Earth are grown in Brazil (USDA, 2025/26), and about half of Brazil's soybean area is in the Cerrado.
  • The off-season decision is made almost blind. Most farmers repeat second-crop corn or leave the field fallow. Embrapa points out that this succession degrades soil structure and long-term productivity: bare soil has no straw to protect it, and the soybean–corn sequence feeds root nematodes.
  • The climate risk is growing. In the Triângulo the dry season usually starts in April, so a crop sown late reaches flowering without water. The 2025/26 drought hit rainfed farms in the region hard, and the 2026/27 season starts under a strong El Niño.
  • Almost no safety net. Only 3.3% of Brazil's planted area was insured in 2025, so every climate loss goes straight to the farmer's income.

3. Our solution: Raiz Orbital

Raiz Orbital is a responsive web app that answers one question for one specific field: "What should I plant after soybeans, and which rotation should I follow for the next 3 years?"

The farmer answers only two things: where the field is and when the soybeans will be harvested. NASA satellites answer the rest. Raiz Orbital replays 20 seasons (2005–2024) of NASA observations for that exact spot, tests six off-season options against the local soil, re-runs everything under 2041–2060 NASA climate projections, and turns it into one clear recommendation, explained in plain language, with the source of every number.

4. How to use it, step by step

The whole path takes about one minute with the demo field. It works on a phone and on a computer, in Portuguese and English (switch in the header).

  1. Open the app at https://frontend-production-62e614b3.up.railway.app and tap the main button on the home screen.
  2. Mark the field. The map opens with a demo field already marked: keep it, tap "Use where I am now", or use "Other ways to mark" to paste coordinates or a Google Maps link. The MVP covers the area around Uberlândia and Uberaba; points outside it get a clear message.
  3. Tell when you harvest the soybeans: an exact date, or early, mid or late February. Not sure? "Still deciding?" compares harvest periods and how much rain is left after each one.
  4. Read your field's X-ray: eight indicators (soil, moisture now, rain, dry spells, heat and more) and the last 10 seasons seen by satellite. Confirm what you planted in the last three off-seasons.
  5. Choose your priority (More safety, Income or Care for the soil) and get one suggestion with "worked in X of 20 years". Tap "Why this suggestion?" to see the NASA data behind it, and compare up to three crops side by side.
  6. Build your 3-year plan. Change any year and the following years are recalculated, with our suggestion always visible. Open "What if the year is dry?" to see Plan A and Plan B.
  7. Open "Your plan": a timeline of what to do and when, the alerts for your area and Print report to take to your agronomist.
  8. Anytime: the Alerts bell and the Guide (27 short articles) are in the header, and "Listen to summary" reads each screen aloud.

5. What the farmer gets

5.1 A detailed X-ray of the land

Eight indicators for the chosen point: soil texture, water the soil can hold, root-zone moisture now (SMAP), crop greenness (MODIS), rain in a typical year and the longest dry spell (GPM IMERG), strong-heat years (NASA POWER) and how the field compares with the region. Each block shows its NASA source and resolution.

It also shows a 10-season history of the field from MODIS NDVI: the satellite detects the soybean crop and whether the field was planted or left fallow after it. The farmer confirms each season, and those answers become the baseline for the plan.

5.2 One recommendation, adjusted to the farmer's priority

The farmer chooses what matters most: more safety, income or care for the soil. Raiz Orbital suggests one option, for example "worked in 20 of 20 years", and lets the farmer compare up to three crops side by side: water, future climate, income risk, soil effect, sowing deadline, pros and cons. Every value opens the math and the source.

5.3 A planting plan for the next 3 years

A rotation suggested year by year, with the reason for each step, scored against how the field is managed today (safety, soil health and 2041–2060 climate). It also shows how much rain is put to use instead of being wasted on bare soil.

What if the year is dry? Using the official NOAA El Niño outlook and the current SMAP soil moisture, the plan gives a Plan A for a normal autumn and a Plan B for a dry one.

5.4 Alerts, reports and guidance

Current alerts (strong heat, dry soil, heavy rain, frost and nearby fire), how the area has changed between 2005–2019 and 2020–2024, the most extreme events of the last 20 years, a printable report to take to the agronomist and links to the official Civil Defense alert channels.

A bilingual guide (Portuguese and English) with 27 short articles on crops, planting, soil care, climate and safety, plus a "How the math works" page listing every rule, threshold and source.

6. How it works

  • Daily climate series for the field's 0.1° cell, 2005–2024: rain from GPM IMERG Final (NASA POWER as fallback); reference evapotranspiration with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith from NASA POWER.
  • Soil from ISRIC SoilGrids sets how much water the soil holds (60 mm clayey, 50 mm medium, 40 mm sandy). The farmer can adjust it.
  • Daily soil-water balance (FAO-56) starting each season from the NASA SMAP root-zone moisture on sowing day.
  • Sowing date follows the harvest date. Crops past their official ZARC sowing deadline are never recommended.
  • A season "worked" if the crop's water satisfaction stayed at or above 55% around flowering (50% in the first 30 days for cover crops), with fewer than 3 days at 35 °C or more.
  • Future climate: monthly changes from three NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models (SSP2-4.5, 2041–2060 vs 1995–2014) are applied and every option is simulated again.
  • Score 0–100: climate safety 30%, future climate 15%, soil health 25% (straw, nitrogen, nematode break) and income 30%. The farmer's priority reorders the ranking.
  • Six options: second-crop corn, sorghum, corn with brachiaria, pearl millet, crotalaria (sunn hemp) and fallow.

7. NASA data in every number

  • GPM IMERG Final, daily V07 (0.1°, 2005–2024): rain in every simulation, rain left after harvest, end of the rainy season, longest dry spell, heavy-rain alerts.
  • NASA POWER, daily agroclimatology: evapotranspiration (FAO-56), heat at flowering, frost risk, current dry-day and heat warnings.
  • SMAP L4 SPL4SMGP v008 (9 km): starting soil water on sowing day, current root-zone moisture percentile, dry-soil alerts.
  • MODIS MOD13Q1 + MYD13Q1 NDVI (250 m): 10-season history of each field: soybean detected, planted or fallow after it.
  • MODIS MCD12Q1 land cover (500 m): cropland mask to compare with neighbouring fields within 30 km.
  • MODIS MCD64A1 burned area (500 m): fire history within 5 km of the field.
  • NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (0.25°, SSP2-4.5, 3 models): every option re-simulated for 2041–2060, with model agreement.

We download the data directly from NASA services (POWER API, GES DISC, ORNL DAAC, NCCS THREDDS and Earthdata). NASA is cited only by name as the source of each number; no NASA logos are used.

8. How Raiz Orbital answers Field Shift

What the challenge asks for, and what Raiz Orbital delivers:

  • NASA Earth observations: GPM IMERG, NASA POWER, SMAP, MODIS and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 in every result.
  • Local soil information: SoilGrids texture and water-holding capacity, adjustable by the farmer.
  • Crop characteristics: cycle, flowering, water demand and sowing deadlines from ZARC and Embrapa.
  • Farmer priorities: ranking by safety, income or care for the soil.
  • Crop rotation strategies: a 3-year plan compared with how the field is managed today.
  • Soil health: score for straw, nitrogen and nematode break, plus the field’s fallow history.
  • Adapting to changing conditions: 20-year risk, a dry-autumn Plan B and a 2041–2060 re-simulation.

9. Design decisions

  • Two questions, one answer. Many farmers in the region are over 45 and have little formal schooling, so the app uses plain language and a "Listen to summary" button on every screen.
  • No invented numbers. Every threshold is stored with its source (ZARC, Embrapa, FAO-56) and the API rejects any value without one. When data is missing, the block is hidden.
  • No AI in the decision. Farmers trust agronomists far more than AI, so the engine is deterministic and auditable. The app "helps you decide; it does not replace your agronomist."
  • No guessed prices. Income is measured by facts: whether the crop gives grain and how often it lost water or suffered heat.
  • A website, not an app store download. It works on a phone in the field and on the computer at the cooperative, with no sign-up.
  • Honest about scale. The prototype covers a pilot area of 226 grid cells around Uberlândia and Uberaba.

10. Impact

  • Environment: fields covered all year instead of bare soil mean less erosion, more water kept in the soil, more straw and nitrogen, and fewer nematodes.
  • Farm income: choosing a crop that fits this field's climate means fewer harvests lost to drought, in a country where almost no area is insured.
  • People: free access, plain language, audio and two languages put 20 years of NASA satellite data in the hands of farmers who never had it.

Our hypothesis: if farmers see, for their own field, how each option performed over 20 years and how it would perform in the 2050s, at least 1 in 3 will try a soil-building option on part of their land.

11. Validation and limitations

Next we will interview farmers and agronomists, run a pilot with 15 to 20 farmers in the 2027 off-season and check our "risky years" against IBGE municipal crop-loss data. Limitations we show to users: satellites observe, they do not forecast weather; SMAP and IMERG describe the region, not a single field; optical NDVI is affected by clouds; crop texts are drafts awaiting agronomist review.

12. What comes next

We built this in 48 hours. Imagine one month.

What we are submitting is an MVP: it covers a pilot area of 226 grid cells around Uberlândia and Uberaba, in the Triângulo Mineiro. The engine, the data pipeline and the screens are ready to grow. Four bets take it from here:

12.1 From one region to every soybean field on Earth

NASA data is global and free; what changes from place to place is the agronomy (sowing deadlines, crop cycles, soil). That makes expansion mostly configuration, not new code. The steps are: the whole Triângulo Mineiro and Alto Paranaíba, then the Cerrado (Minas Gerais, Goiás, Mato Grosso, Bahia, Tocantins), then every soybean region in Brazil, including the South, with wheat, oats and frost rules, and then other countries, replacing ZARC with each country's planting calendar. Along the way we move from MODIS to HLS (30 m) and VIIRS, which see individual fields better. The goal: any farmer who grows soybeans, anywhere, can ask "what do I plant next?" and get an answer for their own field.

12.2 The satellite in every farmer's pocket: fully integrated with WhatsApp

In rural Brazil, WhatsApp is where business happens: 96% of farmers use it for business decisions (9th ABMRA survey), 98% of farms have internet at least on a phone, and 82% of rural internet users go online only through a phone. At the same time, 66.9% of Brazil's soybean production is outside 4G and 5G coverage. A website needs a good signal and a new habit; a WhatsApp message arrives anyway. That is why the next version is not "alerts on WhatsApp" but the whole product inside WhatsApp:

  • Ask and get the answer in the chat: send the field's location pin, tap the harvest period, and receive the recommendation as short text and as audio, with a link to the full plan and the PDF report.
  • Build and follow the plan there: reminders on the plan's dates ("the sowing deadline for sorghum is March 20").
  • Receive alerts that matter: dry soil, dry spells or heat at flowering, heavy rain, frost and fire nearby, at most two a week so they never become noise.
  • Ask by voice: record "can I still plant sorghum?" and get an answer from the same engine.
  • Built the right way: the official WhatsApp Business Cloud API, a verified number, the same engine as the website, opt-in alerts and no personal data beyond the chat.

12.3 Farmers helping farmers: a community that works as a whole

Satellites see the region; neighbours see the field. Rain alone can be 20% above average in Uberlândia and 30% below in Uberaba on the same month, less than 100 km apart. The community turns the farmers of a region into one network:

  • It rained here: farmers with a rain gauge record today's rain in two taps, correcting satellite rainfall for everyone.
  • What I planted and how it went: "12 neighbours planted sorghum; 9 were happy", the kind of trust no algorithm can buy.
  • It happened here: hail, fire, flash flood, pests or a bad road, so a warning reaches the next farm first.
  • Share equipment and labour: a planter for a day, a crew for a firebreak, a shared truck to the cooperative.
  • Plant together: neighbours who choose the same crop can coordinate sowing and logistics.
  • Buy together: group purchases of seed and inputs for a better price, so small farms gain the strength of a large one.
  • Ask the agronomist and get the week in your region: rain, what neighbours planted and the alerts, in one short digest.

Privacy by design: only the 10 km area is stored, never the exact spot; names appear only with permission; reports are cross-checked with satellite data and the community is moderated.

12.4 From harvest to harvest, nothing wasted

From one question to the whole farm year: a signal for when to plant the soybeans, dry-spell and heat alerts at flowering, the after-harvest decision, frost and fire alerts in the dry season, and a satellite check in July and August that the plan was really planted. More starting crops (after corn, cotton, sugarcane, beans) and more options to plant join the six we cover today. More yield from the same land, less soil, water and money wasted.

First steps: month one, a WhatsApp beta with 20 farmers and the whole Triângulo on the map; February–March 2027, an off-season pilot with 15 to 20 farmers in Uberlândia and Uberaba; then the Cerrado and the first partner cooperative. Our north star is the number of hectares that leave fallow and stay covered, checked from space. Full plan: product roadmap.

13. Technology and quality

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, PostgreSQL 17 + PostGIS 3.5. Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, Leaflet. Data pipeline: 14 Python scripts that download data directly from NASA, ISRIC and NOAA and precompute every grid cell. Hosting: Docker and Railway, live 24/7 during judging. No special hardware.

Built test-first. Every behaviour started with a failing test (TDD), in four layers:

  • Unit tests (backend, Pytest), ~1,370 tests: the engine: water balance, success rule, ZARC window, scores, rotation rules, alerts, with fake repositories.
  • Integration tests (backend, Pytest), ~210 tests: API endpoints and the database, against a disposable PostGIS; migrations up, down and up again.
  • Unit and controller tests (frontend, Vitest), ~900 tests: services, API calls, hooks, translations and content.
  • Component and feature tests (frontend, Vitest + Testing Library), ~530 tests: every component and every screen rendered the way the user sees it, and full flows through the routes.
  • Screen reviews: after each delivery, every screen was checked in Portuguese and English, on a phone (360 px) and on a desktop, and the interface was adjusted round after round: plain language, no step counters and a real "Back" button, details in pop-ups, the plan's suggestion always visible and no sideways scroll on a phone.
  • Prototyping: the first screens were prototyped with Lovable, then rebuilt in React with tests.
  • Automated delivery: every pull request runs secret scanning, linters (Ruff, Oxlint), all tests, the production build and the Docker images; every merge deploys to Railway and a final check confirms that the live site runs the new version.

What is on GitHub (https://github.com/Ricardo07g/nasa-challenge): almost 600 commits from four contributors in 48 hours, about half Python and half TypeScript.

  • README: the problem, how we got to it, how to use the app, how it works, architecture, tests, use of AI and how to run it.
  • Product documents: Discovery (research, pains, personas, hypotheses) · Business plan · PRD · Roadmap.
  • Code: the FastAPI backend, the React frontend, the NASA data pipeline, the engine rules with a source for every number, architecture decision records, user stories and diagrams.

14. Use of artificial intelligence

We used AI tools as assistants. No AI produces any number, score or recommendation shown to farmers.

  • Claude (Anthropic): research support for product discovery and data review, documentation drafts, pair programming (FastAPI services, React screens, NASA data-ingestion scripts and tests), interface and guide texts in Portuguese and English, and production of the demo video and the illustrations on this page.
  • Gemini (Google): pair programming, code review and documentation drafts.
  • Lovable: early interface prototyping and the decorative image on the app's home screen, which carries a visible "AI-generated image" mark.
  • Demo video: AI-generated, marked "AI-generated video". The narration is a synthetic voice (Piper TTS) and the soundtrack was composed with code by AI.
  • Images on this page: the illustrations marked "AI-generated image" were produced with AI; the other images are real screenshots of our app.

Every change was reviewed by the team under shared rules for people and AI agents (AGENTS.md in the repository).

15. Team

Team Raiz Orbital, Uberlândia, Minas Gerais, Brazil: Adriano Araújo, Rayanne Lemos and Ricardo Pereira.

Thank you, NASA

Thank you to NASA and the Space Apps community for opening the data of space to the people who take care of the land. Small decisions in one field. A big difference for the planet.

projectDetails.name: RasterRoot – Intelligent Crop Rotation System
projectDetails.summary:
RasterRoot is a mobile, user-friendly and easy to use decision-support application designed to help farmers plan the crop rotation strategies. 
By integrating NASA Earth observation data, local farm information, and agronomic criteria, the platform uses a multi-criteria analysis model to recommend sustainable and productive cropping systems. 
Farmers can map fields, and with the app evaluation of the climate and water conditions, compare different rotation scenarios based on factors such as water availability, soil health, erosion risk, crop diversification, vegetation cover, operational feasibility, and economic potential. 
Initially focused on Uberlândia and the Triângulo Mineiro region in Brazil, RasterRoot aims to transform complex scientific data into accessible insights that support better agricultural decisions. 
The project promotes sustainable land management, increases resilience to climate change, and helps producers balance productivity with environmental conservation, contributing to a smarter and more climate-adaptive future for agriculture.
projectDetails.details:
Problem

Climate change is making agricultural decision-making more difficult than ever. Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, prolonged droughts, and soil degradation directly affect crop productivity, water availability, and long-term farm sustainability. Poor crop rotation choices can lead to nutrient depletion, increased erosion, and reduced resilience to environmental challenges.

Small and medium-sized farmers often have limited access to environmental data, technical support, and planning tools. While valuable scientific and Earth observation data already exist, they are not always easy to access or apply in day-to-day farm management.

As a result, farmers need practical tools that can transform complex environmental information into clear and actionable recommendations tailored to local conditions.

Proposed Solution

RasterRoot is a mobile decision-support platform that combines NASA environmental data, local farm information, and agronomic knowledge to help farmers choose and plan crop rotation strategies.

Using a multi-criteria evaluation model, the platform compares different rotation scenarios and identifies the best alternatives based on factors such as water availability, soil conservation, climate suitability, crop diversification, and operational feasibility. Recommendations are designed to support farmers in making more sustainable and resilient decisions while maintaining productivity.

Rather than replacing professional agronomic advice, RasterRoot provides accessible insights that help farmers better understand the opportunities and trade-offs associated with each strategy.

How It Works

Farmers begin by registering basic information about their property, including location, field size, crops, irrigation availability, and production priorities.

Using GPS or manual mapping tools, users define the boundaries of the field to be analyzed. The platform then processes environmental and agronomic indicators and presents the results through an intuitive dashboard with rankings, scores, visual charts, risk alerts, and technical reports that can be shared with stakeholders.

Key Features

  • Farm and field registration.
  • GPS and satellite-based field mapping.
  • Automatic area calculation and geospatial analysis.
  • Comparison of crop rotation strategies.
  • Indicators for water availability, soil health, erosion risk, and vegetation cover.
  • Technical report generation and sharing.
  • Portuguese and English language support.
  • Offline storage of up to 20 analyzed fields.

RasterRoot initially focuses on Uberlândia and the Triângulo Mineiro region of Brazil, promoting climate-smart agriculture through accessible scientific data and practical decision support.

NASA Data Used

RasterRoot uses NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) as its primary environmental data source.

The platform incorporates variables such as air temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, solar radiation, and other climate indicators to characterize local growing conditions and support crop rotation planning.

Local Data and Agronomic Knowledge

NASA data are complemented by information provided directly by farmers, including farm size, land use, crop history, irrigation availability, and production priorities.

The platform also incorporates agronomic knowledge related to water requirements, climate suitability, soil management practices, crop diversification, and operational feasibility. Technical references from EMBRAPA and Brazil's Agricultural Climate Risk Zoning Program (ZARC) help support the assessment of alternative crop rotation strategies.

Combining Earth observation data with local knowledge helps avoid generic recommendations and ensures that analyses reflect the realities of each farm.

Limitations and Future Work

RasterRoot is currently a prototype, and its results depend on both the quality of local information and the resolution of available environmental data. NASA observations represent environmental conditions at specific spatial and temporal scales and should not replace direct field measurements.

The multicriteria model also relies on weights and parameters that require further validation with farmers, agronomists, and researchers. Therefore, recommendations should be interpreted as decision-support guidance rather than guarantees of success.

Future developments include agronomic validation of recommendations, sensitivity analysis of model parameters, support for additional crops, climate scenario assessments, improved offline functionality, and expansion to new agricultural regions.

Technologies and Tools

Backend & Integrations

  • C#
  • Microsoft Azure
  • Environmental data processing services

Mobile Application

  • React Native

SI - Assisted Development

  • Microsoft Copilot: coding assistance, image generation, and mathematical and statistical support (technically reviewed by a software engineer and a statistician) .
  • Claude and Grok: UI prototyping, storytelling, and visual asset creation.
  • ChatGPT: research support and agricultural reference analysis.
  • Lovable: final presentation video production.

Offline Capabilities

  • Local storage of analyzed fields.
  • Technical report sharing.
  • Portuguese and English support.

projectDetails.name: Mission Mars Game
projectDetails.summary: Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer that lets a child run a Mars colony for eleven sols. Five resources — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — rise and fall in real time while the colony moves through 90-second days and nights. Twenty-five events, from dust storms and marsquakes to crew conflicts, appear in a Mission Log with four trade-off choices each, and ignoring one has its own consequence. Buildings have levels and build timers, research takes time, robots explore the surface and can break down, and a radio link to Houston answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way real deep-space communication does. Every event, site and term is tagged with the open NASA source behind it: DONKI space weather, OSDR life sciences, Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight and SCaN. Losing opens a science debriefing instead of a "game over", so failure becomes a lesson. Three difficulty modes let younger and older players train at their own pace. Mars is the hook; systems thinking is the lesson.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works. Mission Mars is a browser-based mission trainer where a child commands a Mars colony for eleven sols. The screen is a mission control center: a header with the mission clock and a day/night indicator, a COLONY RESOURCES panel with five live bars — water, oxygen, energy, food and materials — and a Mission Log that is the heart of the game. Every event appears there as a large Mars image, a timestamp, a short narrative and four big decision buttons. Time runs on a fixed cycle: 90 seconds of daylight and 90 seconds of night, three minutes per sol. Solar panels produce energy only in daylight, batteries carry the base through the night, and the crew keeps consuming water, oxygen and food the whole time. Twenty-five events are drawn at random and weighted toward pressure — 20% opportunities, 40% dilemmas, 40% crises — and every one of them has four choices with real trade-offs, hidden risks and a consequence if the player ignores the event for 60 seconds. Buildings have five levels and take time to build or upgrade. Ten research technologies reach three levels each and cost 30, 60 or 90 seconds per level. Robots with 100 hit points are built, sent to twenty real Martian sites such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Utopia Planitia and Olympus Mons, and can break down and be repaired or lost. A radio link to Houston costs energy and answers 15 to 20 seconds late, the way deep-space communication really works. Winning means surviving to sol 11 and returning to Earth; losing opens a science debriefing that explains the cause, what was learned and one tip for the next flight.

Benefits and intended impact. The game teaches systems thinking: saving energy can starve oxygen, a fast trip can cost a robot, and a party raises morale but eats the food stores. Children practice reading trends, comparing costs and asking for help before an emergency grows — with no penalty for failing, because every loss is explained. It also makes open NASA data a story kids can touch, and it runs in any browser on a school computer or tablet with nothing to install.

Tools and languages. React 19 with TypeScript and TanStack Start, styled with Tailwind CSS v4. The whole simulation is one pure reducer in a single engine file, so every tab reads the same state and every rule can be unit-tested; 106 automated tests cover resource flow, death rules, research, robots, exploration, radio support and difficulty. Event art is generated imagery, and the project was built and iterated with Lovable.

What makes it creative. Instead of a quiz or a score, failure is rewritten as a debriefing; instead of instant answers, the radio reproduces real signal latency; instead of a "correct" option, each choice is only better or worse for the colony you actually have.

Factors considered. Difficulty for ages 7–12 without unfair punishment, honest sourcing of NASA data, screen simplicity and large touch targets, three difficulty modes, and no names, faces or voices of anyone under 18 anywhere in the project.

The file also has a ≈250-word version, the NASA data links for those fields, and a pre-paste checklist. I ran the tests to confirm the numbers quoted: 106 passing, 25 events, 20 sites, 10 researches, 8 buildings, 15–20 s radio delay.

node.title: Selene Vector 301
node.excerpt: Landing on the Moon’s South Pole is tricky—one shadow can freeze a rover, and one hill can block Earth’s signal. We’re Selene Vector 301 (named after the Moon's NASA ID!), a team from Uberlândia building an intuitive, visual "cosmic GPS" to map sa...

projectDetails.name: Selene Vector 301 — Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary: Planning a landing at the Lunar South Pole is tough: low Sun angles cast long shadows, and nearby ridges can easily block Direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio signals. Existing tools like JPL Horizons and LRO Quickmap hold the answers, but jumping between raw ephemeris tables and heavy terrain maps makes rapid comparison slow. We built Selene Vector 301 to bring those pieces together in one interactive web app. By combining 360° LRO/LOLA horizon elevation profiles and a synchronized 3D lunar globe with NASA JPL Horizons Sun and Earth ephemeris data, the app tracks solar power potential, Earth’s libration wobble, and real-time Sunset and Earthset countdowns on an airless Moon. An AHP-TOPSIS ranking model—tuned to Canadian Space Agency (CSA) rover limits like a 15° max slope and shadow battery life—lets engineers, students, and space fans compare candidate craters or test launch delays in seconds.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

Trying to figure out if a spot near the lunar South Pole actually gets enough sunlight or a clear line of sight to Earth is surprisingly tedious. Normally, you have to cross-reference raw JPL Horizons ephemeris tables with massive elevation maps just to answer a basic question: how long until the Sun drops behind a crater rim?

We built Selene Vector 301 to put those answers on one screen. It combines a 360° polar horizon radar, a synchronized 3D lunar globe, and a multi-criteria site comparison tool so you can test landing sites and launch delays in seconds.

Under the hood, four pieces work together:

- 360° Terrain-Aware Horizon Map: We extracted 72-sector horizon elevation profiles (every 5° of azimuth) and local slope data from NASA LRO/LOLA and LROC Quickmap for 10 sites—nine South Pole Artemis III and CLPS candidates, plus Apollo 11 in Mare Tranquillitatis as a familiar equatorial baseline. Users can also enter any custom Moon coordinates to test spots outside our curated list using an analytical spherical horizon.

- 3D Lunar Orbital Twin: Built with Three.js, the 3D globe syncs real lunar surface imagery with the moving day/night terminator, Sun and Earth direction vectors, and timeline playback (1x, 5x, 20x) across a 336-hour (14-Earth-day) mission window.

- Airless Line-of-Sight Physics: Since the Moon has no atmosphere to bend light or radio signals, our math checks the exact step where the Sun or Earth clears the surrounding crater ridges. This captures Earth's figure-8 libration wobble near the horizon and powers live T-Minus Sunset and Earthset countdowns, <12h warnings, and rover battery State-of-Charge tracking.

- AHP-TOPSIS Ranking & Side-by-Side Comparison: An interactive multi-criteria scoring engine ranks sites by solar uptime, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio windows, longest continuous eclipse, ground slope, and distance to water-ice Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs). Users can pin up to two sites next to their active target in Compare Sites to inspect exact deltas and 336-hour timeline bars side by side.

Engineering Choices & Trade-Offs

Rendering raw 3D Digital Elevation Models straight in a browser usually bogs down or crashes regular laptops. Turning 3D crater rims into lightweight 1D horizon silhouettes—and pairing them with precomputed JPL Horizons ephemeris tables (TARGET='301', APPARENT=AIRLESS, 2-hour intervals)—kept recalculations instant at 60 FPS without waiting on a backend server.

We also wired real hardware constraints from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) lunar rover program into the logic, automatically flagging slopes steeper than 15° and tracking whether rover batteries survive long crater shadows. Because a trajectory engineer and a high school student look for very different things, we split the UI into two modes: Flight Director gives engineers raw Azimuth/Elevation telemetry, weight sliders, launch delay buttons (+7d, +14d, +30d), and CSV/JSON exports, while Explorer swaps heavy jargon for plain-English survival notes (such as -170°C lunar night cold-soak risks) and one-click guided experiments.

Why It Matters

Launch dates slip and lander specs change all the time. When a mission shifts by even a week, science teams chasing PSR water ice and engineering teams needing steady solar power and radio links have to re-check their options fast. Selene Vector 301 makes those trade-offs obvious at a glance—and gives teachers and space fans a straightforward way to see why landing on the lunar South Pole is so tricky.

Tech Stack & NASA Data

Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (WebGL), custom SVG polar charts, and Vitest, hosted on Vercel. Powered by NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data (TARGET='301', APPARENT=AIRLESS), NASA LRO/LOLA & LROC Quickmap elevation masks, NASA Moon Trek, and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) rover mobility parameters.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure

Super Intelligence (SI) tools were used during development to assist with TypeScript/Three.js code scaffolding, debugging, orbital geometry verification, and technical writing refinement. All ephemeris tables, horizon elevation masks, physics calculations, and live demo video/audio recordings were deterministically computed or recorded directly without AI-generated media.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Atlas | Stars & Beyond: preventing fire in microgravity environments
projectDetails.summary:
We are Team Stars & Beyond, driven by the mission to make space exploration safer and democratize access to scientific knowledge about how fire behaves beyond Earth.
To achieve this, we developed Atlas Stars & Beyond (Extinction Atlas), an interactive scientific intelligence platform that consolidates decades of microgravity combustion research from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. Atlas maps documented experiments across oxygen concentrations, atmospheric pressures, and gravity regimes, connecting researchers, students, and engineers to critical experimental evidence with full file- and row-level traceability.
By making existing evidence accessible while explicitly revealing where experimental data is missing, Atlas accelerates the investigation of fire prevention and suppression strategies for future space missions.
projectDetails.details:
Atlas Stars & Beyond is a scientific intelligence and visualization platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Flame in Freefall). Its purpose is to transform decades of microgravity combustion research into accessible, interactive, and actionable engineering knowledge.

The platform addresses the challenge of fragmented aerospace fire safety data by bringing together experimental records, deterministic physical calculations, multidimensional data visualization, and a real-time WebGL2 3D combustion solver within a unified analytical environment.

By combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), deterministic evidence rules implemented in Go, interactive dataset exploration, and real-time 3D visualization, Atlas enables researchers and engineers to investigate hypotheses across different spacecraft habitats and materials. Users can adjust environmental parameters—including gravity regimes, atmospheric pressure, and oxygen concentration—to assess experimental coverage, compare fire suppression strategies (such as CO₂ and helium), and examine scientific evidence with full source traceability down to the original file and row.

Beyond retrieving existing literature, Atlas functions as a discovery engine for space fire safety. Through interactive 3D test maps, evidence knowledge graphs, flammability limit visualizations, and the Next Fire gap-analysis queue, the platform reveals underexplored physical conditions—such as partial gravity on the Moon and Mars—and identifies promising directions for future experiments.

By bridging historical NASA datasets with interactive simulation and evidence-grounded AI synthesis, Atlas accelerates scientific investigation and supports the development of safer fire prevention and suppression protocols for future long-duration space missions.

Repository Access – GitHub

Organization: https://github.com/stars-beyond

Backend & Data Pipelines: https://github.com/stars-beyond/atlas-fire-extintion-backend

Frontend & 3D Lab: https://github.com/stars-beyond/atlas-fire-extintion-front

The Problem

Over several decades, NASA has conducted thousands of experiments and published extensive research on fire behavior in microgravity environments, including 24 combustion investigations available through the NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system.

Despite the critical importance of this knowledge for crewed mission safety, the sheer volume of research—and its distribution across heterogeneous tables, PDFs, and technical reports—makes it difficult to retrieve, interpret, and compare experimental findings.

Researchers and engineers must spend considerable time searching and cross-referencing studies to understand how different materials, atmospheric compositions, and ventilation conditions influence combustion. This fragmentation also makes it harder to identify patterns, compare experimental outcomes, and recognize scientific gaps, limiting the ability of existing research to guide future investigations.

The Gap

Advances in artificial intelligence, data engineering, and real-time browser-based simulation create new opportunities to explore large scientific archives. However, a generic chatbot built on top of PDFs is not sufficient for aerospace fire safety: it cannot reliably guarantee source traceability, distinguish measured outcomes from extrapolations, or reveal where experimental evidence is simply unavailable.

For example, future lunar habitats are expected to operate at oxygen concentrations of 30% or higher and atmospheric pressures of 10.2 psi or lower. However, solid-material combustion tests in the NASA PSI archive were conducted at oxygen concentrations ranging from 13.6% to 22.2%, near 1 atm. Furthermore, PSI contains no combustion tests conducted under partial-gravity conditions representative of the Moon or Mars.

This reveals a critical gap between the availability of historical experimental data and the ability to analyze it systematically—making both existing evidence and missing experimental conditions immediately visible.

Our Solution

Atlas is an integrated platform that enables users to investigate, analyze, compare, and explore fire behavior across diverse space environments.

Its backend consolidates 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations, comprising 1,972 tabulated tests (1,153 of which include oxygen and pressure metadata), a hybrid PostgreSQL + pgvector search index, a deterministic evidence engine implemented in Go, and a RAG pipeline containing 18,436 indexed document chunks from NASA PSI and NTRS.

Rather than generating unsupported risk scores, Atlas computes a transparent, four-level Evidence Verdict for each scenario:

Measured: Experimental tests are available under the target atmospheric conditions (±2% O₂ and ±20% pressure) and gravity regime.

Bounded: No tests exist at the exact gravity level, but experimental data is available at both 0 g and 1 g under comparable atmospheric conditions, providing bounds for analysis.

One-sided: Experimental tests are available at only one of the two reference gravity levels (0 g or 1 g).

Terra Incognita: No NASA PSI experimental tests are available under the target atmospheric conditions.

When experimental evidence exists (Measured), Atlas reports empirical outcomes directly, such as the number of samples that burned completely, self-extinguished, or failed to ignite.

When experimental evidence is unavailable, the platform does not fabricate probabilities or unsupported conclusions. Instead, it clearly communicates the limits of existing knowledge: AI generates the explanation, while the underlying data determines the verdict.

How It Works

When users access Atlas, they can explore the platform through a guided configurator (Test Drive) or navigate directly to its analytical modules.

1. Habitat & Free-Text Inference

Users can select from six preset environments: Space Station, Lunar Base, Rover, Mars Habitat, Spacesuit, or Earth Room. Alternatively, they can manually adjust oxygen concentration, atmospheric pressure, and gravity.

A natural-language input—for example, "lunar rover with 34% oxygen and Nomex seats"—automatically extracts the relevant parameters and configures the Test Drive.

2. Material Selection

Users select a fuel family and material, including cotton fabric, acrylic/PMMA, Nomex, silicone, liquid fuels, or gases. For each selection, Atlas displays the exact number of NASA experiments available.

3. Test Drive & Interactive 3D Stage

Clicking Light activates the flame in the 3D environment and reveals the four-level Evidence Verdict.

Three tabs guide the investigation:

Evidence: Displays the verdict, empirical rates, and the closest matching NASA experiments. Selecting a test opens its exact source file, row, and original experimental record.

Extinguish: Allows users to release CO₂ or helium, reduce cabin ventilation, and examine FLEX droplet burn-rate regressions and extinction behavior.

Ask: Provides a natural-language scientific Q&A interface powered by RAG, featuring Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming, clickable numbered citations, rendered LaTeX equations, and source page references.

4. Multi-View Stage

The main visualization area seamlessly switches between multiple analytical environments:

3D Combustion Lab (lab3d): A real-time WebGL2 3D combustion visualization.

3D Test Map: Maps experimental coverage across gravity regimes, with each floor representing a different gravity condition and visibly exposing empty Moon and Mars floors.

Knowledge Graph: Connects the selected scenario to related experiments, revealing relationships between experimental conditions and available evidence.

Flammability Limits: Provides an interactive view of flammability boundaries.

Thermal Camera: An ONNX-powered prediction tool for PMMA film flame spread.

5. Technical Dossier, Dashboard & Mission Story

Atlas also provides tools for deeper scientific investigation and reporting:

Technical Dossier: Generates downloadable Markdown or printable reports containing relevant technical findings.

Scientific Intelligence Dashboard: Allows users to build custom scatter plots, bar charts, and histograms using 15 API datasets, with CSV/PNG export and row-level drill-down.

Investigation Comparison: Enables side-by-side analysis of different experimental investigations.

Next Fire: Presents a gap-analysis queue highlighting opportunities for future experiments.

Mission Story: Offers interactive 3D mission scenarios powered by precomputed trajectories from mission-fire-engine.

Implementation Details

DATA PIPELINES

  • Data ingestion and preparation are handled by modular Python pipelines (brain/atlas/ and ml/):
  • Sources (psi.py): Retrieves combustion investigations, catalogs, and experimental tables from NASA PSI, with local caching and an offline seed fallback (data/seed/).
  • Adapters (adapters.py): Uses table-specific normalization adapters to map heterogeneous experimental records into a unified schema while preserving original file names, line numbers, raw records, and explicit flags for inferred fields (such as assuming a cabin pressure of 1 atm for solid-material tests when the original value is not specified).
  • Documents & Embeddings (docs.py, rag-index): Extracts text from NASA PSI PDFs and challenge resources using PyMuPDF and pypdf. Atlas documents are embedded locally using fastembed, while the RAG collection (flame_freefall_2026_v6) indexes 18,436 chunks from NASA PSI and NTRS in PostgreSQL + pgvector using OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large.
  • ML & Thermal Models (ml/): Includes cross-validated linear regression for FLEX droplet burn rates, as well as scripts (spread_table.py, export_thermal.py) that export Atlas-MachineL neural models into lookup grids and ONNX networks for predicting PMMA film spread speed and surface temperature under 0 g conditions.

BACKEND

  • API (api/, Go 1.25): A domain-driven Go service covering evidence, catalog, flammability, prediction, Q&A, search, datasets, and simulation modules. Connected to PostgreSQL via pgx/v5, it computes all deterministic verdicts, investigation rankings, empirical burn rates, flammability assessments, knowledge graph topologies, dataset charts, and hybrid RRF search. It also proxies SSE-based Q&A streaming (/api/ask/stream) to the RAG service, with graceful fallback to Anthropic Claude, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, or extractive mode when API keys are unavailable.
  • RAG Service (rag/, Python + FastAPI): Runs the team's rag-Carlin pipeline, adapted to PostgreSQL + pgvector (atlas_pg/), delivering evidence-grounded answers with numbered citations, reviewed equations, and conversation history.
  • Embedder Service (brain/, Python + FastAPI): Generates query embeddings through fastembed and executes ONNX-based thermal camera inference using onnxruntime.

FRONTEND

  • Stack: Built with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, Recharts, react-markdown, remark-math, and rehype-katex. The architecture is organized by feature (configurator, stage, ask, findings, investigations, next-fire, dashboard, and story), with no scientific computations performed on the client side. Every verdict, ranking, and chart calculation is handled by the Go API.
  • 3D Combustion Lab (public/lab3d/): A real-time WebGL2 GPU combustion solver embedded through an iframe bridge (bridge.js) that receives physical constants and scenario parameters from /api/sim/config. The model is an uncalibrated study visualization, clearly labeled as such in the interface and kept strictly independent of the Evidence Verdict.
  • Deployment: Published as static assets on Cloudflare Workers & Pages (wrangler.jsonc), communicating with the Go API over HTTPS/CORS.

INFRASTRUCTURE

  • Containerization: Orchestrated through Docker and Docker Compose (docker-compose.yml), running the database (pgvector/pgvector:pg16), embedder, ingestion pipeline (with fingerprint-based atomic schema swapping from atlas_build to atlas), RAG indexing, RAG service, and API.
  • Production: Deployed behind Nginx and Cloudflare, with automated daily NASA PSI data refreshes through deploy/refresh.sh.

Impact

Atlas transforms complex, fragmented aerospace combustion research into accessible, traceable, and actionable engineering intelligence. By enabling researchers and engineers to compare experiments, visualize evidence coverage, identify knowledge gaps, and inspect original experimental records, the platform makes decades of NASA microgravity research more accessible and useful for future investigations.

Its scientific contribution goes beyond organizing existing data. Atlas helps reveal what current experiments can—and cannot—support, highlights underexplored conditions such as partial gravity and elevated-oxygen exploration atmospheres, and helps prioritize future experiments that could address the most significant knowledge gaps.

In practical terms, this means researchers can investigate scenarios more efficiently, identify where additional testing is needed, and make better-informed decisions when designing future experiments and fire suppression strategies.

The platform also has potential applications beyond aerospace research, including terrestrial environments such as enclosed battery rooms under 1 g conditions. By maintaining a clear distinction between experimental evidence, deterministic analysis, and exploratory simulation, Atlas supports evidence-based technical investigation without presenting itself as a flight-safety certification system.

Ultimately, Atlas helps turn fragmented scientific archives into a practical foundation for identifying risks, directing research efforts, and advancing fire safety in environments where reliable experimental knowledge is essential.

Conclusion

Atlas Stars & Beyond brings together deterministic engineering logic, multidimensional data visualization, real-time 3D simulation, and evidence-grounded AI to bridge the gap between historical microgravity combustion research and the challenges of future space exploration.

By making both experimental findings and their limitations visible, Atlas transforms how researchers access, interpret, and investigate scientific evidence. Its approach empowers a new generation of researchers and engineers to identify knowledge gaps, guide future experiments, and contribute to the development of safer habitats beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: GUARUBA
projectDetails.summary:
We developed GUARUBA, an enterprise environmental intelligence and deterministic aerial simulation platform dedicated to protecting the Brazilian Cerrado, calibrated with territorial data from Araguari, Minas Gerais.

Seasonal wildfires and habitat degradation pose severe threats to the Cerrado, yet local conservationists often lack access to early-warning risk systems or the budget for costly physical drone trials. GUARUBA solves this by unifying official satellite data (NASA POWER meteorological telemetry and INPE thermal observations) with an in-browser spatial physics engine. Operators can compute calibrated wildfire risk indices, track historical hotspots, and safely simulate autonomous tactical drone missions—including tethered firefighting UAVs with ground water hoses—at zero risk and zero operational cost.

GUARUBA is vital because it bridges advanced aerospace simulation with grassroots ecological defense, replacing reactive disaster response with proactive, scientifically verified, and data-backed environmental stewardship.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

GUARUBA is an enterprise-grade environmental management and aerial operations platform designed specifically for the protection of the Brazilian Cerrado (calibrated using real-world territorial data from Araguari, Minas Gerais).

The platform operates through three synchronized layers:

1. Environmental Data Ingestion & Risk Screening: It connects to official public satellite feeds—including NASA POWER (meteorological telemetry: temperature, relative humidity, wind speed) and INPE BDQueimadas (thermal satellite observations)—to compute operational fire risk indices (such as the Fosberg Fire Weather Index) and map spatial recurrence grids across registered rural and conservation properties.

2. Deterministic Drone & Fleet Simulator: It features an in-browser spatial physics engine built with MapLibre and Turf.js that deterministically simulates autonomous drone missions, battery degradation, and flight vectors across five distinct UAV profiles. This includes specialized support for UAVI (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle for Fire Intervention) equipped with ground-fed water hoses and continuous power tethers.

3. Multi-Tenant Enterprise Governance: The platform enforces strict organization-level data isolation via database-level Row-Level Security (RLS) and cryptographic audit trails, managing environmental assets, incident logs, maintenance work orders, and commercial licensing.

A cornerstone rule of GUARUBA is strict data integrity: every single data point is permanently labeled as REAL (official provenance), SIMULATED (virtual flight physics), or DERIVED (computed risk models), ensuring that simulated telemetry is never confused with physical sensor ground truth.

---

2. What benefits does it have?

* Early Fire Risk Triage: By combining real-time meteorological variables with historical thermal hotspots, property managers and civil defense teams can anticipate wildfire outbreaks hours before smoke is visible.

* Safe, Cost-Free Aerial Planning: Operators can test flight corridors, battery thresholds, and water-drop approaches in a virtual sandbox, eliminating the high costs, legal liabilities, and crash risks of physical flight tests.

* Data Provenance & Auditability: Unlike generic dashboards, every boundary revision, weather snapshot, and incident triage has an immutable timestamp and cryptographic origin, providing audit-grade compliance reports for ESG certifications and environmental authorities.

* Instant Educational Accessibility: An air-gapped, zero-backend demonstration mode (`/demo`) allows schools, researchers, and field agents to interact with the full suite of tools without risking production databases or incurring API costs.

---

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The Brazilian Cerrado is one of the most biodiverse yet critically threatened biomes on Earth, frequently ravaged by seasonal wildfires and land clearing. GUARUBA's intended impact is to bridge the gap between complex aerospace technology and local conservation efforts.

By providing rural cooperatives, agroforestry ventures, and environmental monitors with automated risk intelligence and realistic tactical drone simulation, GUARUBA democratizes aerial surveillance and fire-suppression planning. It shifts environmental stewardship from reactive disaster management to proactive, data-backed ecological defense.

---

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

* Core Languages & Architecture: Full-stack TypeScript running on React 19 and TanStack Start v1 (leveraging Server-Side Rendering and Edge server functions).

* Mapping & Spatial Mathematics: MapLibre GL for vector mapping and Turf.js for geodesic calculations, geodesic flight arcs, and spatial clustering; PostGIS within PostgreSQL for spatial boundary validation and WGS84 area recalculation.

* Database, Auth & Cloud Backend: Lovable Cloud (managed PostgreSQL with PostGIS, Row-Level Security policies, database triggers, and transactional RPC functions).

* Styling & UI Components: Tailwind CSS v4 paired with shadcn/ui and Lucide icons, adhering to accessible semantic design tokens.

* External APIs & Real Data Feeds:

* NASA POWER API (meteorological parameters)

* INPE BDQueimadas (satellite thermal anomalies)

* IBGE Web Feature Services (municipal and territorial administrative borders)

* Artificial Intelligence: Integrated AI Gateway for structured environmental recommendation analysis, historical anomaly clustering, and contextual operational assistance.

* Quality Assurance & Verification: Automated testing with Vitest (over 150 regression test suites) and end-to-end browser verification via Playwright.

---

5. How is your project creative?

Culturally Grounded Brazilian Identity: Rather than adopting generic dark-mode, neon-purple "AI" tropes, GUARUBA's visual identity draws inspiration from the native Golden Parakeet (Guaruba guarouba*) and the natural palette of the Cerrado (Earthy Terracotta, Cerrado Gold, Deep Forest Green, and Clean Slate), making high-tech software feel native to Brazilian conservationists.

* Realistic Tethered Firefighting Drone Modeling (UAVI): Instead of romanticizing autonomous sci-fi drones with unrealistic multi-hour flight times, GUARUBA innovates by modeling a tethered system with realistic ground-based fluid hoses and power umbilicals, reflecting real-world engineering constraints for active fire suppression.

* The "Zero False Evidence" Principle: GUARUBA treats thermal satellite pixels as unverified heat anomalies rather than automatic "confirmed fires." A fire is only confirmed after human ground validation, preventing automated alarmist panic and maintaining scientific credibility.

---

6. What factors did your team consider?

* Ethical AI & Boundary Between Simulation and Reality: We established an inviolable rule that synthetic drone telemetry or browser-generated data can never enter production environmental databases or masquerade as real telemetry.

* Multi-Tenant Data Privacy: Corporate and farm boundaries must remain strictly confidential. Isolation is enforced through PostgreSQL Row-Level Security at the database core, ensuring no tenant can ever inspect another's flight plans or compliance reports.

* Low-Bandwidth & Field Feasibility: Because rural areas in the Cerrado often suffer from unstable cellular connectivity, the system emphasizes client-side caching, deterministic mathematical simulation, and lightweight vector tiles to remain responsive even on modest devices.

* Extensibility & Safety Governance: Equipment pairing (e.g., docking drones with battery charging stations) requires verified technical interface ratings and documented maintenance logs, reflecting real-world aviation safety standards.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.summary:
Earth System Detective is an interactive web application developed by Team Startec – SESI Araguari for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge Earth System Trend Detective.

The platform uses real, open NASA POWER data to help users investigate environmental changes across different locations and time periods. Users can select environmental variables, explore maps and time-series charts, examine statistical indicators such as Mann–Kendall and Sen's slope, and download reports for further analysis.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming complex Earth system data into accessible visualizations and evidence-based investigations. It is designed to support students, educators and anyone interested in understanding environmental patterns.

By making scientific data easier to explore and interpret, Earth System Detective promotes scientific curiosity, environmental awareness and informed discussions about our changing planet. The MODIS NDVI module is planned for future expansion and is not yet validated with official imported data.
projectDetails.details:
Earth System Detective, developed by Team Startec – SESI Araguari, is an interactive web application designed to make Earth observation data more accessible and understandable.

The platform allows users to investigate environmental changes by selecting variables, geographic locations and time periods. It presents information through interactive maps, time-series charts and statistical indicators, including the Mann–Kendall test, Sen's slope and linear regression. Users can also download reports in CSV, TXT and PDF formats for further analysis.

The current application uses real, open NASA POWER data, including relative humidity and evapotranspiration variables. These resources help users explore environmental patterns and investigate whether changes over time show statistically significant trends.

The project was developed as a web application using Lovable and Lovable Cloud, with AI-assisted tools supporting code generation, interface development, debugging and testing. ChatGPT also supported scientific research, statistical methodology, documentation and project planning.

Our creative approach is to transform complex scientific datasets into an interactive investigation experience. Instead of simply displaying environmental information, the application encourages users to ask questions, select locations, explore evidence and interpret results.

The intended impact is to support environmental education, scientific literacy and informed discussions about changes in Earth's systems, particularly among students, educators and communities.

Throughout development, we considered scientific validity, data quality, traceability, spatial and temporal resolution, accessibility, transparency and responsible interpretation of statistical results. We also ensured that simulated information would not be presented as real NASA observations.

The MODIS NDVI module is part of our planned expansion. Its interface and processing workflow have been developed, but official MODIS files have not yet been imported and validated. Therefore, NDVI results are not currently presented as verified scientific findings.
