projectDetails.name: Stellar Pixel
projectDetails.summary:
Stellar Pixel is an interactive pixel-art lunar base management game built in Unity WebGL that turns real space-weather data into playable survival decisions. Players command a 4-astronaut lunar outpost over a 30-day mission, building and wiring power, water, food, and oxygen grids while keeping cumulative radiation exposure below NASA’s 250 mSv safety limit.

Using open datasets from NASA DONKI, Curiosity RAD, LRO CRaTER, and Apollo archives, the game simulates historical solar flares and geomagnetic storms such as the August 1972 Superstorm and the May 2024 G5 storm. When alerts arrive, players must manage resource trade-offs such as spending water and power on emergency shielding or upgrading the Habitat against higher daily upkeep. By turning real space radiation and life-support data into a clear browser game, Stellar Pixel helps students and the public understand the survival challenges astronauts face on the Moon.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

Stellar Pixel is a 2D pixel-art lunar base management game that runs directly in the browser. You manage a 4-astronaut outpost over a 30-day mission, keeping life support running while dealing with real space weather.

  • Building & Wiring Grids: You earn Lunar Credits by completing missions and surviving events, then spend them in the Shop ([T]) to place 7 different modules: Solar Panels, Water Generators, Greenhouses, Oxygen Generators, Power Storage, and Water Tanks. To automate resource collection and expand your reserves, you press [C] to drag power cables and water pipes between generators and storage tanks.
  • Daily Life Support: Every lunar day, the central Habitat ([H]) consumes Energy, Water, Food, and Oxygen based on your crew size. You can upgrade the Habitat across 5 levels to raise radiation protection (from 0% up to 70%) and boost production, though higher levels also increase daily energy and water upkeep.
  • Radiation & Solar Storms: A 30-day dosimeter on the top HUD tracks the crew's cumulative radiation against NASA's 250 mSv limit, starting from the Moon's natural 1.37 mSv/day background radiation. When a solar flare or coronal mass ejection is detected, you get a short warning window to stock up on water and power before deciding how to respond—such as pumping water into hydrogen-rich wall shields that block up to 85% of incoming solar protons.


How We Used NASA & Space Agency Open Data

We used open spaceflight datasets to set the numbers, hazards, and survival mechanics in the game:

  1. NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): Used to model real solar flares and coronal mass ejections, including the September 2017 X9.3 Solar Flare and the May 2024 G5 Geomagnetic Storm.
  2. NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) CRaTER: Used for the Moon's baseline radiation rate of 1.37 mSv/day from galactic cosmic rays.
  3. NASA Curiosity RAD & Apollo Records: Used to scale Solar Particle Event radiation spikes, including the August 1972 Solar Superstorm (350+ mSv unshielded) that happened between Apollo 16 and Apollo 17.
  4. NASA ECLSS & Artemis Base Camp Concepts: Used to balance daily crew water, oxygen, food, and power consumption, showing why water is both a daily necessity and a primary radiation shield on the Moon.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Making Radiation Visible: Space radiation numbers like millisieverts (mSv) and solar proton events are hard to picture from a textbook. Turning them into a resource-management problem helps players see how quickly exposure adds up without an atmosphere or magnetic field.
  • Showing Real Engineering Trade-Offs: There is no single upgrade that solves everything. Raising Habitat shielding costs more power and water every day, and using water reserves to block solar storms leaves less water for oxygen production and crops.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Engine & Code: Unity and C#.
  • Art: Aseprite (all sprites, modules, icons, and animations drawn pixel by pixel).
  • Web: Unity WebGL, HTML5, Tailwind CSS and JavaScript.
  • Reference Data: NASA DONKI, NASA-STD-3001 radiation limits, Curiosity RAD, NASA LRO CRaTER lunar dosimetry data.

projectDetails.name: Where the fire data stops
projectDetails.summary: NASA burned 2,299 samples in microgravity, and none of the solid ones in the air a Moon base will breathe. We unified the combustion tables of NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository into one citable dataset (2,299 tests from 13 investigations, 24,905 measurements, a source on every row), measured that evidence gap, and built a dashboard that shows where tests exist, what they say, and which test is missing. We also recovered outcomes the published tables do not carry: 552 tests labeled from experiment script logs. A deterministic video pipeline, with no language model and no generic OCR, read the telemetry burned into 1,248,016 frames of 94 BASS-II videos and joined 86 accepted tests to the test matrix, recovering the fan sequence and how each test ended.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. A dashboard with four views: coverage and gaps (chamber oxygen versus pressure of every test against three target atmospheres), what the evidence says (gas flame sustainment by oxygen band), video to data (fan, air speed and radiometer read from BASS-II video overlays), and the 24 PSI combustion investigations side by side with pillar, fuels, ranges and DOI. An experimental SI agent at /ask/ answers questions from precomputed dataset facts and cites PSI ID and DOI.

How it works. A deterministic Python pipeline harmonizes 32 source tables with curated column maps, converts to SI units, and writes one row per test with PSI ID, DOI, file, sheet and row. Nothing is imputed. 99.7% of cells are filled where the source reports the field (4,702 of 4,714). 39 automated tests. Code and docs: https://github.com/PabloBispo/still-blue-flame. Dataset and 13 annotated clips: https://github.com/PabloBispo/still-blue-flame/releases/tag/v1.0.0

Video pipeline. Solid fuels are the habitat materials, and 250 of the 380 solid-fuel tests in PSI are BASS and BASS-II. BASS-II videos carry telemetry burned into every frame. Our reader learns the digit templates from each video itself (the clock's seconds digit changes at 1 Hz and labels the samples), classifies each character by normalized correlation (minimum 0.80, otherwise null, nothing interpolated), and checks itself: the clock must follow the expected sequence in at least 98% of frames. 86 of 94 files pass. It runs at 245 frames per second on 2 cores.

Findings (descriptive). 0 of 261 solid-fuel tests with reported oxygen reach 30% O2; the highest is 22.7%, none at 70 kPa or less. The closest solid test to the exploration atmosphere (34% O2, 56.5 kPa) is 11.3 O2 points and 41.8 kPa away. In ACME CFI-G, 0 of 64 normal gas flames sustained below 30% O2; in ACME Flame Design, 3 of 58. In BASS-II video, 63 of 86 flames went out at a steady fan setting, 9 were blown out by the operator, 10 recordings stop first, 4 show no radiometer fall.

Limits. Gas flames on a spherical burner are not habitat materials. Counts are descriptive. 97 of 244 BASS-II video files were read; readings were checked by eye on 5 videos. The flame mask illustrates the method and is not a validated measurement. Dashboard charts of video still show the first 16 videos; the release has all 86. PSI holds no partial-gravity test. The SI agent was tested on few questions and can make mistakes.

Benefit. It points to the missing experiment: a solid material burned at 30% to 34% O2 and 57 to 70 kPa.

Tools. Python, pandas, pyarrow, OpenCV, Plotly, uv, pytest, Vercel, GitHub.

projectDetails.name: CosmoSPHERE
projectDetails.summary:
CosmoSPHERE is an interactive web platform that transforms real observations from NASA's SPHEREx space telescope into an accessible exploration of the infrared sky across time and wavelength.
SPHEREx collects an extraordinary amount of scientific information about the universe, but interpreting multidimensional astronomical observations can be challenging for students, educators, and people without specialized training.
Our solution allows users to explore celestial objects through an interactive sky map or astronomical coordinates, visualize observations from different epochs, and investigate infrared spectra across six SPHEREx detector bands covering approximately 0.75–5.0 micrometers.
CosmoSPHERE retrieves authentic observations from NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), processes astronomical FITS images, aligns observations onto a common celestial grid, generates scientifically grounded false-color visualizations, and extracts spectral measurements through multi-epoch photometry.
An interactive timeline helps users explore different observation periods, while spectral charts reveal the infrared characteristics of selected celestial targets. Preprocessed observations of selected objects provide a faster exploration experience.
By combining real NASA data, scientific computing, and interactive visualization, CosmoSPHERE makes infrared astronomy more approachable and encourages scientific curiosity, education, and exploration.
projectDetails.details:
CosmoSPHERE is an interactive scientific exploration platform that transforms real observations from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope into accessible, visually engaging experiences. The platform combines an interactive frontend with a scientific processing backend. When users select astronomical coordinates or a target, the backend queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), retrieves specific FITS image regions, spatially aligns observations onto a common celestial grid, normalizes infrared measurements into false-color image layers across six detector bands, organizes them into chronological temporal sequences, and performs multi-epoch forced photometry for spectral analysis.

The benefits provided by CosmoSPHERE are:

  • Educational Accessibility: Helps students, educators, and astronomy enthusiasts explore real infrared observations through an approachable interface.
  • Scientific Literacy: Encourages users to understand how astronomical observations are collected, processed, and interpreted.
  • Multidimensional Understanding: Combines spatial, temporal, and spectral information to investigate targets from unique perspectives.
  • Efficient Data Processing: Utilizes targeted data retrieval, asynchronous computation, and caching to minimize unnecessary processing.
  • Open-Source Development: Supports transparency, technical learning, and future collaboration.

The primary objective is to reduce barriers between advanced astronomical research data and the public. By making authentic NASA observations approachable in a web-based environment, the project aims to inspire educational demonstrations, independent learning, astronomy outreach, and introductory scientific investigation, demonstrating how open data and software engineering can make the universe more accessible.

The tools the we used to develop the system were, for each topic:

  • Frontend Development: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, CSS Modules, WebGL, Aladin Lite, and Plotly.js.
  • Backend Development: Node.js, Express, Python, FastAPI, and Pydantic.
  • Scientific Computing & Data: Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, NumPy, SciPy, Reproject, Pillow, FITS processing, WCS transformations, and multi-epoch photometric analysis.
  • Data Sources: NASA SPHEREx mission observations and NASA/IPAC IRSA services.
  • Infrastructure & Deployment: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Docker, Docker Compose, Traefik, Portainer, Cloudflare, GitHub Actions, Git, and GitHub. (No specialized physical hardware is required beyond a modern web browser and internet connection).

CosmoSPHERE’s creativity lies in transforming complex, multidimensional astronomical datasets into an intuitive, interactive exploration experience. Instead of presenting observations solely as static files or numerical tables, it integrates spatial, temporal, and spectral exploration into a single environment, translating invisible infrared wavelengths into meaningful false-color representations without requiring specialized software.

The factors that we considered for this project were:

  • Scientific Integrity: Ensuring the use of authentic NASA data with a clear distinction between measured information and false-color visualization.
  • Accuracy and Comparability: Implementing consistent celestial grids, image reprojection, and controlled normalization for multi-epoch comparisons.
  • Performance and Scalability: Utilizing targeted data retrieval, caching, and asynchronous processing to handle large datasets.
  • Accessibility and User Experience: Designing intuitive navigation and controls that do not require advanced programming knowledge.
  • Transparency and Reproducibility: Providing open-source code, technical documentation, and clear API contracts.
  • Scientific Limitations: Acknowledging that the implementation is primarily for exploration and educational visualization, thereby communicating results responsibly.

projectDetails.summary:
AstroLab – Learning Through Space Exploration

AstroLab is an interactive 3D educational game developed using Unity and Blender that transforms learning about space exploration into an immersive experience. Players take on the role of astronauts and experience different stages of a space mission: training on Earth, traveling through space, landing on the Moon, and surviving at a lunar base. Throughout the journey, they must solve challenges, repair equipment, manage resources, and prepare the base for the arrival of a new crew.

The project addresses the challenge of making science education more accessible, engaging, and practical, especially for children and young learners. Through gamification, players explore concepts related to astronomy, physics, technology, and sustainability while developing critical thinking, planning, and problem-solving skills.

AstroLab is important because it connects space science with interactive learning, inspiring curiosity and encouraging interest in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM). More than just a game, AstroLab demonstrates that education can be an adventure, inspiring future generations to explore knowledge and imagine their role in the future of space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
AstroLab – Project Details

AstroLab is an immersive 3D educational game designed to make space exploration and scientific learning more accessible, interactive, and engaging, especially for children and young students. By combining storytelling, realistic space missions, and gamification, the project transforms complex scientific concepts into exciting, hands-on learning experiences.

How Does It Work?

Players take on the role of astronauts preparing for a mission to the Moon. Their journey begins on Earth, where they complete training activities inspired by real astronaut preparation programs. After training, players board a spacecraft, travel through space, experience a cinematic lunar landing, and begin their mission at a lunar research base.

Once on the Moon, players face challenges involving survival, resource management, equipment maintenance, and scientific exploration. They must monitor oxygen and energy supplies, repair solar panels, restore essential systems, and prepare the lunar base for the arrival of another crew.

Each challenge encourages players to apply scientific knowledge, logical reasoning, and problem-solving skills in an interactive environment.

Technology and Development

AstroLab is developed using Unity 6 and C# for gameplay mechanics, interactions, animations, and mission systems. Blender and Python are used for 3D modeling and procedural asset creation. The project also utilizes Unity's Universal Render Pipeline (URP), Cinemachine, custom shaders, and visual effects to create a stylized yet believable space environment.

Git and GitHub support collaborative development, allowing team members to work independently on different systems while maintaining a unified project.

Creativity and Innovation

What makes AstroLab unique is its combination of educational content with immersive gameplay. Rather than simply presenting scientific information, the game allows students to experience the challenges of space exploration through decision-making, experimentation, and interactive missions.

Its cartoon-realistic visual style balances scientific inspiration with an accessible and engaging design for younger audiences.

Benefits and Intended Impact

AstroLab aims to stimulate curiosity about astronomy, physics, engineering, technology, and space exploration while strengthening critical thinking, teamwork, creativity, and problem-solving abilities.

Our team prioritizes educational accessibility, scientific relevance, intuitive gameplay, visual consistency, and technical performance.

Ultimately, AstroLab seeks to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers by demonstrating that learning science can be as exciting as exploring another world.

projectDetails.name: Skybrew
projectDetails.summary:
SPHEREx, NASA's all-sky infrared survey, images the entire sky every six months in 102 wavelength bands. Asteroids, comets, nearby stars and brown dwarfs reveal themselves by shifting position between exposures, but the volume of data is too large for a few specialists to inspect.
SkyBrew bridges citizen science and professional astronomy through a progressive dual-layer architecture. For curious beginners, SkyBrew abstracts complex physics into guided workflows. Users can hunt for asteroids, brown dwarfs, or variable stars using intent-based automated band stacking and time-lapse flipbooks, while learning how to identify celestial objects in images through interactive quizzes. In Professional mode, astronomers choose a field by typing coordinates or by navigating an interactive sky map, pick the infrared detectors, compare the images with the Gaia DR3 catalog, and export a candidate report with its position and time. Every search has its own link, so it can be shared or embedded in other websites. To demonstrate the tool, SkyBrew includes instant one-click benchmarks for NASA-suggested test targets (WISE 0855, Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis).
projectDetails.details:
What it does & how it works

SkyBrew helps people spot changes in the sky by playing real SPHEREx images of the same region in sequence. It retrieves Level-2 images and observation metadata from NASA/IPAC IRSA, checks which exposures can be compared, and aligns them by sky coordinates before playback.

  • Citizen Science Mode: Volunteers select a target category and receive a randomly sampled sky field. SkyBrew automatically configures the appropriate detector bands for that goal and retrieves images with overlapping coverage to build a time-lapse blink sequence. Users can mark candidate objects directly on the blinking viewer, supported by interactive tutorials and a quiz that introduce moving objects, variable brightness, known sources, and detector artifacts. 
  • Professional Mode: Users can enter right ascension and declination, choose a field size and select one or more infrared detectors (D1–D6). An Aladin Lite sky map supports navigation. The viewer provides blink sequences, combinations of overlapping detector images, temporal stacking and subtraction, quick-look spectral graphs, catalog markers, quality flags and an adjustable WISE reference image. Users can also browse the 102 nominal channels of a separate SPHEREx all-sky visual map. Search coordinates, field size and detector selection can be shared in a URL or opened in an iframe.

Benefits

  • Goal-Oriented Infrared Presets: Abstracts complex 102-band near-infrared physics into goal-oriented presets (Asteroids, Brown Dwarfs, Variable Stars), enabling non-experts to analyze multi-spectral data without manual channel management.
  • Training with real examples: Tutorials and a quiz teach volunteers what to examine and how to check artifacts and quality flags before reporting a candidate.
  • Stable blink sequences: SkyBrew groups exposures by shared coverage and places their FITS images on a common sky-coordinate grid, making changes easier to see across frames.
  • Spectral exploration: Professionals can browse 102 nominal channels in the time-combined SPHEREx DR1 sky map. From loaded Level-2 exposures, they can also plot a quick-look spectrum at a selected position or compare bright-pixel signal across wavelengths in the whole field. 
  • Temporal comparisons: Professionals can stack selected exposures from one detector using inverse-variance weights or subtract two aligned images. When both images provide suitable ePSF models, subtraction can optionally match their central point-spread functions. 
  • WISE reference imagery: An adjustable AllWISE infrared image can be overlaid on the professional sky map and image viewer to compare SPHEREx with an earlier survey. It is aligned by sky coordinates but was observed at different times and wavelengths.
  • Reference markers: Gaia DR3, AllWISE and 2MASS catalog positions, along with predicted positions of known Solar System objects from IMCCE SkyBoT, can be displayed over the images. This eliminates user confusion, prevents redundant tagging of established targets, and directs volunteer screening toward genuine candidate discoveries.
  • Image-quality inspection: Users can highlight pixels flagged for caution or lacking usable data and inspect the original flags for individual detector images.
  • Interactive Multi-Candidate Tagging: Users mark candidate objects directly on the time-lapse frames. Each candidate receives its own persistent identifier, so several targets in the same field can be followed across the sequence without their marks being mixed up and their recorded information can be also kept separate. 
  • Sub-Pixel Alignment: A magnified alignment tool with sub-pixel adjustment controls lets users place the center marker precisely on faint sources before recording.
  • Quick Trials: Bundled SPHEREx image sets for Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis open without waiting for a new IRSA image request. The WISE 0855 marker shows a predicted position; its identification in individual SPHEREx exposures has not been verified.
  • Shareable fields: URLs preserve coordinates, field size and detector selection for bookmarking and embedding.

Intended Impact:
By empowering both researchers and the public, Skybrew fosters collaborative innovation, accelerates the pace of scientific discovery in the era of big data, and democratizes space science. 

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software: 

  • Client & Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, CDS Aladin Lite v3 Engine. 
  • Serverless Backend & API: TypeScript Vercel Functions (/api/search, /api/frame, /api/catalog/stars, /api/catalog/solar) Custom TypeScript FITS reader verified against independent Python extractions.

projectDetails.name: Apogeu
projectDetails.summary: We developed a free, browser-based 2D strategy game set in the Cold War space race (1955–1969). Each player runs a space agency (USA or USSR side) racing to complete a ladder of historical missions. A dice-driven circular board provides resources, buildings, shops, espionage and chance events — but the heart of the game is the engineering workshop: players design their spacecraft by choosing a launch vehicle, orbit, instruments and parts, each with explicit trade-offs in cost, mass, power, data and risk, then decide the central dilemma — launch now, cheap and risky, or wait and let rivals pull ahead. Launches are simulated stage by stage, and every failure comes with a clear explanation of why it happened, plus a "In real history" card connecting it to actual events. This addresses the challenge directly: players define mission goals, design under constraints, simulate, and learn from feedback. It matters because it makes real mission-design reasoning — budgets, trade-offs, risk — accessible and fun for beginners and youth, solo or with up to four players, with no installation required.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / how it works: A browser-based 2D board game where 1–4 players each run a space agency (US/USSR) during the 1955–1969 space race. Gameplay alternates between a shared circular board (dice movement, buildings, shops, espionage, chance events, rival bots) and an engineering workshop where players design spacecraft — picking launch vehicles, orbits, instruments, and parts, each with explicit cost/mass/power/data/risk trade-offs. Each turn, players choose to research, build, upgrade, or attempt launch. Launches run through a staged simulation (src/sim/simulate.js, flight.js) that computes success/failure with transparent causes, tied to a historical "In real history" card. Years advance in 3-round cycles (1955→1969), building a ladder of missions players race to complete first.

Benefits: No installs, no cost, runs entirely in-browser; supports solo (sandbox) or hot-seat/networked multiplayer up to 4; teaches real mission-design reasoning (budget, mass, power, data, risk) through consequence rather than lecture; failure is explained, not just penalized, turning mistakes into learning moments.

Intended impact: Make space mission engineering trade-offs approachable and engaging for beginners/youth, per the challenge's goal of broadening access to mission design concepts, while also teaching real space race history.

Tools/languages: Plain JavaScript (ES modules), no build step/framework, node --test for testing; custom peer-to-peer networking (src/net/peer.js, lobby.js, sync.js, roomCode.js) for multiplayer; HTML/CSS for UI/rendering (src/ui/*, src/board/board.js).

Creativity: Combines a Monopoly-style board (resource/social layer) with a serious engineering/simulation layer underneath; frames the core tension as "launch now (cheap, risky) vs. wait (safer, rivals advance)"; adds narrative texture via espionage, rumors, dilemma cards, and historical callouts tying game outcomes to real Cold War space history.

Factors considered: Every mechanic was checked against whether it affects the core launch-now-vs-wait decision (cut if it's just flavor); balance was tuned to avoid snowballing (rising upgrade costs, discounts for players who fall behind); the team was explicit about not fabricating real rocket/instrument/mission data — approximated balance values are flagged as such in code/docs.

projectDetails.summary: Earth Jukebox makes NASA Earth science audible. It turns seven NASA Earth Information Center visualization sequences—near-surface temperature, wind, precipitation, specific humidity, PM2.5, ozone, and carbon monoxide—into browser-generated sound. Listeners can navigate with a keyboard and screen reader, choose the whole planet, a continent, or a country without relying on a mouse, move through frames, hear frame readings, and combine variables. An optional spoken guide for controls and a metronome support the listening experience. A jukebox-inspired interface gives each variable a distinct, repeatable sound mapping. The project offers blind and low-vision audiences another way to explore changing Earth patterns, while remaining open to everyone. The sounds follow documented rules applied to image-derived values; wind and PM2.5 use qualitative visual-signal indexes.
projectDetails.details:
Earth Jukebox turns seven NASA Earth Information Center visualization tracks into sound. The browser player decodes image colors using each visualization’s color scale, then maps image-derived values to musical notes, timbre, brightness, or rhythm using fixed rules. Tone.js synthesizes the sound live as the frames play.

Designed for keyboard navigation and screen readers, the experience lets listeners choose the whole planet, a continent, or a country without using a mouse. They can play or pause, move between frames, hear a frame’s readings, and combine variables in a separate mode. An optional spoken guide announces focused controls, and an optional metronome marks time intervals.

The jukebox concept turns Earth science into a collection of tracks to explore. It offers blind and low-vision audiences another way to engage with changing planetary patterns, while also inviting sighted visitors to listen.

The interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules. The offline image-processing and evaluation pipeline uses Python, NumPy, Pillow, Requests, scikit-image, SciPy, imageio-ffmpeg, and Matplotlib. Natural Earth country boundaries support geographic selections.

The team considered how to keep the sound mappings consistent across places and time, make the controls usable without a mouse, and avoid implying more scientific certainty than the image-derived values support. Wind and PM2.5 use qualitative visual-signal indexes; their sounds do not represent direct measurements of wind speed or pollutant concentration. AI tools assisted with selected coding, data analysis, research, and documentation tasks; the team chose the project concept and sound mappings.

projectDetails.name: "TREM" DE FERRO: Minas Gerais Banded Iron Formations as Geochemical Analogs for Martian ISRU
projectDetails.summary: We developed an interactive web platform and in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) simulator, positioning the Banded Iron Formations (BIFs) of Brazil's Iron Quadrangle (Minas Gerais) as functional geochemical analogs for hematite-rich Martian regolith at Meridiani Planum and Gale Crater. Our solution moves beyond surface visual resemblances to terrestrial deserts by targeting mineral extraction. Based on the fundamental reduction reaction (2Fe₂O₃ → 4Fe + 3O₂), we model two mature metallurgical pathways Hydrogen Direct Reduction (H₂-DRI) and Molten Oxide Electrolysis (MOE) to co-produce breathable life-support oxygen, rocket propellant, and structural metallic iron for additive habitat manufacturing. This work addresses a primary constraint of deep space missions: return propellant (LOX) represents the single largest mass penalty from Earth (~25 metric tons for a four-person crew under NASA DRA 5.0). Testing these processing routes using Minas Gerais ores enables early calibration of specific energy consumption, chemical yields, and equipment reliability in terrestrial pilot facilities before launching payloads to Mars.
projectDetails.details:
"TREM" DE FERRO is an open-access web platform and ISRU simulator establishing a functional and geochemical bridge between terrestrial Banded Iron Formations (itabirites and hematites from Minas Gerais, Brazil) and Martian iron-oxide deposits identified by NASA rovers. Rather than seeking morphological desert analogs, we target chemical and mineral parity: extracting oxygen and metallic iron from ferric oxide (2Fe₂O₃ → 4Fe + 3O₂). The platform models two core industrial pathways: Hydrogen Direct Reduction (DRI-H₂), which thermochemically reduces ore into sponge iron and water vapor before recovering H₂ through water electrolysis, and Molten Oxide Electrolysis (MOE), which electrochemically cracks molten iron oxide at ~1,600 °C directly into pure liquid iron and gaseous oxygen without requiring water.

The primary benefit is substantially derisking surface operations and reducing launch mass. According to NASA’s Mars Design Reference Architecture 5.0 (DRA 5.0), return descent/ascent vehicles require approximately 25 metric tons of liquid oxygen (LOX). While NASA’s MOXIE experiment proved that atmospheric oxygen generation works, it produced 122 grams total throughout its mission. Sustained surface habitats require regolith mineral processing. By benchmarking processing routes in Minas Gerais pilot facilities, researchers can validate specific energy consumption (kWh/kg O₂), powder fluidization, and reduction kinetics on Earth prior to flight hardware fabrication.

The interactive platform was developed using React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and custom numerical models for stoichiometric and thermodynamic balances. Planetary datasets were retrieved from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) Geosciences and Atmospheres nodes, integrating APXS/CheMin spectrometry from Curiosity, PIXL data from Perseverance, Mössbauer hematite spectra from Opportunity, and MOXIE operational telemetry. Terrestrial geological grades and mineralogical baselines were sourced from CPRM/Geological Survey of Brazil (SGB) database surveys.

Our key conceptual shift was discarding passive landscape analogies in favor of active geochemical and metallurgical testing. Brazil possesses one of the world's most advanced mining and direct-reduction industrial ecosystems; mobilizing this infrastructure as an accessible proving ground for space exploration turns a major terrestrial industry into an operational asset for Mars.

The team established an explicit boundary for the analogy: what can be directly validated on Earth (dry magnetic pre-concentration efficiency, reduction kinetics, and thermodynamic efficiency) versus what strictly requires environmental simulation chambers (0.38 g Martian gravity, a 6 hPa CO₂ atmosphere, and reactive perchlorate salts in the regolith).

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Uai-Fi: Brazil's Hidden Moon and Mars Analogs
projectDetails.summary: Uai-Fi maps Brazilian places that can stand in for the Moon and Mars. Classic analogs are always the same few sites (Atacama, Antarctica, Iceland), while Brazil, with craters, iron-rich soils, caves, dunes and a large semi-arid region, has never been scanned systematically. We built a Moon/Mars reference table (temperature, regolith, relief, sunlight, rain, water, wind, radiation, fire), scored 14 under-studied Brazilian sites on 8 dimensions into a 0-100 similarity to Mars and to the Moon, and matched each site to the part of a base it can train: farming, habitats, geology, astrobiology, mobility or resources. We also scanned Brazil on a 2,729-point grid with NASA AppEEARS (MODIS LST, NDVI, burned area, SRTM). First results (558 points, northern and northeastern Brazil) point to the semi-arid Northeast as the strongest new analog region, next to two of our researched sites. For every site we state where the analogy breaks.
projectDetails.details: WHAT IT DOES: Finds and characterizes Brazilian terrestrial analogs for Moon and Mars bases. Instead of asking whether a site matches the Moon or Mars in everything (none does), we ask which dimensions it matches and which mission it can train. HOW IT WORKS: (1) Reference table of 16 Moon/Mars conditions with Earth values and sources (NASA fact sheets, LRO Diviner, Phoenix lander chemistry, TES hematite). (2) 14 under-studied Brazilian sites (Araguainha and Serra da Cangalha impact craters, Carajas iron caves, Iron Quadrangle hematite, Peruacu and Toca da Boa Vista caves, Cabaceiras semi-arid, Lencois Maranhenses and Sao Francisco dunes, Nhecolandia soda lakes, Lagoa Salgada stromatolites, Pocos de Caldas caldera, Uberlandia basalt soils, Embrapa Cerrados) scored 0-3 on soil, relief, aridity, subsurface, water chemistry, life, wind and temperature, weighted into 0-100 Mars and Moon scores plus mission profiles. Top results: Peruacu Caves (Moon 53), Toca da Boa Vista (Moon 49), Carajas (Mars 42), Araguainha crater (Moon 42), Iron Quadrangle (Mars 38). (3) A nationwide 2,729-point grid (0.5 deg) sent to NASA AppEEARS; from MODIS NDVI, day/night land surface temperature and burned area we built a satellite analog index (bare ground + large day-night swing + no fire). The 558 points returned so far rank the semi-arid Northeast highest (day surface 36-38 C, NDVI 0.31-0.41 vs 0.73 median), next to Cabaceiras and Toca da Boa Vista, confirming the research ranking. (4) A Plan B pipeline with NASA POWER climatology and SRTM relief. IMPACT: Gives mission planners new, accessible, low-cost analogs in Brazil and an honest list of where each analogy breaks (no vacuum, extreme cold, low gravity or ice). TOOLS: Python (pandas, matplotlib), NASA AppEEARS API, NASA POWER API, OpenTopoData SRTM, Leaflet map. FUTURE: finish the national scan, add SGB geology maps, validate top sites in the field.

projectDetails.name: MarsWalk
projectDetails.summary:
MarsWalk is an interactive 3D planetary exploration and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) planning platform engineered to assist future Mars astronauts and mission planners. Future human crews on Mars will operate under a 4 to 24-minute communication delay with Earth, strict suit oxygen and battery budgets, and extreme surface hazards. MarsWalk addresses these critical constraints by integrating NASA Mars Trek orbital cartography and regional elevation data into an intuitive web interface. 

Crews can analyze high-resolution 3D terrain, identify crucial in-situ resources (water ice, clay minerals, silica deposits), evaluate terrain slope and radiation risks, and preview traverses in an interactive first-person EVA simulation. The system features Ares, an intelligent, zero-persistence on-suit voice and text copilot operating in English and Brazilian Portuguese. MarsWalk bridges high-level mission planning and real-time surface safety, empowering autonomous decision-making when instant Earth support is impossible.
projectDetails.details:
What it does & How it works

MarsWalk is a comprehensive Martian EVA planner and surface exploration system designed for both strategic mission planning and operational astronaut assistance. The application is structured in three interconnected layers:

1. Planetary 3D Cartography: A global, interactive Mars globe rendered with NASA Mars Trek WMTS orbital tiles, showcasing scientifically validated landing sites (Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons, Utopia Planitia, Meridiani Planum). It includes neighboring planets and starfields for celestial navigation orientation.

2. Regional Resource & Hazard Heatmaps: High-resolution local topographic overlays that map critical resources (water-ice deposits, clay minerals, volcanic basalt, silica) alongside terrain slope, dust traps, and radiation exposure zones.

3. First-Person Walk Simulation & Life Support Dynamics: A 3D Martian surface environment running at 0.38g gravity, featuring procedural regolith textures, real-time suit telemetry (O2 consumption, battery discharge, distance traveled), emergency base resupply hubs, and headlamp illumination.

4. Ares Support Companion: A zero-persistence mission assistant accessible via text and real-time bidirectional voice (supporting English and Portuguese), providing contextual EVA guidance without logging sensitive mission logs.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Human exploration of Mars cannot rely on real-time Earth intervention due to the 4 to 24-minute speed-of-light communication latency. MarsWalk directly addresses cognitive overload and mission autonomy by giving surface astronauts immediate, local situational awareness. By correlating terrain roughness with life-support burn rates, MarsWalk ensures crews select safe, scientifically valuable traverse routes, minimizing life-threatening suit exhaustion incidents.

Tools, Languages & Frameworks

- Frontend & Core Architecture: React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Start (full-stack edge routing), Vite 7, and Tailwind CSS.

- 3D Graphics & Simulation: Three.js and React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber, @react-three/drei) with custom GLSL shaders and procedural heightmaps.

- Voice & AI Infrastructure: Lovable AI Gateway with streaming WebSockets and WebRTC for low-latency, bilingual audio dialogue.

- Data Integration: NASA Mars Trek REST/WMTS tile services and USGS/PDS MOLA elevation models.

- Desktop Packaging: Electron sandbox runner for offline field deployment.

Creativity & Factors Considered

The project uniquely unifies orbital remote sensing data with an immersive tactical simulation. We accounted for real-world environmental extremes: low atmospheric density, 38% Earth gravity, thermal day/night swings, communication blackouts, fine electrostatic dust, and the psychological necessity of clear, unencumbered HUD interfaces.

projectDetails.name: CrewVitals
projectDetails.summary: CrewVitals is a web app that lets an astronaut on a long mission check their own health in about a minute a day. The crew member logs six indicators: blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood. The app compares each reading with a clinical reference range, shows a green, yellow or red status with plain-language guidance, tracks trends across mission days, and says when a result should go to the Crew Medical Officer or the flight surgeon on the ground. A clickable body map explains how spaceflight affects each body system, with every statement linked to its NASA source. A radiation panel compares dose rates measured by real instruments in six environments, from the International Space Station to the surface of Mars, and a banner reports recent solar events, all from NASA databases. On missions far from Earth, communication with the ground is delayed and crews carry much of the responsibility for noticing changes in their own health. CrewVitals is built for that situation.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

  • Daily check-in. One short form for six indicators, with a note beside each field on how to take the measurement. A status badge updates as the crew member types.
  • Dashboard. The mission day, an overall status, and one card per indicator with the reading, its position against the reference range, and what to do next.
  • Guidance and escalation. Green means keep the routine. Yellow gives self-care steps and asks for a new reading the next day. Red gives the next step for that indicator and says when to inform the Crew Medical Officer. A red trend goes to the Crew Medical Officer and the flight surgeon on the ground. A small set of critical values triggers an urgent message.
  • Trends. One chart per indicator across mission days, with the reference band shaded and out-of-range days marked. Four trend rules look at three consecutive days, for example sleep under six hours three nights in a row, and raise an alert that a single reading would not.
  • Body map. A figure with six regions. Selecting a region shows its latest readings, how spaceflight affects that body system, the related hazards of human spaceflight, related open-science studies, and the reason for tracking it.
  • Radiation across six environments. The radiation panel shows absorbed dose measured on the same day, 1 December 2022, by instruments on the ISS, in lunar orbit, inside the Orion capsule during Artemis I, in deep space, in Mars orbit and on the surface of Mars. The crew member can select each one to see its dose rate through the day. The panel states that the instruments differ in design, shielding and location, so the values are what each instrument measured and not comparable crew doses.
  • Space weather. A banner reports solar flares and solar energetic particle events from the last seven days.
  • Mission setting. The crew member chooses ISS, Lunar surface or Mars transit. On Mars transit, every instruction that sends the crew to the ground adds a reminder that communication is delayed and the onboard procedure comes first. The panel also says plainly where no measured data exists for the chosen setting.
  • Two languages. The app opens in English and can be switched to Brazilian Portuguese with one selector. Links to NASA pages are marked as English-language pages when the app is in Portuguese.
  • Demo mission. One button loads 30 days of simulated crew data, clearly labelled as simulated, so the trends and alerts can be seen at once.

How it works

CrewVitals is a single-page web app that runs in the browser. Health entries are stored only on the device, in the browser's local storage, and nothing the crew member types is sent to a server. Status rules and reference ranges live in one file, so a flight surgeon could review or replace them in one place. Three small server functions fetch NASA data and fall back to a saved copy when a source is unavailable. The app always shows whether NASA data is live or a saved snapshot, and always labels simulated crew data.

What we were careful about

  • The alert thresholds are adult clinical reference ranges used on Earth, and the app says so on every card. We did not invent spaceflight-specific thresholds. They were reviewed by the team's biomedical engineer.
  • NASA statements are paraphrased and shown with a link to the NASA page they come from. A team member checked each paraphrase against its NASA source. The team's own reasoning is shown separately and labelled as ours.
  • No environment is presented as another. There is no measured lunar-surface or Mars-transit radiation data in the source database, and the app says so instead of substituting a different environment.
  • Status is never shown by colour alone. Each status has an icon and a text label. An automated accessibility check reports no violations on any screen.
  • The app is a hackathon prototype and not a medical device, and it says so on every page.

Benefits and goals

On a Mars mission a message to the ground can take up to 20 minutes to arrive, and the answer as long to come back. A crew member needs a tool that helps them notice a change early, tells them what they can do themselves, and makes clear when to involve the crew's medical officer. Our goal was a tool simple enough to use every day and honest about what it knows. Next steps would be readings taken directly from onboard medical devices, thresholds set by flight surgeons, and a personal radiation dose record fed by the crew member's own dosimeter.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, React Router, Lucide icons, Vitest. Hosted on Cloudflare Pages with Pages Functions. Source code: https://github.com/pedronogueira21/crewvitals

How we used NASA and partner data

  • NASA Human Research Program, "5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight": the frame for the whole app. Each indicator and body region is linked to the hazards that affect it.
  • NASA, "The Human Body in Space": source of the paraphrased statements in the body map.
  • NASA RadLab (Open Science Data Repository): absorbed dose rates for one common day, 1 December 2022, from six instruments: ISS (DosTel1), lunar orbit (LRO, CRaTER), inside Orion on Artemis I (HERA), deep space (BioSentinel, BPD), Mars orbit (TGO, Liulin-MO) and Mars surface (Curiosity, MSL-RAD).
  • NASA CCMC DONKI: recent solar flares and solar energetic particle events for the space-weather banner.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository search: related open-science studies for each indicator, shown with organism and study type because many are animal or ground studies.
  • ESA: the Mars-orbit measurements come from the Liulin-MO dosimeter on the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, a joint ESA–Roscosmos mission. We accessed them through NASA's RadLab database.
  • The alert ranges are adapted from ACC/AHA blood pressure categories and American Diabetes Association glucose criteria.

Use of AI

The application code was written with Claude Code (Anthropic) and reviewed and tested by the team. Claude also helped plan the project and drafted the interface text, the paraphrases of NASA pages (each checked by a team member against its source), the Portuguese translation and the demo slides. Gemini (Google) was used as an aid in the clinical review, which the team's biomedical engineer approved. The body map figure and the app icon are simple schematics drawn in code with AI assistance, identified as such in the app. The demo mission is simulated data and is labelled as simulated. No NASA logos or mission identifiers are used.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: Project UBTeam
projectDetails.summary:
NASA's MODIS sensors have tracked active fires for over two decades, but they are being retired, and their successor, VIIRS, sees fire differently: with smaller pixels, it detects almost four times more hotspots over the same area. Without a bridge, the fire history stops being comparable with today.

We built the Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar. A Python pipeline places 34 million NASA FIRMS hotspots for 14 South American countries (MODIS 2002–2020, VIIRS NOAA-20 2018–2025) on a common daily grid. Using the years when both sensors flew together, it works out what a VIIRS hotspot is worth in MODIS terms for each region and month. Tested on years it had never seen, the converted total was off by just 0.1%, and it tracked monthly country totals with R² = 0.99.

A web app turns the result into a 24-year calendar: pick a country or draw any area, compare any year with the 2002–2020 baseline, spot anomalies, and download the data. With it, emergency teams like CONAE's keep a consistent fire baseline after MODIS goes dark.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

The Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar turns two incompatible NASA fire records into one. MODIS (Terra and Aqua) observed active fires from 2002 to 2020. VIIRS (NOAA-20, 375 m) observes them from 2018 on, but detects almost four times more hotspots over the same area. Our system converts VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent hotspots and delivers a single, consistent series for South America from 2002 to 2025, explored through a web app.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Common grid: a Python pipeline reads 34 million hotspots from NASA FIRMS archives for 14 South American countries and counts them per 0.1° cell (about 11 km) per day, together with fire radiative power, day/night flag and confidence.

2. Conversion factor: in the overlap period (April 2018 to December 2020), we compute how many MODIS hotspots one VIIRS hotspot corresponds to, for each 2° region and each month of the year. Where data are sparse, the factor is pulled toward the continental value (0.26 MODIS hotspots per VIIRS hotspot), so quiet places do not get noisy factors.

3. Testing: we compared nine variants of this conversion, plus nonlinear models, by fitting on two overlap years and testing on the third, repeated for each year. The selected model tracked monthly country totals with R² = 0.99 and cell-by-month values with R² = 0.80, and the converted total was off by only 0.1%.

4. Harmonized series: MODIS is kept as observed through 2020, and VIIRS is converted from 2021 on. Every converted value carries an uncertainty taken from those tests.

5. Web app: a FastAPI service answers most queries in under 0.1 s, and a React app shows a years-by-months calendar (activity, or anomaly versus the 2002-2020 average), a map of where it burned, a day-by-day calendar, the seasonal cycle, annual totals with uncertainty bars, and CSV downloads. Users pick a country or draw any area on the map.

BENEFITS

- One baseline from 2002 to today, so a season can be called normal or abnormal regardless of which satellite saw it. Example: 2024 appears as the 3rd most active fire year in South America since 2002, 36% above the 2002-2020 average.

- Fires do not follow borders: any area can be analyzed, not only countries.

- Trust through transparency: for 2018-2020 the app shows converted VIIRS next to observed MODIS, so users can check the validation themselves.

- Raw MODIS and VIIRS counts are kept in every export.

INTENDED IMPACT

Keep burning activity calendars alive for emergency teams such as CONAE's after MODIS is switched off, and give fire managers and researchers a consistent record to follow trends and anomalies as fire weather becomes more frequent and intense. The pipeline is generic: changing the country list runs it for any region of the world.

CREATIVE ASPECTS

- We treat the two satellites like two currencies. The "exchange rate" between them changes with place and season, so we estimate it per region and month instead of using one global number.

- We convert VIIRS into MODIS units, not the reverse: the 19-year history is MODIS, and detections MODIS never made cannot be invented.

- We let the data decide. The intuitive idea of merging 375 m VIIRS pixels into 1 km clusters to imitate MODIS did not improve results, and nonlinear models performed worse. We report both findings.

- Validation and uncertainty are part of the product, not hidden in a report.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project Ares
projectDetails.summary:
Project Ares is a pixel-art game, in Portuguese and English, where children aged 7 to 12 command a mission to Mars: a 180-day journey and 10 sols at the base. Each turn, players split limited energy (8 points, only 4 during a dust storm) among air and water, greenhouse, radiation shield and radio, which sends science to Earth (goal: 30). Decision cards offer two options, and both have a cost; the active option leads to a 15-second minigame. Crew members Lia, Davi and Yara have their own bonuses, and the robot Orbi guides the tutorial. The ending is punishment-free: a 1-to-3-star debriefing and a certificate with the player’s name.

The game answers the challenge of teaching real space engineering decisions to young learners: energy is limited and every system competes for the same resources. It uses real NASA data: radiation measured by the Curiosity rover and 1,036 solar flares from 2024 in the DONKI archive. The storm warning only arrives with the radio on, forcing a choice between science and safety. The data is archived and shown with its date and source. The game rules are separate from the interface and covered by automated tests.

It matters because children learn through consequences: they discover why radiation is the biggest obstacle on the way to Mars and how engineers decide under uncertainty. It is free, bilingual, accessible (keyboard, screen reader, optional minigames) and runs in any browser, reaching schools and families at no cost.
projectDetails.details:
Project Ares is an interactive, bilingual educational browser game that simulates the challenges of a human mission to Mars. Designed for children aged 7 to 12, it combines pixel-art visuals, storytelling, resource management, and interactive minigames to make space science more engaging and accessible.

How It Works

Players take command of a three-member astronaut crew: Lia, the commander; Davi, the engineer; and Yara, the botanist. Each character has a unique bonus, while Orbi, a companion robot, guides players through the tutorial and provides contextual hints throughout the experience.

The gameplay is divided into two phases: a 180-day journey to Mars, represented by six turns, followed by ten Martian sols at the base. During each turn, players manage a limited energy supply generated by solar panels, allocating resources among four essential systems: air and water, greenhouse food production, radiation protection, and radio communications. Players must balance crew survival with scientific research, aiming to transmit 30 science points back to Earth.

Random events introduce additional challenges through decision cards with two possible outcomes. Each active decision leads to a short minigame that can improve or worsen its result. The experience concludes with a non-punitive performance assessment, encouraging players to learn from their decisions and try again.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Project Ares promotes scientific literacy, critical thinking, strategic planning, and resource management. Rather than presenting space science through passive explanations, it allows children to understand scientific concepts through consequences and experimentation.

The game incorporates authentic NASA information, including radiation measurements collected by the Curiosity rover, solar flare records from NASA's DONKI database, and references to real technologies and missions such as the ISS water recycling system, Perseverance's MOXIE experiment, and the Opportunity rover.

This approach helps children understand the real difficulties of space exploration, particularly radiation exposure, environmental hazards, energy limitations, and the importance of scientific communication. The intended impact is to encourage curiosity about science, technology, engineering, and space exploration from an early age.

Technologies and Development Tools

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5: Page structure and game interface.
  • CSS3: Visual design, pixel-art presentation, animations, and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript: Gameplay mechanics, resource management, event systems, character bonuses, and minigames.
  • Python: Data collection and processing scripts for NASA datasets.
  • Node.js Test Runner: Approximately 25 automated tests covering the core game logic.
  • Vercel: Deployment and hosting, providing public access to the game.
  • NASA Open Data: Scientific datasets and mission information used to support gameplay accuracy.
  • Git and GitHub: Version control, source code management, and collaborative development.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/germanoafb/Base_Mars

The architecture separates the game rules from the user interface, making the system easier to maintain, test, and expand. The game runs directly in the browser without requiring installation.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Project Ares lies in transforming complex scientific information into meaningful gameplay mechanics. Radiation exposure, solar storms, energy scarcity, and scientific communication are not merely background details; they directly influence player decisions and mission outcomes.

For example, maintaining radio communications allows players to receive early warnings about solar storms, creating a strategic trade-off between scientific progress and crew safety. Similarly, radiation protection requires careful resource allocation, demonstrating why shielding is essential for long-duration space missions.

The combination of pixel-art aesthetics, character-driven storytelling, interactive minigames, and real scientific data creates an educational experience that connects entertainment with authentic scientific challenges.

Factors Considered During Development

The team considered several important factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: NASA data is presented with its original dates and sources, without being misrepresented as real-time information.
  • Age-appropriate design: Mechanics, language, and visual elements are designed for children aged 7–12.
  • Accessibility: Keyboard navigation, screen-reader compatibility, reduced-motion support, and the ability to skip minigames.
  • Educational value: Every major gameplay mechanic reinforces a scientific concept or encourages strategic thinking.
  • Fairness and engagement: The non-punitive ending encourages experimentation and learning rather than discouraging players for making mistakes.
  • Accessibility of technology: Free hosting, browser compatibility, and bilingual support make the experience available to schools and families without additional costs.

Ultimately, Project Ares aims to demonstrate that scientific education can be interactive, inclusive, and entertaining while remaining grounded in real-world research. It invites children to experience the challenges of Mars exploration and inspires them to think like scientists, engineers, and explorers.

challengeDetails.title: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
challengeDetails.excerpt: Space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies the engineering trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Few tools make those trade-offs both tangible and fun. Your challenge is to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing competing demands like life support, radiation shielding, power, and food production, so they experience firsthand the decisions that determine whether a mission fails or succeeds.

projectDetails.name: Project XBigDevs
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Route Planner (MRP) is a web app for planning a Marswalk (EVA) in Jezero crater. The astronaut marks a start point and science stops on a map built from several NASA missions (MRO HiRISE and CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA). The app computes a safe route over the real relief, avoiding slopes of 25° and more, and estimates the time and oxygen with a walking model scaled to Mars gravity. The EVA can be replayed in 2D or 3D.

The challenge asks for an integrated, layered view of one Martian site that answers three questions. MRP shows where to go and at what cost, comparing the return to the habitat and to the start. It shows current conditions from the latest Perseverance MEDA data. It also highlights which science targets are worth visiting and which mission revealed each one.

On Mars, a bad route can mean running out of oxygen. MRP gives a GO / NO-GO verdict with a 10% O₂ reserve and marks the point of no return. Every layer cites its mission and date, and every estimate is labeled as one, so planners can trust what they see.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Route Planner (MRP) is a web app for planning a Marswalk in Jezero crater. The astronaut marks a start point and science stops on a map built from NASA mission data (MRO HiRISE and CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA). An A* algorithm then finds a safe route over the real terrain, avoiding slopes of 25° and more. A walking model scaled to Mars gravity estimates the time and oxygen of each plan. With the 0.73 kg of oxygen of NASA’s lunar suit design and a 10% reserve, the app gives a GO / NO-GO verdict for returning to the habitat or to the start. It also marks the point of no return and can reorder the stops to save oxygen. The EVA can be replayed in 2D or 3D, and a Conditions screen shows the latest Perseverance MEDA weather data.

Its main benefit is making the most critical limit visible before going outside: will the oxygen last? Every layer cites its mission and date, and every estimate is labeled as one, so planners know what is measured and what is modeled.

We built it with TypeScript, React, Leaflet and CesiumJS, and processed the NASA data with Python. It is a static site on Cloudflare, so it runs on any browser, including phones. Its creative core is turning a route into a survival decision, while staying transparent about every assumption.

This project is an MVP, ready to expand by processing more data. The Python pipeline turns NASA rasters into light files with a fixed format, and the routing engine works on any grid in that format. Adding new landing sites, finer terrain, more map layers or a longer MEDA weather history means running the pipeline on new data, not rewriting the app.

challengeDetails.title: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map
challengeDetails.excerpt: NASA has explored Mars robotically for decades, studying its extreme environment, mapping its surface, and collecting many types of data. Far from home, the first astronauts to set foot on Mars will want the best map possible, with information on the details of their routes and destinations, updates on current conditions, and the data needed to complete their mission quickly and safely. Your challenge is to create a layered, integrated view of a location or route on the Martian surface that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions and could help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk while conducting new and exciting science along the way.
